A decision tree classifier can handle missing attribute values in a number of ways, both in the training and the test sets. When there are missing values in the test set, the classifier must decide which branch to follow if the value of a splitting node attribute is missing for a given test instance. One approach, known as the probabilistic split method, which is employed by the C4.5 decision tree classifier, distributes the data instance to every child of the splitting node according to the probability that the missing attribute has a particular value. In contrast, the CART algorithm uses the surrogate split method, where the instance whose splitting attribute value is missing is assigned to one of the child nodes based on the value of another non-missing surrogate attribute whose splits most resemble the partitions made by the missing attribute. Another approach, known as the separate class method is used by the CHAID algorithm, where the missing value is treated as a separate categorical value distinct from other values of the splitting attribute. Figure 3.18 shows an example of the three different ways for handling missing values in a decision tree classifier. Other strategies for dealing with missing values are based on data preprocessing, where the instance with missing value is either imputed with the mode (for categorical attribute) or mean (for continuous attribute) value or discarded before the classifier is trained.

Handling Irrelevant Attributes: An attribute is irrelevant if it is not useful for the classification task. Since irrelevant attributes are poorly associated with the target class labels, they will provide little or no gain in purity and thus will be passed over by other more relevant features. Hence, the presence of a small number of irrelevant attributes will not impact the decision tree construction process. However, not all attributes that provide little to no gain are irrelevant (see Figure 3.19 ). Hence, if the classification problem is complex (e.g., involving interactions among attributes) and there are a large number of irrelevant attributes, then some of these attributes may be accidentally chosen during the tree-growing process, since they may provide a better gain than a relevant attribute just by random chance. Feature selection techniques can help to improve the accuracy of decision trees by eliminating the irrelevant attributes during preprocessing.

Every numerical or binary attribute is typically represented using a single node on this layer, while a categorical attribute is either represented using a different node for each categorical value, or by encoding the k -ary attribute using input nodes. Every hidden node operates on signals received from the input nodes or hidden nodes at the preceding layer, and produces an activation value that is transmitted to the next layer. The final layer is called the output layer and processes the activation values from its preceding layer to produce predictions of output variables. For binary classification, the output layer contains a single node representing the binary class label. In this architecture, since the signals are propagated only in the forward direction from the input layer to the output layer, they are also called feedforward neural networks .

A cluster is fundamentally defined as a set of objects in which each object is closer (or more similar) to every other object in the cluster than to any object not in the cluster. This idealistic definition is satisfied only when the data contains natural clusters that are quite far from each other, and well-separated clusters do not need to be globular but can have any shape. Sometimes a threshold is used to specify that all the objects in a cluster must be sufficiently close (or similar) to one another. 

More generally, a cluster can be defined as a set of objects that share some property. For example, objects in a center-based cluster share the property that they are all closest to the same centroid or medoid. In this prototype-based approach, a cluster is a set of objects in which each object is closer (more similar) to the prototype that defines the cluster than to the prototype of any other cluster. For data with continuous attributes, the prototype is often a centroid, i.e., the average (mean) of all the points in the cluster. When a centroid is not meaningful, such as when the data has categorical attributes, the prototype is often a medoid, i.e., the most representative point of a cluster. Such clusters tend to be globular.

If the data is represented as a graph, where the nodes are objects and the links represent connections among objects, a cluster can be defined as a connected component; i.e., a group of objects that are connected to one another, but that have no connection to objects outside the group. An important example of graph-based clusters is a contiguity-based cluster, where two objects are connected only if they are within a specified distance of each other. This definition is useful when clusters are irregular or intertwined, but it can have trouble when noise is present since a small bridge of points can merge two distinct clusters.

A density-based definition of a cluster describes it as a dense region of objects that is surrounded by a region of low density. This definition is often employed when the clusters are irregular or intertwined, and when noise and outliers are present. By contrast, a contiguity-based definition would not work well for such data because the noise would tend to form bridges between clusters.

In many applications, the notion of a cluster is not well defined, and the best definition depends on the nature of data and the desired results. The process of finding clusters that require a very specific concept of a cluster to be successfully detected is called conceptual clustering. However, too sophisticated a notion of a cluster would take us into the area of pattern recognition, and thus, simpler types of clusters are typically considered in standard data mining contexts.

expert_reference: Intra-cluster distance, also referred to as intra-cluster dissimilarity, measures the internal cohesion of a cluster by quantifying the distances between objects and the cluster's centroid. In K-means clustering, this metric is calculated as the summation of distances between the objects and the centroid of the cluster to which they are assigned. The centroid represents the mean value of the objects within that cluster. The primary objective of clustering is to divide a data set into groups based on object similarity while minimizing this intra-cluster dissimilarity. In the context of K-means Clustering Imputation (KMI), the distance between a centroid and an object is denoted as d(vk, xi), where vk is the centroid of cluster k and xi is the object. The KMI procedure involves randomly selecting K complete data objects as centroids, iteratively modifying the partition to reduce the sum of distances for each object from its cluster centroid, and finally filling in non-reference attributes for incomplete objects using a nearest neighbor algorithm. The process terminates when the summation of distances falls below a user-specified threshold or when no changes occur to the centroids in the last iteration. In hierarchical clustering, intra-cluster distances are explicitly excluded from inter-cluster distance calculations; for example, distances between points within the same cluster are not used to determine the height at which two distinct clusters are merged in a dendrogram. Clustering generally requires a meaningful distance or similarity measure to function effectively.

expert_reference: The distinction between classification and clustering is defined by the source of the labels used to group objects. Classification involves assigning particular objects to pre-existing groups, a process that relies on a model developed from objects with known class labels to assign labels to new, unlabeled objects. In contrast, clustering involves dividing objects into groups based on shared common characteristics, where the labels are derived solely from the data itself. Because clustering creates a labeling of objects with class (cluster) labels without using pre-existing known labels, it is sometimes referred to as unsupervised classification. While both processes result in objects being grouped, clustering is the study of techniques for automatically finding these classes, whereas classification is the assignment of objects to those classes. This distinction is a core concept in understanding how data mining techniques divide data objects into groups.

expert_reference: A core point is a data point located in the interior of a density-based cluster. Formally, a point is a core point if there are at least MinPts points within a distance of Eps, where MinPts and Eps are user-specified parameters. The count of points in the neighborhood includes the point itself. In density-based clustering algorithms like DBSCAN and SNN density-based clustering, core points are defined as points that strongly belong to one cluster. A core point can directly reach a border point, but a border point cannot directly reach back as a core-expanding point. In the DBSCAN algorithm, any two core points that are close enough—within a distance Eps of one another—are put in the same cluster. The use of core points adds considerable power and flexibility to density-based clustering approaches.

expert_reference: A border point is a data point that is not a core point because it does not have enough points in its neighborhood to satisfy the core point condition, but it falls within the neighborhood of at least one core point. In the context of density-based clustering, a border point is located on the edge of a dense region. While a core point starts and expands dense regions, a border point can be attached to a dense region but does not expand it. This limitation exists because direct density-reachability requires the starting point to be a core point; consequently, a core point can directly reach a border point, but a border point cannot directly reach back as a core-expanding point. In cluster construction, border points attach to the core component formed by mutually connected core points. If a border point is close to core points from different clusters, a border tie occurs, requiring a convention to resolve the assignment, such as assigning the point to the first cluster that reaches it or the closest core point. A border point is distinct from a noise point, which is neither a core point nor a border point and is not assigned to any cluster.

In the context of density-based clustering, a noise point is defined as any point that is neither a core point nor a border point. This classification arises from a center-based approach to density, which categorizes data points into three distinct types: those in the interior of a dense region (core points), those on the edge of a dense region (border points), and those in sparsely occupied regions (noise or background points). A noise point is specifically characterized by its location in a sparsely occupied region, meaning it does not meet the density requirements to be a core point and is not within the neighborhood of a core point to qualify as a border point.

In the DBSCAN algorithm, noise points are handled by being discarded or omitted from the clustering process. This mechanism allows the algorithm to automatically classify low-density points as noise and remove them, thereby eliminating their negative effects on the clustering results. This is particularly important because atypical points or outliers can severely degrade the performance of clustering algorithms, especially prototype-based methods like K-means, or cause techniques like single link to join clusters that should not be joined. By identifying and discarding noise points, DBSCAN maintains the integrity of the discovered clusters.

The classification of a point as noise is sensitive to the algorithm's parameters. If the distance threshold (epsilon) is set too small, most neighborhoods become too small, causing many points to be classified as noise. Conversely, if the minimum points parameter (minPts) is set too large, real small clusters may disappear and be classified as noise. Thus, a noise point is a point that fails to satisfy the density connectivity conditions required to be part of a cluster under the given parameter settings.

expert_reference: DBSCAN requires two user-specified parameters, Eps and MinPts, to define its clustering behavior. Eps represents the maximum distance threshold for neighborhood calculations, while MinPts is the minimum number of points required within that Eps radius for a point to be classified as a core point. The point itself is included in the count of points within the Eps-neighborhood. For example, if MinPts is set to 3, a point must have itself and at least two other points within the Eps distance to be considered core. These parameters are global, meaning a single Eps and MinPts value are applied to the entire dataset. The selection of these parameters is critical because they determine the density threshold used to distinguish clusters from noise. A common method for determining Eps involves computing the k-dist (the distance to the k-th nearest neighbor) for all points, sorting these values, and identifying a sharp increase in the plot, which indicates a suitable Eps value. The value of k used in this process typically corresponds to the MinPts parameter. DBSCAN's reliance on a single global density threshold can be a limitation when cluster densities vary widely, as it may fail to separate clusters of different densities or merge them incorrectly depending on the chosen Eps.

To determine suitable values for these parameters, a basic approach involves analyzing the k-dist, which is the distance from a point to its k-th nearest neighbor. The procedure is as follows:
1. Compute the k-dist for all data points for a chosen value of k.
2. Sort these k-dist values in increasing order.
3. Plot the sorted values.
4. Identify the value at which there is a sharp change or increase in the plot; this value corresponds to a suitable Eps.
5. Set the value of k used in the process as the MinPts parameter.

Under this selection method, points with a k-dist less than Eps are labeled as core points, while others are labeled as noise or border points.

DBSCAN may fail or have trouble when the density of clusters varies widely because it uses one global density threshold. In such cases, an Eps threshold that allows the algorithm to find lower-density clusters as distinct may cause higher-density clusters and their surrounding noise to merge into a single cluster. Conversely, an Eps threshold that separates higher-density clusters may cause lower-density clusters to be marked as noise.

Selection of DBSCAN Parameters

There is, of course, the issue of how to determine the parameters Eps and MinPts . The basic approach is to look at the behavior of the distance from a point to its nearest neighbor, which we will call the k -dist. For points that belong to some cluster, the value of k -dist will be small if k is not larger than the cluster size. Note that there will be some variation, depending on the density of the cluster and the random distribution of points, but on average, the range of variation will not be huge if the cluster densities are not radically different. However, for points that are not in a cluster, such as noise points, the k -dist will be relatively large. Therefore, if we compute the k -dist for all the data points for some k , sort them in increasing order, and then plot the sorted values, we expect to see a sharp change at the value of k -dist that corresponds to a suitable value of Eps . If we select this distance as the Eps parameter and take the value of k as the MinPts parameter, then points for which k -dist is less than Eps will be labeled as core points, while other points will be labeled as noise or border points.

DBSCAN can have trouble with density if the density of clusters varies widely. Consider Figure 7.24 , which shows four clusters embedded in noise. The density of the clusters and noise regions is indicated by their darkness. The noise around the pair of denser clusters, A and B , has the same density as clusters C and D . For a fixed MinPts , if the Eps threshold is chosen so that DBSCAN finds C and D as distinct clusters, with the points surrounding them as noise, then A and B and the points surrounding them will become a single cluster. If the Eps threshold is set so that DBSCAN finds A and B as separate clusters, and the points surrounding them are marked as noise, then C , D , and the points surrounding them will also be marked as noise.

expert_reference: Directly density-reachable is a directional relationship between two points in density-based clustering. A point q is directly density-reachable from a point p if and only if two conditions are met: q must be in the ε-neighborhood of p (denoted as q ∈ Nε(p)), and p must be a core point. This relationship is asymmetric; specifically, a core point can directly reach a border point, but a border point cannot directly reach back as a core-expanding point. Consequently, while a border point can be assigned to a cluster, it does not expand the cluster because the definition requires the starting point of the reachability relation to be core. This concept serves as the foundational step for defining density-reachability, where a point q is density-reachable from p if there exists a chain of points from p to q such that each subsequent point in the chain is directly density-reachable from the previous one.

expert_reference: Density-reachability is a relationship defined between two points, p and q, within the framework of density-based clustering. A point q is considered density-reachable from p if there exists a chain of points starting at p and ending at q, denoted as p = p1, p2, ..., pn = q, such that each subsequent point in the chain is directly density-reachable from the preceding point. This concept relies on the definition of direct density-reachability, where a point q is directly density-reachable from p if q is contained in the epsilon-neighborhood of p (q ∈ Nε(p)) and p is a core point. Density-reachability is distinct from density-connectedness, which holds when there exists some point o such that both p and q are density-reachable from o. The framework assumes that the entire dataset can be evaluated using a single density standard. This approach contrasts with centroid-based methods like K-means, which may identify dense compact blobs but optimize for centroid compactness rather than density reachability.

expert_reference: Density-connected is a relationship between two points in a density-based clustering context. Two points, p and q, are density-connected if there exists some point o such that both p and q are density-reachable from o. This definition relies on the concept of density-reachability, where a point q is density-reachable from p if there is a chain of points from p to q such that each subsequent point in the chain is directly density-reachable from the previous one. The relationship is symmetric: if p and q are density-connected, they belong to the same cluster. This concept is central to DBSCAN, which identifies clusters as dense regions of objects surrounded by low-density regions. Unlike centroid-based methods that may cut through curved dense shapes, DBSCAN can follow dense connected regions when parameters are suitable. Density-connectedness allows DBSCAN to label points as noise instead of forcing them into a cluster, which is an advantage over K-means when density connectivity is the appropriate cluster model.

In Section 7.4 , we considered DBSCAN, a simple, but effective algorithm for finding density-based clusters, i.e., dense regions of objects that are surrounded by low-density regions. This section examines additional densitybased clustering techniques that address issues of efficiency, finding clusters in subspaces, and more accurately modeling density. First, we consider gridbased clustering, which breaks the data space into grid cells and then forms clusters from cells that are sufficiently dense. Such an approach can be efficient and effective, at least for low-dimensional data. For a data space with n dimensions, potentially subspaces2n−1 need to be searched, and thus an efficient technique is needed to do this. CLIQUE is a grid-based clustering algorithm that provides an efficient approach to subspace clustering based on the observation that dense areas in a high-dimensional space imply the existence of dense areas in lowerdimensional space. Finally, we describe DENCLUE, a clustering technique that uses kernel density functions to model density as the sum of the influences of individual data objects. While DENCLUE is not fundamentally a grid-based technique, it does employ a grid-based approach to improve efficiency.

expert_reference: DBSCAN is a density-based clustering algorithm that locates regions of high density separated by regions of low density. Unlike K-means, which uses a prototype-based or centroid-based notion of a cluster, DBSCAN defines clusters based on a single density threshold. This approach allows DBSCAN to handle clusters of arbitrary shapes and sizes and makes it relatively resistant to noise. DBSCAN produces a partitional clustering where the number of clusters is automatically determined by the algorithm, rather than being specified as a parameter. A key characteristic of this definition is that points in low-density regions are classified as noise and omitted; consequently, DBSCAN does not produce a complete clustering of all objects. The algorithm operates by connecting core points that are within a distance Eps of one another into the same cluster, attaching border points that are close enough to a core point to that core point's cluster, and discarding noise points. Because it relies on a global density threshold, DBSCAN may struggle with data where cluster characteristics vary widely, and it can be computationally expensive for high-dimensional data where density is difficult to define.

As a partitional clustering algorithm, DBSCAN assigns each object to a single cluster, but it does not produce a complete clustering because points in low-density regions are classified as noise and omitted. The number of clusters is automatically determined by the algorithm based on a single density threshold, rather than being specified as a parameter in advance.

The algorithm forms clusters through the following procedure:
1. Connect core points that are within a distance Eps of one another into the same cluster.
2. Attach border points to the same cluster as any core point they are close enough to (ties are resolved if a border point is close to core points from different clusters).
3. Discard noise points.

DBSCAN is particularly effective when the natural clusters in the data are noisy, non-spherical, and density-separated, or when the number of clusters is unknown. However, it can be computationally expensive when calculating nearest neighbors requires all pairwise proximities, and it struggles with high-dimensional data where density is more difficult to define.

Because DBSCAN uses a density-based definition of a cluster, it is relatively resistant to noise and can handle clusters of arbitrary shapes and sizes. It also has trouble with high-dimensional data because density is more difficult to define for such data. Another problem is that most clustering techniques have a global (static) model of clusters. For instance, K-means assumes that the clusters will be globular, while DBSCAN defines clusters based on a single density threshold. Clustering schemes that use such a global model cannot handle cases in which cluster characteristics, such as size, shape, and density, vary widely between clusters. As an example of the importance of the local (dynamic) modeling of clusters, consider Figure 8.18 . If we use the closeness of clusters to determine which pair of clusters should be merged, as would be the case if we used, for example, the single link clustering algorithm, then we would merge clusters (a) and (b). However, we have not taken into account the characteristics of each individual cluster. Specifically, we have ignored the density of the individual clusters. For clusters (a) and (b), which are relatively dense, the distance between the two clusters is significantly larger than the distance between a point and its nearest neighbors within the same cluster.

Both DBSCAN and K-means are partitional clustering algorithms that assign each object to a single cluster, but K-means typically clusters all the objects, while DBSCAN discards objects that it classifies as noise.
K-means uses a prototype-based notion of a cluster; DBSCAN uses a density-based concept.

Given the previous definitions of core points, border points, and noise points, the DBSCAN algorithm can be informally described as follows. Any two core points that are close enough—within a distance Eps of one another—are put in the same cluster. Likewise, any border point that is close enough to a core point is put in the same cluster as the core point. (Ties need to be resolved if a border point is close to core points from different clusters.) Noise points are discarded. This algorithm uses the same concepts and finds the same clusters as the original DBSCAN, but is optimized for simplicity, not efficiency.

expert_reference: Internal indices are unsupervised measures of cluster validity that evaluate the goodness of a clustering structure without respect to external information. These measures are termed internal indices because they rely exclusively on information present in the data set itself. Unsupervised measures of cluster validity are often further divided into two classes: measures of cluster cohesion, which determine how closely related the objects in a cluster are, and measures of cluster separation, which determine how distinct or well-separated a cluster is from other clusters. Within the broader classification of cluster validity indices, internal indices represent the category that assesses clustering quality based solely on internal data characteristics rather than external reference labels.

SSE (Sum of Squared Errors) is an unsupervised, internal cluster evaluation measure that quantifies the goodness of a clustering structure without relying on external information. It functions as a centroid-quality measure, assessing how tightly data points sit around their assigned centroids; a smaller SSE indicates that points are closer to their centroids. In the context of K-means clustering, SSE serves as the objective function to be minimized, and for a fixed number of clusters (K), a lower SSE represents a better clustering solution.

The formal definition of SSE is the sum of the squared distances between each point and its assigned cluster centroid. This is expressed as SSE = ∑(i=1 to K) ∑(x ∈ Ci) (ci - x)², where K is the number of clusters, Ci is the set of points in cluster i, ci is the centroid of cluster i, and x is a data point. An equivalent formulation using a distance function is SSE = ∑(i=1 to K) ∑(x ∈ Ci) dist(ci, x)². The total SSE of a clustering is the sum of the SSE contributed by each individual cluster.

SSE is sensitive to the number of clusters used. Increasing the number of clusters (K) almost always reduces the SSE. In the extreme case where K equals the total number of points (n), every point becomes its own cluster, resulting in an SSE of 0, which is generally considered a useless clustering. Because of this property, SSE can be used to determine the number of clusters by observing where the measure stops decreasing significantly as K increases.

While K-means typically converges to a local minimum of SSE, various postprocessing techniques can be used to "fix up" the resulting clusters to achieve a lower SSE without increasing K. These techniques include alternating phases of splitting and merging clusters. Splitting strategies often involve dividing the cluster with the largest SSE or the largest standard deviation for a specific attribute, and introducing a new centroid (often the point farthest from any existing center). Merging strategies combine clusters to reduce the total number while attempting to minimize the overall SSE. Additionally, per-cluster SSE is useful as a diagnostic tool to identify which specific clusters are loose or spread out.

Cohesion is an internal measure of cluster validity that quantifies how closely related the objects within a single cluster are, often described as the compactness or tightness of the group. It is used to evaluate the goodness of a clustering structure without relying on external labels, using only information present in the dataset. Cohesion is distinct from separation, which measures how distinct or well-separated a cluster is from other clusters.

For prototype-based clusters, cohesion is defined as the sum of the proximity between each object in the cluster and the cluster's prototype (centroid). The formula is cohesion(C_i) = ∑_{x∈C_i} proximity(x, c_i), where C_i is the cluster, c_i is the prototype or centroid of the cluster, and proximity is a function that can represent either similarity or dissimilarity. When proximity is defined as squared Euclidean distance, this measure is equivalent to the cluster Sum of Squared Errors (SSE). For graph-based clusters, cohesion is defined as the sum of the pairwise proximities between all objects in the cluster, expressed as cohesion(C_i) = ∑_{x∈C_i} ∑_{y∈C_i} proximity(x, y).

The interpretation of the cohesion value depends on the type of proximity function used. If the proximity function is a similarity measure, higher values indicate better cohesion. If the proximity function is a dissimilarity measure, lower values indicate better cohesion. In the context of K-means clustering, which is a centroid-based algorithm, centroid-based cohesion is the appropriate measure. For non-Euclidean data, such as document data represented as a document-term matrix, cohesion can be defined using cosine similarity, where the objective is to maximize the similarity of documents to the cluster centroid. The total cohesion across all clusters is the sum of the cohesion of each individual cluster.

Cohesion is often related to separation. For some validity measures, the sum of total SSE (cohesion) and total SSB (separation) is a constant, meaning that minimizing cohesion is equivalent to maximizing separation. Cohesion can also be used to evaluate individual objects within a cluster; objects that contribute more to the overall cohesion are typically near the interior of the cluster, while those contributing less are near the edge. This information can guide clustering improvements, such as splitting a cluster with low cohesion into subclusters or merging clusters that are cohesive but not well separated.

7.5.2 Unsupervised Cluster Evaluation Using Cohesion and Separation

Many internal measures of cluster validity for partitional clustering schemes are based on the notions of cohesion or separation. In this section, we use cluster validity measures for prototype- and graph-based clustering techniques to explore these notions in some detail. In the process, we will also see some interesting relationships between prototype- and graph-based measures.

expert_reference: Separation is an internal cluster validity measure that quantifies how distinct or well-separated a cluster is from other clusters. It is used to evaluate clustering quality by assessing the distance or dissimilarity between clusters, often in conjunction with cohesion measures. For prototype-based clusters, such as those produced by K-Means, separation is defined as the proximity (distance or dissimilarity) between the cluster's prototype (centroid or medoid) and either another cluster's prototype or an overall prototype. Specifically, the separation between two clusters Ci and Cj is given by separation(Ci, Cj) = proximity(ci, cj), where ci and cj are the prototypes of the respective clusters. Alternatively, the separation of a single cluster Ci from the overall dataset is given by separation(Ci) = proximity(ci, c), where c is the overall prototype. In graph-based or object-level definitions, separation is calculated as the sum of pairwise proximities between all objects in one cluster and all objects in another cluster: separation(Ci, Cj) = ∑_{x∈Ci} ∑_{y∈Cj} proximity(x, y). Another formulation, often used in normalized contexts, defines separation(Y) as the average normalized distance from a cluster's centroid to the centroids of all other clusters: separation(Y) = (1 / (|ζ| - 1)) ∑_{Y'∈ζ, Y'≠Y} d_N(center(Y), center(Y')). The choice of proximity function (similarity or dissimilarity) affects interpretation: for similarity, lower separation values indicate better separation; for dissimilarity, higher values indicate better separation. Separation is distinct from cohesion, which measures internal cluster compactness, and from external indices like Rand Index or Purity, which require ground truth labels.

The silhouette coefficient is an internal cluster evaluation measure that does not use class labels. It evaluates whether a point is closer to its own cluster than to the nearest competing cluster by combining both cohesion (compactness) and separation.

For a point x in cluster X, the coefficient is computed using two components. First, a(x) is the average distance from x to the other points in its own cluster, defined as a(x) = (sum of d(x, u) for u in X excluding x) / (|X| - 1). Second, for another cluster Y not equal to X, the average distance from x to the members of Y is defined as bb(x, Y) = (sum of d(x, u) for u in Y) / |Y|. The value b(x) is the smallest average distance to another cluster, defined as b(x) = min over Y in the set of clusters excluding X of bb(x, Y).

The silhouette coefficient for point x is given by the formula: silhouette(x) = (b(x) - a(x)) / max(a(x), b(x)). When a(x) < b(x), the denominator is b(x), and the expression can be written as (b(x) - a(x)) / b(x) = 1 - a(x)/b(x). The value of the silhouette coefficient can vary between -1 and 1. We want the silhouette coefficient to be positive, and for a(x) to be as close to 0 as possible, since the coefficient assumes its maximum value of 1 when a(x) = 0.

The average silhouette coefficient of a cluster is computed by taking the average of the silhouette coefficients of points belonging to the cluster. An overall measure of the goodness of a clustering can be obtained by computing the average silhouette coefficient of all points.

When used with a partitional clustering algorithm such as K-means, the silhouette coefficient tends to decrease until the 'natural' set of clusters is found and start increasing once clusters are being split 'too finely' since separation will suffer and cohesion will not improve much. Thus, these measures can provide a way to determine the number of clusters. However, if the definition of a cluster used by the clustering algorithm differs from that of the cluster evaluation measure, then the set of clusters identified as optimal by the algorithm and validation measure can differ. In addition, if there actually are subclusters that are not separated very well from one another, then methods that incorporate both cohesion and separation may provide only a coarse view of the cluster structure of the data. The silhouette index did well on handling issues such as noise and differing sizes and density, but did not do well on handling arbitrary shapes.

Most unsupervised cluster evaluation measures, such as the silhouette coefficient, incorporate both cohesion (compactness) and separation. When used with a partitional clustering algorithm such as K-means, these measures will tend to decrease until the 'natural' set of clusters is found and start increasing once clusters are being split 'too finely' since separation will suffer and cohesion will not improve much. Thus, these measures can provide a way to determine the number of clusters. Another consideration is that when clustering for summarization, we are not interested in the 'natural' cluster structure of the data, but rather want to achieve a certain level of approximation, e.g., want to reduce SSE to a certain level.

Statistical testing procedures provide a useful way of measuring the significance of a discovered clustering. In particular, we can consider the null hypothesis that there is no cluster structure among the instances and the clustering algorithm is producing a random partitioning of the data. The approach is to use the cluster validity measure as a test statistic. The distribution of that test statistic under the assumption that the data has no clustering structure is the null distribution. We can then test whether the validity measure actually observed for the data is significant. In the following, we consider two general cases: (1) the test statistic is an internal clustering validity index computed for unlabeled data, such as SSE or the silhouette coefficient, or (2) the test statistic is an external index, i.e., the cluster labels are to be compared against class labels, such as entropy or purity.

expert_reference: The Rand Index and Jaccard Coefficient are external validation measures used to evaluate clustering by comparing the discovered cluster structure against an external structure, usually known class labels. They are classified as similarity-oriented measures because they operate by comparing pairs of objects rather than using classification-oriented metrics like purity or F-measure. The key distinction between the two lies in how they handle pairs that are correctly separated in both the class structure and the clustering (denoted as f00). The Rand Index includes these f00 pairs in its calculation, whereas the Jaccard Coefficient ignores f00 and focuses exclusively on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures. In a specific worked example where f00=4, f01=2, f10=2, and f11=2, the Rand statistic is computed as (2+4)/10 = 0.6, and the Jaccard coefficient is computed as 2/(2+2+2) = 0.33. The general methodology for computing these indices involves constructing class similarity and cluster similarity matrices. Additionally, a statistical significance assessment can be performed by generating M randomized sets of labels, computing the external index for each randomization, and defining the p-value as the fraction of randomizations where the index value exceeds the value obtained for the original set of labels.

expert_reference: Recall is an external index used in cluster evaluation to measure the extent to which a cluster contains all objects of a specified class. It is a classification-oriented measure that assesses how well the discovered clustering structure matches an external structure, typically known class labels. The recall of cluster i with respect to class j is defined by the formula recall(i,j) = m_ij / m_j, where m_j represents the number of objects in class j. This metric is one of several external indices, including purity, precision, F-measure, and similarity-oriented measures like the Rand Index and Jaccard Coefficient, used to evaluate clustering performance against ground truth data.

expert_reference: A dendrogram is a tree-like diagram used to graphically display hierarchical clustering. It visualizes both the cluster-subcluster relationships and the order in which clusters were merged (agglomerative view) or split (divisive view). In the diagram, the vertical height at which two clusters are merged reflects the distance between those two clusters. For example, if the distance between two points is 0.11, they are joined at a height of 0.11 in the dendrogram. Hierarchical clustering is sometimes used to generate K clusters by taking the clusters at the K-th level of the dendrogram, where the root is at level 1. This allows for the evaluation of hierarchical clustering behavior and comparison with K-means. If a final flat clustering is desired, the dendrogram must be cut at a specific level. When drawing a dendrogram by hand, the exact horizontal spacing does not matter, but the vertical merge heights and nested structure are critical. The leaf order must match the nested structure exactly, though branches can be flipped left-to-right. The dendrogram is distinct from the linkage criteria (such as single link, complete link, or group average) used to calculate the distances that determine the merge heights.

expert_reference: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering is a bottom-up method that produces a hierarchical clustering by starting with each point as a singleton cluster and repeatedly merging the two closest clusters until a single, all-encompassing cluster remains or a stopping rule is reached. This approach is a collection of closely related techniques where the definition of cluster similarity depends on the particular algorithm used. Some agglomerative algorithms, such as group average, base their notion of similarity on the strength of the connections between the two clusters (e.g., the pairwise similarity of points in the two clusters), while other techniques, such as the single link method, use the closeness of the clusters (e.g., the minimum distance between points in different clusters) to measure cluster similarity. The single-linkage distance is defined as the minimum distance between any point in one cluster and any point in the other: d_single(C_i, C_j) = min_{x∈C_i, y∈C_j} d(x, y). Other merging strategies include the centroid method, which merges the clusters with the closest centroids, and Ward's method, which is a greedy bottom-up clustering using the K-means SSE objective to merge the two clusters that result in the smallest increase in total SSE. Agglomerative clustering is distinct from divisive clustering, which splits clusters downward; in contrast, agglomerative clustering merges clusters upward. A key limitation of agglomerative hierarchical clustering is that it can never separate objects that have been wrongly put together, meaning it will only compound errors if the initial partitioning or merging decisions are incorrect. Additionally, if the data is very large, an agglomerative hierarchical clustering technique cannot be directly applied, often necessitating the use of divisive techniques or other methods like BIRCH that do not require all data to be in main memory.

The specific definition of cluster similarity used to decide which clusters to merge depends on the algorithm. CURE (Clustering Using REpresentatives) is a clustering algorithm that uses a variety of different techniques to create an approach that can handle large data sets, outliers, and clusters with non-spherical shapes and non-uniform sizes. CURE represents a cluster by using multiple representative points from the cluster. These points will, in theory, capture the geometry and shape of the cluster. The first representative point is chosen to be the point farthest from the center of the cluster, while the remaining points are chosen so that they are farthest from all the previously chosen points. In this way, the representative points are naturally relatively well distributed. The number of points chosen is a parameter, but it was found that a value of 10 or more worked well. Once the representative points are chosen, they are shrunk toward the center by a factor, α . This helps moderate the effect of outliers, which are usually farther away from the center and thus, are shrunk more. For example, a representative point that was a distance of 10 units from the center would move by 3 units (for ), while a representative point at a distance of 1 unit would only move 0.3 units. CURE uses an agglomerative hierarchical scheme to perform the actual clustering. The distance between two clusters is the minimum distance between any two representative points (after they are shrunk toward their respective centers). While this scheme is not exactly like any other hierarchical scheme that we have seen, it is equivalent to centroid-based hierarchical clustering if , and roughly the same as single link hierarchical clustering if . Notice that while a hierarchical clustering scheme is used, the goal of CURE is to find a given number of clusters as specified by the user. CURE takes advantage of certain characteristics of the hierarchical clustering process to eliminate outliers at two different points in the clustering process. First, if a cluster is growing slowly, then it may consist of outliers, since by definition, outliers are far from others and will not be merged with other points very often. expert_reference: Divisive hierarchical clustering is a top-down method that begins with all objects in a single cluster and repeatedly splits clusters into smaller clusters until singleton clusters or a stopping rule is reached. This approach is distinguished from agglomerative clustering, which merges clusters upward, by its downward splitting mechanism. Divisive clustering can be useful if the top-level split is meaningful or if a good splitter is available. One specific divisive hierarchical technique is the minimum spanning tree (MST) algorithm, which starts with the minimum spanning tree of the proximity graph and can be viewed as an application of sparsification for finding clusters; this algorithm produces the same clustering as single link agglomerative clustering. Divisive clustering is often considered when data is very large and agglomerative techniques cannot be directly applied, though the MST algorithm only works if the data set is not too large. Bisecting K-means is another divisive technique that works for many data sets, but it runs into problems if the data set is large enough that it cannot be contained completely in memory. In such large-scale situations, a technique such as BIRCH, which does not require that all data be in main memory, becomes more useful. The choice of clustering algorithm is often determined by the need to create a hierarchical clustering that extends only to the point of splitting data into a few hundred clusters rather than a complete hierarchy to individual objects.

expert_reference:
MIN (Single Linkage) is a linkage criterion used in hierarchical clustering to define the proximity between two clusters. The proximity of two clusters is defined as the minimum of the distance (or the maximum of the similarity) between any two points in the two different clusters. Formally, the distance between two clusters Ci and Cj is given by the formula: dsingle(Ci, Cj) = min d(x, y), where the minimum is taken over all pairs x in Ci and y in Cj. In this formula, dsingle(Ci, Cj) represents the single-linkage distance between clusters Ci and Cj, d(x, y) is the distance between individual points x and y, and the minimization is performed over all x in Ci and y in Cj.

The single-linkage technique operates by starting with all points as singleton clusters and adding links between points one at a time, shortest links first, which combines the points into clusters. This method is characterized by the "nearest bridge" intuition, meaning two clusters are considered close if at least one point in one cluster is close to at least one point in the other cluster. In terms of implementation, single linkage can use a precomputed distance matrix; the original point-distance matrix is computed once, and after a merge, the current matrix is updated using the minimum value.

The single-linkage technique is good at handling non-elliptical shapes, but it is sensitive to noise and outliers. It is distinct from complete linkage, which uses the farthest cross-pair, and centroid linkage, which uses the cluster centers.

expert_reference: MAX (Complete Linkage) is a version of hierarchical clustering in which the proximity of two clusters is defined as the maximum of the distance (or the minimum of the similarity) between any two points in the two different clusters. In graph terminology, if one starts with all points as singleton clusters and adds links between points one at a time, shortest links first, a group of points is not considered a cluster until all the points in it are completely linked, meaning they form a clique. This method is less susceptible to noise and outliers, but it can break large clusters and it favors globular shapes. The distance calculation is demonstrated by the formula d_complete({A, B}, C) = max(2, 1) = 2, where the distance between the cluster {A, B} and point C is the maximum of the individual distances. Another example is d_complete({A, B, C, D}, E) = max(4, 3, 2, 1) = 4. The procedure for complete linkage involves computing the original point-distance matrix once, and after a merge, updating the current matrix using the maximum value. Complete linkage says two clusters are close only if even the farthest cross-cluster pair is not too far. This contrasts with single linkage, which uses the nearest bridge, and centroid linkage, which uses the cluster centers.

expert_reference: Group Average Linkage is a graph-based agglomerative clustering technique that defines the proximity between two clusters as the average of the pairwise proximities (or average length of edges) of all pairs of points from different clusters. This approach bases its notion of similarity on the strength of the connections between the two clusters, such as the pairwise similarity of points, rather than relying solely on the closeness of the clusters measured by the minimum distance between points. In a full agglomerative clustering run, the distance between two specified clusters is calculated as one candidate distance, which must be compared with all other current cluster-pair distances before choosing a merge. The weighted version of group average, known as WPGMA, uses coefficients that are constants independent of cluster sizes, specifically alpha_A = 1/2, alpha_B = 1/2, beta = 0, and gamma = 0. General unweighted approaches are preferred unless there is reason to believe that individual points should have different weights. For clustering approaches like group average, outliers are potentially less problematic because they tend to form singleton or small clusters that do not merge with other clusters until much later in the merging process, allowing them to be removed by discarding these small clusters.

Ward's method is a greedy bottom-up hierarchical clustering technique that uses the same objective function as K-means clustering: minimizing the sum of squared errors (SSE). In this approach, each cluster is represented by its centroid, and the proximity between two clusters is defined as the increase in the total SSE that results from merging them. The algorithm proceeds by repeatedly evaluating all possible merges of existing clusters, computing the total SSE after each candidate merge, and selecting the merge that causes the smallest increase in total SSE. This process builds a hierarchy of clusters until all points are merged into a single cluster.

The SSE for a cluster C is defined as the sum of the squared distances of its points from the cluster centroid: SSE(C) = Σ ||x - μ_C||², where x is a point in C and μ_C is the centroid of C. The total SSE across all clusters is the sum of the individual cluster SSEs: SSE_total = SSE(C₁) + SSE(C₂) + ... + SSE(Cₖ).

Ward's method is distinct from centroid linkage, which also uses centroids but defines cluster proximity as the distance between centroids rather than the increase in SSE. Ward's method is mathematically similar to the group average method when the proximity between two points is taken to be the square of the distance between them. However, Ward's method is the correct hierarchical analog of K-means, as it directly optimizes the same SSE objective.

A key limitation of Ward's method is that once a merge is made, it cannot be undone, which prevents a local optimization criterion from becoming a global one. The clusters at each level do not represent local minima with respect to the total SSE, and a point in one cluster can be closer to the centroid of another cluster than to its own. Despite this, Ward's method is often used as a robust method for initializing K-means clustering. Outliers pose the most serious problems for Ward's method because they increase SSE and distort centroids, whereas in methods like single link, complete link, and group average, outliers tend to form singleton clusters that can be discarded.

Agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithms tend to make good local decisions about combining two clusters because they can use information about the pairwise similarity of all points. However, once a decision is made to merge two clusters, it cannot be undone at a later time. This approach prevents a local optimization criterion from becoming a global optimization criterion. For example, although the 'minimize squared error' criterion from Kmeans is used in deciding which clusters to merge in Ward's method, the clusters at each level do not represent local minima with respect to the total SSE. Indeed, the clusters are not even stable, in the sense that a point in one cluster can be closer to the centroid of some other cluster than it is to the centroid of its current cluster. Nonetheless, Ward's method is often used as a robust method of initializing a K-means clustering, indicating that a local 'minimize squared error' objective function does have a connection to a global 'minimize squared error' objective function.

expert_reference: Hierarchical clustering complexity refers to the computational and storage requirements of agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithms, which are defined by their use of a proximity matrix and iterative merging of clusters. The total space complexity is O(m²), where m is the number of data points, because the algorithm must store the proximities between all pairs of points (assuming a symmetric matrix) and track the state of the clusters. The time complexity is O(m² log m) when using a sorted list or heap to optimize the search for the two closest clusters; without such optimization, the time complexity is higher due to linear searches over the proximity matrix. These complexity bounds severely limit the size of data sets that can be processed directly, making the algorithm impractical for large-scale applications. The high computational cost arises because the general clustering problem is computationally infeasible to solve exactly, and the local merging strategy, while avoiding hard combinatorial optimization, still incurs significant overhead. Scalable alternatives, such as bisecting K-means or graph sparsification techniques, are often used to address these limitations by reducing the effective number of points or partitions before applying hierarchical methods.

Supervised evaluation of a hierarchical clustering is more difficult for a variety of reasons, including the fact that a preexisting hierarchical structure often does not exist. In addition, although relatively pure clusters often exist at certain levels in the hierarchical clustering, as the clustering proceeds, the clusters will become impure. The key idea of the approach presented here, which is based on the F -measure, is to evaluate whether a hierarchical clustering contains, for each class, at least one cluster that is relatively pure and includes most of the objects of that class. To evaluate a hierarchical clustering with respect to this goal, we compute, for each class, the F -measure for each cluster in the cluster hierarchy, and then take the maximum F -measure attained for any cluster. Finally, we calculate an overall F -measure for the hierarchical clustering by computing the weighted average of all per-class F -measures, where the weights are based on the class sizes. CURE (Clustering Using REpresentatives) is a clustering algorithm that uses a variety of different techniques to create an approach that can handle large data sets, outliers, and clusters with non-spherical shapes and non-uniform sizes. CURE represents a cluster by using multiple representative points from the cluster. These points will, in theory, capture the geometry and shape of the cluster. The first representative point is chosen to be the point farthest from the center of the cluster, while the remaining points are chosen so that they are farthest from all the previously chosen points. In this way, the representative points are naturally relatively well distributed. The number of points chosen is a parameter, but it was found that a value of 10 or more worked well. Once the representative points are chosen, they are shrunk toward the center by a factor, α . This helps moderate the effect of outliers, which are usually farther away from the center and thus, are shrunk more. For example, a representative point that was a distance of 10 units from the center would move by 3 units (for ), while a representative point at a distance of 1 unit would only move 0.3 units. CURE uses an agglomerative hierarchical scheme to perform the actual clustering. The distance between two clusters is the minimum distance between any two representative points (after they are shrunk toward their respective centers). expert_reference: K-Means is a partitional clustering algorithm that directly divides data into K clusters, where K is a user-specified parameter representing the desired number of clusters. Each cluster is represented by a centroid, which is the representative centre of the cluster. For Euclidean K-Means, the centroid is defined as the mean of all points in the cluster; it is a mean position and does not have to be one of the original data points. expert_reference: The SSE Optimization Criterion is an objective function used in clustering that aims to minimize the total squared error (SSE). When applied to clustering, this criterion frames the task as an optimization problem where the goal is to find a partition of points that minimizes the total SSE. The evidence indicates that finding the global optimum for this criterion is computationally infeasible because it would require enumerating all possible ways of dividing points into clusters. Consequently, practical clustering algorithms, such as agglomerative hierarchical clustering, use local criteria to decide which clusters to merge at each step. This local approach avoids the difficulty of solving the hard combinatorial optimization problem associated with the global SSE minimization. For instance, Ward’s method uses the “minimize squared error” criterion to decide which clusters to merge, although the resulting clusters at each level do not represent local minima with respect to the total SSE. The criterion is also relevant to K-means clustering, where it serves as the objective function. The evidence notes that a local “minimize squared error” objective function has a connection to a global “minimize squared error” objective function, as Ward’s method is often used to initialize K-means clustering. The distinction between global and local minima is illustrated by examples where a clustering solution can be a global minimum of the SSE for a given number of clusters, while another solution is only a local minimum.

expert_reference: Centroid Initialization Sensitivity refers to the susceptibility of K-means clustering algorithms to the specific choice of initial centroids, a factor that can significantly impact the resulting cluster quality and Sum of Squared Errors (SSE). Standard K-means is particularly prone to this issue, whereas variants like bisecting K-means are less susceptible because they perform several trial bisections and select the one with the lowest SSE, maintaining only two centroids at each step. To mitigate this sensitivity, specific initialization procedures are employed. One approach involves selecting the first point at random or as the centroid of all points, then iteratively selecting the point farthest from any already-selected initial centroid to ensure well-separated centroids; this method is often applied to a sample of points to avoid selecting outliers and to reduce computational expense. Another advanced technique, K-means++, picks centroids incrementally where each point has a probability of being selected as a new centroid proportional to the square of its distance to its closest centroid, a method guaranteed to find a solution optimal to within a factor of O log(k). These strategies address the core limitation that random initialization may lead to suboptimal clustering or the selection of outliers, which can reduce the number of centroids available for forming clusters for the majority of points.

expert_reference: Bisecting K-Means is a hierarchical clustering algorithm that extends the basic K-Means method by producing a hierarchy of clusters through a sequence of binary splits. Unlike standard K-Means, which initializes K centroids simultaneously and jointly updates them, Bisecting K-Means starts with a single cluster containing all data points. The algorithm repeatedly selects one existing cluster and splits it into two subclusters using basic K-Means with K = 2. This process continues until the desired number of leaf clusters is reached. A key characteristic of this approach is that it makes local split decisions, meaning it does not jointly optimize all centroids at once; consequently, it can produce different results than standard K-Means with the same target number of clusters. The algorithm is often used to speed up clustering by reducing the number of similarity computations, as it only calculates distances for a subset of points to two centroids at each step rather than all points to all centroids. It is also noted for being less susceptible to initialization problems because it can perform several trial bisections and select the one with the lowest Sum of Squared Errors (SSE). If a flat clustering with lower total SSE is required, the final centroids from Bisecting K-Means can be used as initial centroids for a subsequent standard K-Means refinement step, although Bisecting K-Means itself is a valid standalone algorithm.

expert_reference: A distance function d(x, y) between two points x and y is characterized by three well-known properties: positivity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality. Positivity requires that d(x, y) ≥ 0 for all x and y, and that d(x, y) = 0 only if x = y. Symmetry requires that d(x, y) = d(y, x) for all x and y. The triangle inequality requires that d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all points x, y, and z. These properties are common to all distances, including the Euclidean distance. A dissimilarity measure that fails to satisfy these properties can be modified to become a valid distance function. For example, the measure d(A, B) = size(A - B) between two sets A and B, where size returns the number of elements in a set, is an integer value greater than or equal to 0 but does not satisfy the second part of the positivity property, the symmetry property, or the triangle inequality. This measure can be modified to d(A, B) = size(A - B) + size(B - A) to make these properties hold. In the case of A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {2, 3, 4}, A - B = {1} and B - A = ∅, so the original measure gives d(A, B) = 1, while the modified measure gives d(A, B) = 1. The distance function is assumed to return a distance of 0 only for objects that are the same, which is a condition relevant to algorithms that rely on distance comparisons.

expert_reference: Euclidean distance is a metric distance measure used to quantify the proximity between two points in Euclidean space. It is a specific case of the Lp norm distance family and is the most commonly used proximity measure in the literature for dense, continuous data. The measure is defined by the formula d_E(x, y) = sqrt((x_1 - y_1)^2 + (x_2 - y_2)^2), where x and y are the coordinates of the two points. As a distance function, it satisfies the properties of positivity (d(x, y) ≥ 0), identity of indiscernibles (d(x, y) = 0 only if x = y), symmetry (d(x, y) = d(y, x)), and the triangle inequality (d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z)). In clustering algorithms such as K-means, Euclidean distance is used to determine the closest centroid for each data point and to compute the sum of squared errors (SSE) as an objective function for evaluating cluster quality. It is distinct from similarity measures like cosine similarity, which compares direction or pattern rather than location, and from other distance metrics like Manhattan distance, which measures distance by moving step-by-step along the axes.

expert_reference: Manhattan distance is a distance measure that quantifies the separation between two points by summing the absolute differences of their coordinates, effectively measuring the distance if one moves step by step along the axes, like walking through city blocks. The formal definition is given by the formula d_Manhattan(x, y) = Σ_{i=1}^{m} |x_i - y_i|, where x and y are the points being compared, m is the number of dimensions, and x_i and y_i are the coordinates of the points in the i-th dimension. This measure is distinct from similarity scores, such as cosine similarity, where larger values indicate greater similarity, whereas Manhattan distance is a distance metric. The value of Manhattan distance is always non-negative and finite, satisfying the condition 0 ≤ d_Manhattan(x, y) < ∞. In the context of clustering, when the objective is to minimize the sum of distances, the appropriate centroid for a cluster using Manhattan distance is the median of the points in that cluster. An example calculation for two points A and B is d_Manhattan(A, B) = |1 − 4| + |1 − 5| = 3 + 4 = 7, illustrating the summation of absolute coordinate differences.

expert_reference:
Cosine similarity is a similarity score, distinct from distance measures like Manhattan and Euclidean distance, where a larger value indicates greater similarity. It measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors, x and y. When the cosine similarity is 1, the angle between the vectors is 0 degrees, meaning they point in the same direction and are identical except for length. When the cosine similarity is 0, the angle is 90 degrees, indicating the vectors are perpendicular and do not share any terms. When the cosine similarity is -1, the vectors point in exactly opposite directions.

The calculation involves normalizing the vectors by dividing them by their lengths, which results in vectors of length 1. This normalization means cosine similarity does not take the length of the data objects into account. For unit-length vectors, the cosine measure is calculated by taking a simple inner product. This approach is useful for sparse data, such as documents represented as vectors where components record word frequencies, and can reduce computation time when many similarities are calculated.

In the context of clustering, cosine similarity is used as a proximity measure in K-means style algorithms, where the objective is to maximize the similarity of objects to the cluster centroid. It is also included in the class of Bregman divergences, which can serve as the basis for clustering algorithms with convergence properties similar to standard K-means.

expert_reference: The Rand Index is an external validation measure used to evaluate clustering by comparing the cluster structure against true class labels. It is a similarity-oriented measure that operates by comparing pairs of objects. The index is calculated using the formula: Rand Index = (f11 + f00) / (f11 + f10 + f01 + f00). In this formula, f00 represents the pairs of objects that are correctly separated in both the class structure and the clustering. The Rand Index includes these f00 pairs in its calculation, which distinguishes it from the Jaccard Coefficient, a sibling measure that ignores f00 and focuses only on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures. Consequently, the Rand Index is often higher than the Jaccard Coefficient. The calculation counts only pairs of distinct objects; self-pairs are not included in the Rand Index computation. The Rand Index does not require the original feature values once the cluster assignments and class labels are available. It is computed through class similarity and cluster similarity matrices. An adjusted version of the Rand Index exists and is based on the multivariate hypergeometric distribution, which can be used to compute a p-value.

expert_reference: The Jaccard coefficient is a similarity measure used to evaluate the similarity between two binary vectors, particularly in contexts involving asymmetric binary attributes such as transaction data where a 1 indicates an item was purchased and a 0 indicates it was not. It is frequently employed as a cluster validity measure and is often symbolized by j. The coefficient is defined by the formula Jaccard Coefficient = f11 / (f11 + f10 + f01), where f11, f10, and f01 represent specific frequency counts from a contingency table. A key characteristic of the Jaccard coefficient is that it ignores f00, focusing only on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures. This distinguishes it from other measures like the Rand statistic (or Simple Matching Coefficient), which includes f00 in its calculation. For example, given f00=4, f01=2, f10=2, and f11=2, the Jaccard coefficient is calculated as 2 / (2 + 2 + 2) = 0.33. The measure can be extended to more than two variables using multidimensional contingency tables, and an extended version, known as the Extended Jaccard Coefficient or Tanimoto Coefficient, is used for document data and reduces to the standard Jaccard coefficient for binary attributes.

expert_reference:
A similarity matrix is a square matrix that stores the pairwise similarity between every pair of objects in a data set. The similarity between two objects is a numerical measure of the degree to which they are alike; higher values indicate greater similarity. Similarities are usually nonnegative and are often scaled to the interval [0, 1], where 0 represents no similarity and 1 represents complete similarity. This scaling is frequently achieved through linear transformations that map the original range of similarity or dissimilarity values to [0, 1], preserving the relative distances between points.

In the context of clustering, the similarity matrix is used to evaluate the 'goodness' of a clustering by comparing it against an ideal cluster similarity matrix. The ideal matrix is constructed by assigning a value of 1 to an entry if the corresponding pair of points belongs to the same cluster, and 0 otherwise. When the rows and columns of the matrix are sorted so that objects belonging to the same cluster are grouped together, the ideal cluster similarity matrix exhibits a block diagonal structure, with non-zero values inside the blocks representing intra-cluster similarity and zero values elsewhere. The correlation between the actual similarity matrix and this ideal matrix serves as a measure of cluster validity, a metric known in the clustering validation literature as Hubert's Γ statistic.

The similarity matrix can also be used for visual inspection of clustering results. By ordering the matrix with respect to cluster labels and plotting it, the patterns displayed can reveal the relationships and separation between clusters. For instance, well-separated clusters are illustrated by a reordered similarity matrix where high similarity values are concentrated within cluster blocks. Additionally, in supervised or semi-supervised contexts, the cluster similarity matrix can be compared against a class similarity matrix—defined as 1 if two objects belong to the same class and 0 otherwise—to derive validity measures such as the Rand Index or Jaccard Coefficient. In these pair-by-pair comparisons, diagonal entries (comparing an object to itself) are typically excluded, as only pairs of distinct objects are counted.

A missing value is a data quality issue where an attribute value or an entire data object is absent from a dataset. This can occur because information was not collected or because certain attributes are not applicable to all objects. Missing values are distinct from other data quality issues such as spurious or duplicate objects, and inconsistencies where data is present but logically incorrect. 

Handling missing values is a critical step in data analysis because even partially specified data objects contain information, and ignoring them can make reliable analysis difficult or impossible. The approach to handling missing values depends on the specific machine learning algorithm being used. For example, Naïve Bayes classifiers handle missing values by ignoring them during training and using only non-missing values for testing, though this can be inaccurate if the frequency of missing values depends on the class label. Bayesian networks handle missing values by treating them as unobserved nodes and marginalizing out their effect. In contrast, logistic regression and artificial neural networks (ANN) cannot handle missing values and typically require instances with missing values to be discarded. 

Decision tree classifiers offer several specific methods for handling missing values in test instances: the probabilistic split method (used by C4.5) distributes the instance to every child node based on probability; the surrogate split method (used by CART) assigns the instance to a child node based on a surrogate attribute; and the separate class method (used by CHAID) treats the missing value as a distinct categorical value. 

General strategies for dealing with missing values include deletion and imputation. Deletion involves eliminating objects or attributes with missing values, which is expedient if only a few objects are affected but risky if many are missing or if the attributes are critical. Imputation involves estimating missing values, such as by interpolating in time series, using nearest neighbors, or using the mean (for continuous attributes) or mode (for categorical attributes). There is no universal imputation method that performs best for all classifiers.

Different classifiers handle missing values in varying ways. Naïve Bayes classifiers can handle missing values in the training set by ignoring them when computing conditional probability estimates, and in test instances by using only non-missing attribute values for posterior probabilities. Bayesian networks can handle missing values during both training and testing; for test instances, they perform inference by treating the missing attribute as an unobserved node and marginalizing out its effect on the target class. Decision tree classifiers employ several methods for test sets: the probabilistic split method (used by C4.5) distributes the instance to every child node based on the probability of the missing attribute's value; the surrogate split method (used by CART) assigns the instance to a child node based on a non-missing surrogate attribute that resembles the missing attribute's partitions; and the separate class method (used by CHAID) treats the missing value as a distinct categorical value.

In contrast, some models cannot handle missing values. Logistic regression and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) cannot handle instances with missing values in the training or testing phase. For logistic regression, training instances with missing values can be discarded, but missing values in a test instance will cause the model to fail to predict the class label.

General strategies for dealing with missing values include data preprocessing steps such as discarding instances or attributes with missing values, or using imputation. Imputation involves estimating missing data, such as using interpolation for smooth time series or using the average (for continuous attributes) or mode (for categorical attributes) of nearest neighbors. Additionally, similarity calculations for clustering can be performed using only the attributes that are not missing, though this results in an approximate similarity.

Imputation is the process of replacing missing values (MVs) in a dataset with estimated values. It is distinguished from deletion strategies, which remove cases containing missing data, and from the classification of missingness mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, NMAR), which describe how data is lost rather than how to fill it. The goal of imputation is to obtain values for non-reference attributes (attributes with missing values) for incomplete objects, using the available reference attributes (attributes with known values).

Imputation methods generally fall into two broad categories: statistical methods and machine learning (ML) methods. Statistical methods, such as Maximum Likelihood Imputation and Expectation-Maximization (EM), model the underlying probability distribution of the data. For example, in a simple coin-flipping scenario where the probability of heads is θ, the maximum likelihood estimate is derived as θ̂ = h/n, where h is the number of heads and n is the total number of flips. More formally, the likelihood is based on a binomial distribution. EM algorithms, often used with Gaussian mixture models, iteratively estimate parameters like the mean (μ) and covariance (Σ) to impute missing values via regression.

Machine learning methods, such as K-means Clustering Imputation (KMI) and Fuzzy K-means Imputation, do not require assuming a specific underlying distribution but still rely on the Missing At Random (MAR) assumption. KMI works by clustering data into K groups, where each cluster is represented by a centroid. The algorithm proceeds in three steps: (1) randomly select K complete data objects as initial centroids; (2) iteratively update the partition to minimize the sum of distances between objects and their assigned centroids until a threshold ε is met or centroids stabilize; and (3) impute missing values for incomplete objects using the cluster information, treating objects in the same cluster as nearest neighbors. Fuzzy K-means imputation extends this by allowing objects to belong to multiple clusters with different membership degrees, calculating imputed values as a weighted sum of cluster centroids based on these memberships. Other approaches include Support Vector Machines Imputation (SVMI) and Hot Deck imputation, which is a historical method used by the Census Bureau.

Evaluating imputation methods is challenging. In unsupervised settings, Mean Squared Error (MSE) or Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) are commonly used to compare imputed values against known true values (by artificially introducing missingness). In supervised settings, such as classification, the goal is to improve classifier accuracy, which is harder to measure directly with MSE/RMSE. Metrics like Wilson’s Noise Ratio may be used to assess the impact of imputation on the learning task.
