Data integration is the process of merging data elements from different sources into a single data set. This task is required when there are several or heterogeneous sources of data, as gathering all data elements together is not an easy task. Different attribute names or table schemes from various sources produce uneven examples that need to be consolidated, and attribute values may represent the same concept with different names, creating inconsistencies in the instances obtained.

An essential part of the integration process is to build a data map that establishes how each instance should be arranged in a common structure to present a real-world example. When data is obtained from relational databases, it is usually flattened and gathered together into one single record. Some database frameworks enable the user to provide a map to directly traverse the database through in-database access utilities. While using in-database mining tools has the advantage of not having to extract and create an external file for the data, it is not the best option for its treatment with preprocessing techniques. In this case, extracting the data is usually the best option. Preprocessing takes time, and when the data is kept in the database, preprocessing has to be applied repeatedly. If the data is extracted to an external file, then processing and modeling it can be faster if the data is already preprocessed and completely fits in memory.

If the integration process is not properly performed, redundancies and inconsistencies will soon appear, resulting in a decrease of the accuracy and speed of the subsequent data mining processes. Matching the schema from different sources presents a notorious problem that usually does not come alone: inconsistent and duplicated tuples as well as redundant and correlated attributes are problems that the data set creation process will probably show sooner or later. Automatic approaches used to integrate the data can be found in the literature, from techniques that match and find the schemas of the data to automatic procedures that reconcile different schemas.

After the data is correctly integrated into a data set, it does not mean that the data is free from errors. The integration may result in an inordinate proportion of the data being dirty. Broadly, dirty data include missing data, wrong data and non-standard representation of the same data. If a high proportion of the data is dirty, applying a data mining process will surely result in an unreliable model. Dirty data has varying degrees of impact depending on the data mining algorithm, but it is difficult to quantify such an impact.

An attribute is redundant when it can be derived from another attribute or set of them, or when it is strongly correlated with another attribute in the data. Redundancy is a problem that should be avoided as much as possible because it usually causes an increment in the data set size, meaning that the modeling time of data mining algorithms is incremented as well, and may also induce overfitting in the obtained model. Inconsistencies in dimension or attribute names can cause redundancies as well. When examples come from different sources and have to be merged in a single data set, if some attributes are calculated from the others, the data sets will present a large size but the information contained will not scale accordingly, making detecting and eliminating redundant attributes needed.

Redundancies in attributes can be detected using correlation analysis, which measures how strong the implication of one attribute to the other is. When the data is nominal and the set of values is finite, the chi-squared test is commonly applied. In numeric attributes, the use of the correlation coefficient and the covariance is typical. For two nominal attributes A and B containing c and r distinct values each, a contingency table is created with the joint events (Ai, Bj) in which attribute A takes the value ai and attribute B takes the value bj. The chi-squared value is computed as the sum over i from 1 to c and j from 1 to r of (oij - eij)^2 / eij, where oij is the observed frequency of the joint event (Ai, Bj) and eij is the expected frequency of (Ai, Bj) computed as count(A = ai) × count(B = bj) / m. Here, m is the number of instances in the data set, count(A = ai) is the number of instances with the value ai for attribute A, and count(B = bj) is the number of instances having the value bj for attribute B. The chi-squared test checks the hypothesis that A and B are independent, with (r-1) × (c-1) degrees of freedom. The chi-squared statistic is compared against a chi-squared table using the suitable degrees of freedom or available software. If the significance level of the table is below the established one, or the statistic value computed is above the needed one in the table, the null hypothesis is rejected and A and B are statistically correlated.

For two numerical attributes, the correlation coefficient rA,B is computed as the sum over i from 1 to m of (ai - A_bar)(bi - B_bar) / (m σA σB), which is equivalent to (sum over i from 1 to m of (ai bi) - m A_bar B_bar) / (m σA σB). Here, m is the number of instances, ai and bi are the values of attributes A and B in the instances, A_bar and B_bar are the mean values of A and B respectively, and σA and σB are the standard deviations of A and B. Checking whether numerical attributes are highly correlated is useful to determine if they are redundant.

Different classifiers handle redundant attributes in different ways. Decision trees can handle the presence of redundant attributes because redundant attributes show similar gains in purity if they are selected for splitting, so only one of them will be selected as an attribute test condition. Logistic regression can handle redundant attributes that are duplicates of each other by learning equal weights for every redundant attribute without degrading classification performance, although a large number of irrelevant or redundant attributes in high-dimensional settings can make it susceptible to model overfitting. Linear SVM can handle redundant attributes by learning similar weights for the duplicate attributes, and its ability to regularize its learning makes it more robust to the presence of a large number of irrelevant and redundant attributes than other classifiers. Rule-based classifiers can easily handle the presence of redundant attributes that are highly correlated with one other because once an attribute has been used as a conjunct in a rule antecedent, the remaining redundant attributes would show little to no information gain and would thus be ignored. Bayesian networks can easily handle the presence of correlated or redundant attributes because they do not use the naive Bayes assumption about conditional independence, but instead are able to express richer forms of conditional independence. Artificial neural networks can handle redundant attributes by receiving similar weights for them without degrading the quality of the classifier, although if the number of irrelevant or redundant attributes is large, the learning of the ANN model may suffer from overfitting. The presence of a large number of redundant attributes that are highly correlated with each other can bias proximity measures toward such attributes, resulting in improper estimates of distance and adversely affecting the performance of nearest neighbor classifiers.

ANN can easily handle irrelevant attributes, by using zero weights for attributes that do not help in improving the training loss. Also, redundant attributes receive similar weights and do not degrade the quality of the classifier. However, if the number of irrelevant or redundant attributes is large, the learning of the ANN model may suffer from overfitting, leading to poor generalization performance.

Linear SVM can handle irrelevant attributes by learning zero weights corresponding to such attributes. It can also handle redundant attributes by learning similar weights for the duplicate attributes. Furthermore, the ability of SVM to regularize its learning makes it more robust to the presence of a large number of irrelevant and redundant attributes than other classifiers, even in high-dimensional settings. For this reason, nonlinear SVMs are less impacted by irrelevant and redundant attributes than other highly expressive classifiers that can learn nonlinear decision boundaries such as decision trees.

Rule-based classifiers can easily handle the presence of redundant attributes that are highly correlated with one other. This is because once an attribute has been used as a conjunct in a rule antecedent, the remaining redundant attributes would show little to no FOIL's information gain and would thus be ignored.

This can occur when information is sourced from different systems with varying measurement standards, leading to instances that are actually the same but not identified as such. In the context of duplicate detection, inconsistent values must be resolved when two objects represent a single entity but have differing attribute values. Data cleaning is the first step in data preprocessing, specifically defined as the detection and correction of data inaccuracies. It is a necessary phase that occurs after data has become computer-readable and constitutes a unique source, but before any data mining (DM) technique is applied. The primary goal of data cleaning is to filter or repair dirty data to ensure that the knowledge extracted by DM algorithms is accurate and that the algorithms can effectively handle the data. Without this step, the presence of dirty data can lead to less reliable models or prevent algorithms from functioning properly.

Dirty data typically manifests in two main forms: missing data and wrong (noisy) data. The sources of these errors include data entry errors, data update errors, data transmission errors, and bugs in the data processing system. It is important to distinguish data cleaning from other preprocessing steps; for instance, having a uniform data set without measurable inconsistencies does not automatically mean the data is clean. Furthermore, data cleaning is distinct from data normalization and transformation, which are used to adapt the data set to the specific needs of the DM algorithm (such as handling nominal attributes or subtle transformations) rather than correcting inaccuracies. The impact of dirty data varies by algorithm; for example, decision trees (especially those of higher order), artificial neural networks (ANNs), and distance-based algorithms like KNN are known to be susceptible to noise. Therefore, data cleaning is a foundational technique required to improve the accuracy and efficiency of subsequent data mining processes.

Normalization and transformation are data preprocessing techniques used to adapt a data set to the needs of a subsequent data mining algorithm. A variable transformation is a transformation applied to all the values of a variable, meaning that for each object, the transformation is applied to the value of the variable for that object. For example, if only the magnitude of a variable is important, the values can be transformed by taking the absolute value.

In the literature, 'normalization' usually refers to a particular case of min-max normalization in which the final interval is [0, 1], meaning the new minimum is 0 and the new maximum is 1. The interval [-1, 1] is also typical when normalizing data. An alternative, but equivalent, formulation for min-max normalization is obtained by using a base value (new-min_A) and the desired new range (R) in which the values will be mapped after the transformation. The formula for this transformation is: v' = new-min_A + R * ((v - min_A) / (max_A - min_A)), where max_A and min_A are the original maximum and minimum attribute values respectively.

This type of normalization is very common in data sets being prepared for learning methods based on distances. Rescaling all data to the same range of values avoids attributes with a large max_A - min_A difference dominating over others in distance calculations, which would otherwise mislead the learning process by giving more importance to those attributes. Normalization is also known for speeding up the learning process in artificial neural networks (ANNs), helping weights to converge faster. In some cases, transformation or normalization of the data is needed to obtain a proper similarity measure, such as when time series have trends or periodic patterns that significantly impact similarity.

A specific transformation useful for obtaining a new variable that is very likely to behave like a normally distributed one involves using the rank of the observation and the cumulative normal function. However, this transformation cannot be applied separately to the training and test partitions; it is only recommended when the test and training data is the same.

expert_reference: A confusion matrix is a table that summarizes the performance of a classifier by comparing predicted labels against the true labels of instances in a test set. It is the most basic approach for representing classification performance and provides a concise, detailed representation of how a model predicts correctly or incorrectly. For a binary classification problem, the matrix is organized with rows representing the true class and columns representing the predicted class. It contains four specific counts: True Positives (TP), which are actual positives predicted as positive; False Negatives (FN), which are actual positives predicted as negative; False Positives (FP), which are actual negatives predicted as positive; and True Negatives (TN), which are actual negatives predicted as negative. The confusion matrix is used to evaluate models trained on independent training and test sets to ensure accurate prediction of unseen instances. While the matrix provides the necessary information to determine model performance, it is often difficult to interpret and compare classifiers using the four-dimensional representation of these counts. Consequently, the counts are often summarized into single-value evaluation measures, such as accuracy, to facilitate the comparison of relative performance between different models. The confusion matrix is also applicable in contexts such as clustering, where it provides the most detailed information for evaluating the performance of a specific cluster against a class.

expert_reference: Accuracy is a metric used to evaluate the quality of classification rules and classifiers. In the context of a specific classification rule, accuracy (also referred to as the confidence factor) is defined as the fraction of instances triggered by the rule whose class labels are equal to the predicted class. For binary classification, accuracy is calculated as the sum of true positives and true negatives divided by the total number of predictions (true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives). It can also be expressed generally as the number of correct predictions divided by the number of all predictions. Accuracy is an estimate based on a finite test set and is not guaranteed to be the exact true accuracy of the classifier. A higher raw accuracy alone is not always a significant win; a raw accuracy difference is not automatically a significant win. Accuracy can be misleading because it can hide poor positive-class performance, especially under class imbalance. Larger test sets reduce sampling uncertainty associated with the measured accuracy.

expert_reference: Precision is an evaluation measure for binary classification that quantifies the fraction of correct predictions of the positive class over the total number of positive predictions. It is also referred to as the positive predicted value (PPV). The standard formula for precision is p = TP / (TP + FP), where TP represents true positives and FP represents false positives. A classifier with high precision is likely to have most of its positive predictions correct, making it a useful measure for highly skewed test sets where positive predictions, even though small in numbers, are required to be mostly correct. Precision is sensitive to class skew; when selecting a score threshold for a classifier, if the evaluation measure is precision, the skew of the validation set used for selection must be similar to that of the test set to ensure optimal performance. In the context of statistical testing, precision is closely related to the false discovery rate (FDR), with the relationship precision = 1 - FDR. Precision captures the effect of false positives but not false negatives; a classifier that is very conservative in classifying instances as positive to reduce false positives may end up having high precision but very poor recall. A perfect classifier is characterized by precision = 1 and recall = 1.

expert_reference: Specificity, also known as the true negative rate (TNR), is a classifier evaluation metric defined as the fraction of negative test instances correctly predicted by the classifier. Formally, it is calculated as the number of true negatives (TN) divided by the sum of true negatives and false positives (FP), expressed as Specificity = TN / (TN + FP). This metric specifically checks how many actual negatives were correctly rejected by the model. It is distinct from precision for the negative class because specificity uses actual negatives in the denominator, whereas negative predictive value uses predicted negatives. In a worked example, a classifier with 5 true negatives and 2 false positives yields a specificity of 5/7, or approximately 71.4%. Specificity is used alongside other metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F-measure to provide a comprehensive view of classifier performance, particularly when the correct rejection of negative cases is a priority.

expert_reference: The significance level, denoted by the Greek letter alpha (α), is a fixed constant in hypothesis testing whose value is decided before any tests are performed. It is defined as the probability of incurring a type I error, which is equal to the probability of the critical region under the null hypothesis. In practice, a result is called statistically significant if it has a p-value lower than the pre-specified threshold α. This threshold is equivalent to the boundary of the critical region; rejecting the null hypothesis if the test statistic falls in the critical region is equivalent to rejecting it if the p-value falls below α. While every result has a different p-value, the significance level remains a fixed constant for the testing procedure. Common choices for the level of significance are 0.05 (5%) and 0.01 (1%). In specific applications, such as a one-sided test, the significance level determines the critical value used for decision-making; for example, at a significance level of 0.05, the critical value for a one-sided test is Z = 1.64. The significance level also serves as the target for controlling the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) in multiple testing scenarios, where procedures like Bonferroni adjust the per-test significance level to ensure the overall FWER remains below α.

expert_reference: In the context of model evaluation, one-sided and two-sided tests are statistical procedures used to determine whether an observed result is a significant departure from the null hypothesis. The test statistic, typically a count or real-valued quantity, measures how 'extreme' an observed result is under the null hypothesis. One-sided tests are categorized as right-tailed or left-tailed, while two-sided tests evaluate whether the result is extreme in either direction. The distinction is reflected in the distribution of the significance level (alpha) across the tails of the null distribution: a two-sided test with an alpha of 0.05 allocates 0.025 probability to each tail, whereas a one-sided test allocates the entire 0.05 probability to a single tail. A low p-value indicates smaller probabilities in the tails of the null distribution, providing sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. For example, a one-sided test asking whether model A is better than model B is distinct from a two-tailed test, which asks whether the classifiers are different in either direction and would normally use a threshold of |Z| > 1.96 at alpha = 0.05.

There is a trade-off associated with sample size: larger sample sizes increase the probability that a sample will be representative, but they simultaneously reduce the primary advantages gained from sampling. For example, in a dataset of 8000 two-dimensional points, a sample of 2000 points may preserve most of the data structure, whereas a sample of 500 points may result in much of that structure being missing. expert_reference: An ensemble classifier is a method that constructs a set of base classifiers from training data and performs classification by taking a vote on the predictions made by each base classifier. The base classifiers are often individually imperfect, but their combined decision can be more robust. For classification, a common combination rule is majority voting, where the final prediction is determined by the majority of the individual predictions. An alternate approach is to take a weighted majority vote, where the weight of a base classifier denotes its accuracy or relevance. The ensemble classifier predicts the class label of a test example by taking a majority vote on the predictions made by the base classifiers. If the base classifiers are identical, then all the base classifiers will commit the same mistakes, and the error rate of the ensemble remains the same as the individual classifiers. On the other hand, if the base classifiers are independent—i.e., their errors are uncorrelated—then the ensemble makes a wrong prediction only if more than half of the base classifiers predict incorrectly. In this case, the error rate of the ensemble classifier is lower than that of the individual classifiers. The ensemble classifier performs worse than the base classifiers when the base classifier error rate is larger than 0.5. Two necessary conditions for an ensemble classifier to perform better than a single classifier are: (1) the base classifiers should be independent of each other, and (2) the base classifiers should do better than a classifier that performs random guessing. In practice, it is difficult to ensure total independence among the base classifiers, but improvements in classification accuracies have been observed in ensemble methods in which the base classifiers are somewhat correlated. The ensemble of classifiers can be constructed in many ways, including by manipulating the training set, where multiple training sets are created by resampling the original data according to some sampling distribution and constructing a classifier from each training set. Bagging and boosting are two examples of ensemble methods that manipulate their training sets. The base classifiers for most of these approaches can be generated sequentially (one after another) or in parallel (all at once). Once an ensemble of classifiers has been learned, a test example is classified by combining the predictions made by the base classifiers. The final prediction of the ensemble classifier is obtained by taking a weighted average of the predictions made by each base classifier. The ensemble classifier can also enhance the representation of the target function; even though each base classifier is a decision stump, combining the classifiers can lead to a decision boundary that mimics a decision tree of depth 2. The ensemble classifier is a general method that can be applied to any classifier, and it is used to improve the performance of a single classifier by combining the predictions of multiple base classifiers.

expert_reference: Majority voting is a combination rule used in ensemble classification to derive a single final prediction from the outputs of multiple base classifiers. In this approach, each base classifier predicts a class label for a given instance, and the final prediction is the class that receives the most votes. This method is particularly common in random forests, where the final prediction is obtained by majority voting over the individual decision trees. The ensemble is strongest when the individual trees are reasonably accurate and their errors are not perfectly correlated, as this diversity helps reduce the high variance associated with single decision trees. A weighted majority vote is an alternative approach where the weight of a base classifier denotes its accuracy or relevance, but in standard majority voting, every vote has equal impact. In the context of k-nearest neighbors, majority voting assigns the test instance to the majority class of its nearest neighbors, with ties potentially resolved by random choice. The procedure involves sending a test instance through all base classifiers or trees and combining their predictions using this voting mechanism.

expert_reference: A random forest is an ensemble of decision trees, where each tree is trained using randomness so that the trees are not all identical. The method manipulates both the training instances and the input features to create diversity among the base classifiers. The training data is represented as a set of instances D = {(x1, y1), (x2, y2), ..., (xN, yN)}. The induction process for each tree b = 1, 2, ..., B involves drawing a bootstrap sample Db from the original training set by sampling N instances with replacement. A decision tree is then trained on Db, often grown deeply and without heavy pruning, meaning the trees are unpruned and allowed to grow until every leaf is pure. At every split, the tree considers only a random subset of features and chooses the best split from that subset. The number of attributes to be selected at every node, p, is a hyper-parameter of the random forest classifier. For classification, the final prediction is made by combining the trees using majority voting: ŷ = majority{h1(x), h2(x), ..., hB(x)}, where x is the test instance, hb is the b-th base classifier, and ŷ is the final ensemble prediction. The two main random components are bootstrap sampling of instances and random feature selection at each split. This approach reduces the variance of the trees without negatively impacting their low bias, making random forests robust to overfitting and computationally fast even in high-dimensional settings.

expert_reference: Boosting is an iterative ensemble procedure that adaptively changes the distribution of training examples so that base classifiers increasingly focus on examples that are hard to classify. Unlike bagging, boosting assigns a weight to each training example and may adaptively change the weight at the end of each boosting round. The algorithm begins by assigning equal weights to all examples, then draws a sample according to the sampling distribution to obtain a new training set. A classifier is built from this training set and used to classify all examples in the original data. At the end of each boosting round, the weights of the training examples are updated: examples that are classified incorrectly have their weights increased, while those classified correctly have their weights decreased. As the boosting rounds proceed, examples that are the hardest to classify tend to become even more prevalent in the sampling distribution. The final ensemble is obtained by aggregating the base classifiers obtained from each boosting round. In the AdaBoost implementation, the prediction made by each classifier is weighted rather than using a majority voting scheme, which allows the algorithm to penalize models that have poor accuracy. If any intermediate round produces an error rate higher than 50%, the weights are reverted back to their original uniform values and the resampling procedure is repeated. The training error of the ensemble decreases exponentially, leading to fast convergence, although the technique can be susceptible to overfitting due to its tendency to focus on wrongly classified examples.

expert_reference: The class imbalance problem is a practical issue in classification where the training set has an unbalanced representation of classes, typically with a minority class that is not well-represented. This imbalance poses two challenges for classification: first, many classification methods work well only when the training set has a balanced representation of both classes, and second, a classifier trained over an imbalanced data set shows a bias toward improving its performance over the majority class, which is often not the desired behavior. In the context of binary classification, the minority class is referred to as the positive class, while the majority class is referred to as the negative class. The problem is particularly relevant in model evaluation, where detection rate and false alarm rate are metrics that are not sensitive to skewness in the class distribution. In the presence of class imbalance, the behavior of an algorithm over small false positive rate values (also termed as early retrieval) is often more meaningful for comparison than the performance over all false positive rate values. This is because, in many applications, it is important to assess the true positive rate achieved by a classifier in the first few instances with highest scores, without incurring a large false positive rate. The precision-recall (PR) curve is an alternate approach for measuring the aggregate performance of a classifier, which is especially useful in the presence of class imbalance. The PR curve generally helps to magnify the differences between classifiers in the left portion of the PR curve, providing a deeper insight into the performance of classifiers than the ROC curves, especially in the early retrieval range of operating points.

The class imbalance problem occurs when there is a skewness in the class distribution of a dataset. In binary classification, this is typically framed as a scenario where the minority class is the positive class and the majority class is the negative class.

Class imbalance poses challenges for classification because many methods only work well when the training set has a balanced representation of both classes. While some classifiers, such as k-NN and rule-based classifiers, are more effective at handling imbalance in training data than others, all are impacted if the minority class is not well-represented. Generally, a classifier trained on an imbalanced dataset exhibits a bias toward improving performance on the majority class, which is often not the desired behavior.

Evaluating performance in the presence of class imbalance requires specific considerations. Metrics such as the false alarm rate and detection rate are not sensitive to skewness in class distribution. While the Area Under the ROC curve (AUC) summarizes aggregate performance, it may be less meaningful than analyzing the behavior of an algorithm over small False Positive Rate (FPR) values, a process termed early retrieval. This is because it is often important to assess the True Positive Rate (TPR) achieved in the first few instances with the highest scores without incurring a large FPR.

To address these evaluation challenges, the precision-recall (PR) curve is an alternative approach for measuring aggregate performance that is especially useful for imbalanced data. Analyzing PR curves generally provides deeper insight than ROC curves, particularly in the early retrieval range, as the PR curve helps magnify differences between classifiers in its left portion.

candidate_system_evidence.text: A method for comparing classifier performance using the convex hull of ROC curves was suggested by Provost and Fawcett in [ 286 ]. Bradley [ 208 ] investigated the use of area under the ROC curve (AUC) as a performance metric for machine learning algorithms. expert_reference: Oversampling is a technique used to create a balanced training set by artificially generating new positive examples to address class imbalance. A simple approach involves duplicating every positive instance a specific number of times, where the duplication factor is determined by the ratio of the number of negative training instances to the number of positive training instances. This duplication method is analogous to doubling the weight of positive instances during the training stage, an effect that can alternatively be achieved by assigning higher weights to positive instances than negative instances, a method compatible with classifiers such as logistic regression, artificial neural networks, and support vector machines. However, a limitation of the duplication method is that replicated positive examples have an artificially lower variance compared to their true distribution, which can bias the classifier to the specific distribution of training instances and lead to poor generalizability. To overcome this limitation, the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) generates synthetic positive instances in the neighborhood of existing positive instances. The SMOTE procedure first determines the k-nearest positive neighbors of every positive instance, then generates a synthetic positive instance at some intermediate point along the line segment joining the instance to one of its randomly chosen k-nearest neighbors. This process is repeated until the desired number of positive instances is reached. A limitation of SMOTE is that it can only generate new positive instances within the convex hull of the existing positive class, meaning it does not improve the representation of the positive class outside the boundary of existing positive instances. Despite their complementary strengths and weaknesses, undersampling and oversampling provide useful directions for generating balanced training sets in the presence of class imbalance.

expert_reference: Undersampling is a sampling method used to create balanced training sets in the presence of class imbalance by reducing the frequency of the majority class to match the frequency of the minority class. This approach is one of two primary strategies for ensuring that a learning algorithm is trained over a data set with adequate representation of both the majority and minority classes, the other being oversampling. To overcome the skew among the classes, a random sample of 100 examples is selected from the negative class and used with the 100 positive examples to create a balanced training set. One limitation is that some useful negative examples, particularly those closer to the actual decision boundary, may not be chosen for training, which can result in an inferior classification model. Another limitation is that the smaller sample of negative instances may have a higher variance than the larger original set. Undersampling and oversampling provide complementary directions for generating balanced training sets, each with distinct strengths and weaknesses.

expert_reference: RIPPER is a widely-used rule induction algorithm that implements a direct method for generating classification rules directly from data, distinguishing it from indirect methods that derive rules from decision trees. It is designed to work well with noisy data by using a validation set to prevent model overfitting. The algorithm typically employs a sequential covering scheme to induce rules. After generating a rule, RIPPER eliminates all positive and negative examples covered by that rule. The rule is added to the rule set provided it does not violate specific stopping conditions. One stopping condition is based on the minimum description length principle: if a new rule increases the total description length of the rule set by at least d bits, RIPPER stops adding rules; by default, d is chosen to be 64 bits. Another stopping condition requires that the error rate of the rule on the validation set must not exceed 50%. RIPPER also prunes rules to improve generalization errors based on their performance on the validation set. Pruning is done starting from the last conjunct added to the rule, removing a conjunct if a specific metric improves after pruning. This metric is monotonically related to the rule's accuracy on the validation set and involves the number of positive and negative examples in the validation set covered by the rule. While the original rule covers only positive examples, the pruned rule may cover some negative examples in the training set.

expert_reference: The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is a measure used to summarize the aggregate behavior of a classifier across all operating points. It serves as a performance metric for machine learning algorithms, providing a single value that reflects overall classification quality. In terms of scale, a perfect classifier yields an AUC of 1, while an algorithm that performs random guessing results in an AUC of 0.5. The AUC is also described as the number of correctly ranked positive-negative pairs. A key property of the AUC is that it is insensitive to class skew in the test set, distinguishing it from the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUC-PR), which varies with changing skew. However, the AUC has significant limitations when used to compare classifiers. A higher AUC for one algorithm does not guarantee that it is strictly better than another, as this would require the ROC curve of the first algorithm to dominate the second across all operating points. If the ROC curves of two classifiers intersect, it is difficult to assess their relative quality using the AUC alone. Additionally, the AUC has been considered an incoherent measure of performance because it may use different scales when comparing different classifiers, although coherent interpretations have been proposed in the literature.

expert_reference: The holdout method is a model evaluation technique in which the available dataset is split once into two parts: a training set and a test set. The model is learned over the training set, and the resulting test error rate corresponds exactly to the performance of that specific model learned over that specific training set. expert_reference: Random subsampling is a model evaluation technique that repeats random hold-out splits several times and averages the resulting performance scores. This approach is more stable than a single hold-out split, which suffers from high dependence on one specific division of the data. However, random subsampling does not guarantee that every instance is tested exactly once; some instances may be tested repeatedly while others may not be tested at all. In the broader context of sampling techniques, random subsampling is related to simple random sampling, where there is an equal probability of selecting any particular object. Sampling can be conducted with or without replacement; in sampling with replacement, objects are not removed from the population as they are selected, allowing the same object to be picked more than once. This method is simpler to analyze because the probability of selecting any object remains constant during the sampling process, particularly when samples are relatively small compared to the data set size.

k-Fold cross validation is a model evaluation technique that generalizes the holdout approach by segmenting the labeled data D (of size N) into k equal-sized partitions, or folds. In each of the k runs, one partition is designated as the test set (D.test(i)) while the remaining k-1 partitions are used as the training set (D.train(i)). This process is repeated until every fold has served as the test set exactly once, ensuring that every data instance in D is used for both training and testing across the full procedure. A different model is learned at every run, and the performance of each model on its respective test fold is aggregated to compute the overall test error rate. This aggregated estimate reflects the expected generalization error rate of the model selection approach when applied to a training set of the same size as one of the training folds, rather than the performance of a single specific model learned over a fixed training set.

The choice of k depends on the characteristics of the problem. A small value of k results in smaller training sets for each run, which can lead to a larger estimate of generalization error rate than expected for a model trained on the entire labeled set. Conversely, a high value of k results in larger training sets, reducing the bias in the estimate of generalization error rate. For most practical applications, choosing k between 5 and 10 provides a reasonable approach for estimating generalization error rate, as each fold can utilize 80% to 90% of the labeled data for training. An extreme case occurs when k equals N, known as the leave-one-out approach, where every run uses exactly one data instance for testing and the remainder for training. While this utilizes as much data as possible for training, it can be computationally expensive for large datasets because the procedure must be repeated N times.

Standard k-fold cross validation produces a single estimate of the generalization error rate without providing information about the variance of that estimate. To obtain variance information, one can run cross-validation for every possible partitioning of the data into k partitions, an approach known as complete cross-validation. However, this is usually too expensive for large datasets. A more practical solution is to repeat the cross-validation approach multiple times using different random partitionings of the data into k partitions at each iteration, and use the average test error rate as the estimate. Additionally, standard k-fold cross validation does not guarantee that the fraction of positive and negative instances in every partition is equal to the fraction observed in the overall data. A solution to this issue is stratified cross-validation, which performs stratified sampling of positive and negative instances into the k partitions to preserve class distribution.

2. For each of the k runs, choose one partition as the test set (D.test(i)) and use the remaining k-1 partitions as the training set (D.train(i)).
3. Learn a different model at every run.

The hyper-parameter value providing the lowest overall validation error rate across all folds is then used to learn the final model on the entire training set.

expert_reference: Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) is a special case of k-fold cross-validation where the number of folds k equals the total number of data instances N. In this approach, the cross-validation procedure is repeated N times. In each run, exactly one data instance is held out for testing, and the model is trained on the remaining N − 1 instances. This configuration provides the maximum possible training data per run, which reduces the bias in the estimate of the generalization error rate compared to using a smaller number of folds. However, LOOCV is computationally expensive for large data sets because the model must be trained and evaluated N times. Additionally, because there is only one possible partitioning of the data for the leave-one-out approach, it is not possible to estimate the variance of the generalization error rate. LOOCV is distinct from standard k-fold cross-validation (where k is typically between 5 and 10), stratified cross-validation (which preserves class proportions), and bootstrap sampling (which samples with replacement and tests on out-of-bag instances).

expert_reference: Bootstrap sampling is a statistical resampling technique in which data instances are randomly selected with replacement from an original data set to create a synthetic collection of the same size as the original. Because the sampling is done with replacement, some instances may appear several times in the same training set, while others may be omitted. On average, a bootstrap sample of size N contains approximately 63.2% of the unique instances from the original data, leaving about 36.8% of the instances unselected. These unselected instances are known as out-of-bag instances and can be used as a test set for model evaluation. The procedure is typically repeated multiple times to generate different training and test sets, allowing for the computation of distributions of performance measures such as accuracy, precision, and recall, or to estimate the distribution of the support of a frequent itemset. In the context of ensemble methods like bagging (bootstrap aggregating), bootstrap sampling is used to train multiple classifiers on different subsets of the data, with the final prediction determined by majority voting. expert_reference: Stratified k-fold cross validation is a model evaluation technique that extends standard k-fold cross validation by ensuring that each fold approximately preserves the class distribution of the full dataset. In standard k-fold cross validation, the labeled data is segmented into k equal-sized partitions, or folds. During each run, one partition is used for testing while the remaining partitions are used for training. This process is repeated until every fold has served as the test set once. A key limitation of standard k-fold cross validation is that it does not guarantee that the fraction of positive and negative instances in every partition is equal to the fraction observed in the overall data. Stratified cross validation addresses this by performing a stratified sampling of the positive and negative instances into the k partitions. This ensures that the proportion of class labels in every fold is kept the same as that of the overall data. This approach is particularly useful for classification tasks where class imbalance might otherwise skew the evaluation results. An empirical study by Kohavi suggests that ten-fold stratified cross validation is the best estimation method for performance metrics when compared to random subsampling and other k-fold variants. The method is distinct from leave-one-out cross validation, which is a special case where k equals the total number of instances N, and from bootstrap sampling, which samples with replacement to form training sets and evaluates on out-of-bag instances.

expert_reference: Feature selection chooses a subset of the original features according to an evaluation criterion. Its purpose is to remove irrelevant or redundant features, reduce dimensionality and acquisition or computational cost, and simplify the resulting model while retaining useful information. The source describes feature selection as a search over possible feature subsets, organized around a subset-evaluation measure, a search strategy, a stopping criterion, and validation. Standard approaches include embedded, filter, and wrapper methods. Unlike feature-construction methods, feature selection retains a subset of the original attributes rather than creating new combined attributes.

Feature selection (FS), also known as feature subset selection, is the process of choosing an optimal subset of features from the original set according to a certain criterion. Unlike some dimensionality reduction techniques that create new transformed attributes, feature selection keeps the original features.

Conceptually, this is a search over all possible subsets of features. The process is viewed as consisting of four parts: a measure for evaluating a subset, a search strategy that controls the generation of a new subset of features, a stopping criterion, and a validation procedure. Because the number of subsets involving n attributes is 2^n, a systematic search over all possibilities is often impractical, necessitating trade-offs between computational expense and the ability to find optimal or near-optimal sets.

Feature selection is used to address the obstacle of dimensionality, which can make learning algorithms computationally expensive. Specifically, it is performed to remove redundant and irrelevant features, reduce acquisition and computational costs, improve model quality and efficiency, and reduce model complexity. It is also used to remove noise and visualize data for model selection.

In practice, the choice of criterion depends on the task. For supervised learning, accuracy-based feature selection is used, which requires a target label. For unsupervised tasks like clustering, where target labels are unavailable, accuracy is replaced by internal cluster validity measures such as silhouette, SSE, cohesion, or separation.

expert_reference: An attribute is defined as irrelevant if it is not useful for the classification task. Because irrelevant attributes are poorly associated with the target class labels, they provide little or no gain in purity and are typically passed over by other more relevant features. Consequently, the presence of a small number of irrelevant attributes will not impact the decision tree construction process. However, if the classification problem is complex, such as involving interactions among attributes, and there are a large number of irrelevant attributes, some of these attributes may be accidentally chosen during the tree-growing process because they may provide a better gain than a relevant attribute just by random chance. For example, students' ID numbers are irrelevant to the task of predicting students' grade point averages. Redundant and irrelevant features can reduce classification accuracy and the quality of the clusters that are found. Feature selection techniques can help to improve the accuracy of decision trees by eliminating the irrelevant attributes during preprocessing. In minimum subset techniques, an algorithm returns a minimum feature subset and no difference is made for features in the subset; whatever is relevant within the subset is otherwise irrelevant. In search directions where the feature set shrinks and the subset grows, the subset may store only the irrelevant features.

expert_reference: The curse of dimensionality is the phenomenon that data analysis becomes increasingly difficult as the number of attributes grows. The data space expands rapidly and observations become sparse, which can make distances and density differences less informative and local neighborhoods less meaningful. These effects can degrade methods that depend on proximity or density, including clustering and classification methods. This is a major motivation for dimensionality reduction and feature selection. Kernel methods can avoid explicitly constructing coordinates in a transformed high-dimensional feature space, but that computational device does not eliminate the broader high-dimensional data problem.

The curse of dimensionality is the phenomenon where many types of data analysis become significantly harder as the dimensionality of the data—defined as the number of attributes that objects in a data set possess—increases.

As dimensionality increases, the data space grows very quickly, causing the data to become increasingly sparse in the space it occupies. For example, if each dimension is split into 10 bins, the number of cells grows as 10^d; with a fixed data size, the average occupancy of these cells collapses.

This sparsity has several negative effects on data analysis:
- For clustering, differences in density and distances between points become less meaningful. Distances may become less discriminative, meaning nearest and farthest points can become less clearly separated.
- In density-based clustering like DBSCAN, the density idea becomes unstable because DBSCAN defines density by counting points inside a radius. In high dimensions, neighborhoods may become nearly empty unless the radius (epsilon) is very large, but if epsilon is too large, neighborhoods may stop being locally meaningful.
- Many clustering and classification algorithms struggle with high-dimensional data, which can lead to poor quality clusters and reduced classification accuracy.

Because of these difficulties, dimensionality reduction is an important motivation in data preprocessing. Dimensionality reduction can eliminate irrelevant features, reduce noise, allow for easier data visualization, and lead to more understandable models with fewer attributes. Additionally, certain techniques like kernel functions in SVMs allow for the representation of nonlinear decision boundaries without suffering from the curse of dimensionality by working with inner products in a transformed space.

expert_reference: The Filter Approach is one of three standard approaches to feature selection, alongside embedded and wrapper methods. It operates independently of the data mining method subsequently employed, a property that distinguishes it from wrapper approaches which are typically coupled to a specific learner. The name 'filter' derives from the process of filtering undesirable features out before the learning phase begins. Within a common feature selection architecture, filter methods share components such as a measure for evaluating a subset, a search strategy, a stopping criterion, and a validation procedure; however, they differ from wrapper methods specifically in the way they evaluate a subset of features. Because the filter approach is independent of the downstream model, filter methods are usually faster than their wrapper counterparts. While the literature also recommends filtering for the detection and treatment of noisy data, the Filter Approach in the context of feature selection is defined by its pre-learning feature evaluation and selection mechanism.

expert_reference: The wrapper approach is a feature selection strategy that uses a learning algorithm as a black box to evaluate feature subsets, aiming to improve the predictive performance of that specific learner. Unlike filter methods, which cannot allow a learning algorithm to fully exploit its bias, wrapper methods are designed to select features that accomplish the highest predictive accuracy for a fixed learning algorithm. The process typically involves two stages: first, feature subset selection where the best subset is chosen using the accuracy provided by the learning algorithm on training data as the criterion; and second, re-learning the data mining model with the best subset. To avoid overfitting, the wrapper approach employs statistical validation, such as cross-validation, to agree on a predictive measure. While wrapper approaches are an interesting choice in some domains, they require higher computational costs and are usually slower than filter methods, which can be a crucial factor under time constraints. Experimental studies have shown that results vary among learners, often recommending wrapper approaches for each kind of learner to optimize performance.

expert_reference: Sequential Forward Generation (SFG) is a forward feature-subset search direction. It starts with an empty selected set S and adds one feature at a time according to the feature-subset criterion until the stopping condition is met or all features have been considered. A stopping rule may specify the desired number of selected features or another criterion. In the source taxonomy, forward generation describes the direction of search; whether the overall search strategy is exhaustive, heuristic, or nondeterministic is a separate design choice.

expert_reference: Sequential Backward Generation (SBG) is a heuristic feature selection method that starts with the full set of features and iteratively removes features one at a time. The algorithm is defined by the function SBG(F, U), where F is the full set of features and U is the measure or criterion used to evaluate subsets. The procedure initializes a set S to hold the removed features. In a repeat loop, the algorithm selects the next feature to remove using f = GetNext(F) (or f = FindNextWorst(F, U) in the heuristic variant), removes it from the current set via F = F \setminus \{f\}, and adds it to the removed set via S = S \cup \{f\}. The loop continues until the remaining set F fails to satisfy the criterion U or until F becomes empty. When the stopping condition is met, the algorithm returns F \cup \{f\}, where f is the last removed feature. This return value is justified because f was the last feature removed, and after removing it, the remaining set failed the criterion. SBG is distinguished from Sequential Forward Generation (SFG), which starts from an empty set and adds features, and from Bidirectional Generation (BG), which combines forward and backward search directions. SBG is a heuristic method because it uses greedy choices to select the next worst feature to remove.

The search terminates under one of two conditions: (1) when one search finds the best subset comprised of m features before it reaches the exact middle, or (2) when both searches achieve the middle of the search space. expert_reference: Random Generation (RG) is a feature set generation algorithm that produces subsets of features at random. It starts the search in a random direction, and the choice of adding or removing a feature is a random decision. RG tries to avoid stagnation into a local optima by not following a fixed way for subset generation. Unlike Sequential Forward Generation (SFG) or Sequential Backward Generation (SBG), the size of the subset of features cannot be stipulated. A random generation scheme is based on a good random number generator attached with a function called RandGen(F) in such a way that every combination of features F has a chance to occur and only once. The formal relation is S = RandGen(F). RG generates random subsets and returns the best satisfactory subset found when the stopping criterion is reached. RG is non-deterministic because the generated subsets are random.

expert_reference: Exhaustive search is a feature selection strategy that explores the entire search space to identify the optimal subset of features. It is defined by its completeness: it covers all possible combinations of features, distinguishing it from heuristic or non-deterministic approaches that may prune the search space. The method can be implemented in two primary directions: forward search, which grows the feature subset gradually, and backward search, which reduces the subset by removing features one at a time. In backward search, the process starts with the full set of features and iteratively removes features to find the optimal subset. The space complexity of exhaustive search is O(2^M), where M is the total number of features. If a threshold m is established for the minimum number of features to be selected, the search space is defined by the sum of combinations from 0 to m, independent of whether the search is forward or backward. Exhaustive search is the only method that guarantees the optimality of the selected feature subset. However, because of its high computational cost, it is often impractical for large datasets. In such cases, exact algorithms like backtracking and branch and bound can be used to find an optimal subset without visiting all possible states. Exhaustive search is typically paired with evaluation measures such as probability, consistency, or accuracy, and it is considered a "complete" search strategy in the taxonomy of feature selection methods.

expert_reference: Heuristic search is a feature selection strategy that employs heuristics to carry out the search, preventing brute force exploration while ensuring the discovery of a non-optimal subset of features. It is positioned as a middle ground between exhaustive search, which guarantees optimality but is impractical for high-dimensional data, and nondeterministic search, which improves quality over time without a defined stopping point. The search process draws a path connecting the beginning and the end in a manner similar to depth-first search, where the maximum length of this path is M and the number of subsets generated is O(M). The choice of the heuristic is crucial to finding a subset closer to the optimal one in a faster operation. In the categorization of feature selection methods, heuristic search is one of the three values for the Search Strategy dimension, alongside Complete and Nondeterministic. It can be combined with different search directions, such as forward or backward, and evaluation measures. One specific implementation mentioned is the Mutual Information based Feature Selection (MIFS), which uses a greedy algorithm to replace impossible exhaustive search by choosing the next feature that maximizes information about the class relative to the average mutual information with already selected features.

expert_reference: Non-Deterministic Search is a feature selection strategy also known as random search. It is characterized by the random choice of search direction, meaning the algorithm does not pursue a fixed path or specific direction for subset generation. This approach is non-deterministic because the generated subsets are random, which allows the method to avoid stagnation in local optima. A key property of this strategy is that it can generate best subsets constantly and keep improving the quality of selected features as time goes by. There are two specific properties associated with this type of search: first, it is unnecessary to wait until the search ends to obtain results, and second, while the optimal set is not known to be obtained at a specific moment, the algorithm knows which subset is better than the previous one and which one is the best at the moment. In the categorization of feature selection methods, Non-Deterministic Search is one of the values for the Search strategy dimension, alongside Complete and Heuristic search. It is typically paired with a Random search direction, as combinations of non-deterministic search with forward or backward generation of features are considered impractical.

expert_reference: The Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient is a dependence measure used to quantify the degree of linear correlation between two numerical variables. It is described as the most well-known correlation coefficient and is specifically applied to numerical features to assess linear relationships. The coefficient is calculated using the values of the two attributes, their respective means, and their standard deviations. For two variables A and B, the correlation coefficient r_{A,B} is given by the formula: r_{A,B} = (Σ_{i=1}^{m} (a_i - A̅)(b_i - B̅)) / (m σ_A σ_B), which is equivalent to (Σ_{i=1}^{m} (a_i b_i) - m A̅ B̅) / (m σ_A σ_B). In this expression, m represents the number of instances, a_i and b_i are the values of attributes A and B in the instances, A̅ and B̅ are the mean values of A and B respectively, and σ_A and σ_B are the standard deviations of A and B. An alternative formulation for variables X and Y is ρ(X,Y) = Σ_i (x_i - x̄)(y_i - ȳ) / [ (Σ_i (x_i - x̄)^2) (Σ_i (y_i - ȳ)^2) ]^{1/2}, where x_i and y_i are the measurements and x̄ and ȳ are the means. This measure is distinct from rank-based or categorical measures, as it specifically targets linear association in numeric data.

Covariance is a statistical measure used to determine how much two variables change together. It is defined as the expected value of the product of the deviations of two attributes from their respective means. Formally, the covariance between attributes A and B is given by the formula: Cov(A, B) = E((A - A̅)(B - B̅)) = (1/m) * Σᵢ₌₁ᵐ (aᵢ - A̅)(bᵢ - B̅). In this expression, m represents the number of instances, aᵢ and bᵢ are the values of attributes A and B in the instances, A̅ and B̅ are the mean values of A and B respectively, and E(A) and E(B) denote the expected values of the attributes.

The sign of the covariance indicates the direction of the relationship between the variables. If two attributes vary similarly, such that when A is greater than its mean A̅, B is also likely to be greater than its mean B̅, the covariance is positive. Conversely, if one attribute tends to be above its expected value while the other is below its expected value, the covariance is negative. When the two variables are independent, the expected value of their product equals the product of their expected values (E(A·B) = E(A)·E(B)), which results in a covariance of zero. However, a covariance of zero does not necessarily imply that the attributes are independent, as some random variables may have a covariance of zero while still being dependent. Additional assumptions, such as the data following multivariate normal distributions, are necessary to determine independence from a zero covariance.

Covariance is closely related to the Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient. The correlation coefficient r(A,B) is calculated by dividing the covariance of A and B by the product of their standard deviations: r(A,B) = Cov(A, B) / (σA * σB), where σA and σB are the standard deviations of A and B. This relationship allows covariance to be used in assessing redundancy between numerical attributes, as high correlation (derived from covariance) may indicate that one attribute can be removed.

expert_reference: Spearman Rank Correlation is a measure of association defined as the Pearson correlation computed on the ranks of the variables. Formally, it is expressed as r_s = ρ(R(X), R(Y)), where r_s denotes the Spearman correlation coefficient, ρ represents the Pearson correlation function, and R(X) and R(Y) represent the ranks of variables X and Y. This measure is specifically used for ordinal variables, ranked variables, or numerical variables where a monotonic relationship is more important than a linear relationship. In contrast to Pearson correlation, which measures linear relationships between numerical variables, Spearman correlation measures monotonic relationships by applying the Pearson calculation to ranks. The resulting value falls within the range [−1, 1], with a value of 0 indicating no monotonic relationship. When calculating Spearman correlation in the presence of tied values, the procedure requires using average ranks and computing the Pearson correlation on those ranks, rather than using a shortcut formula.

expert_reference: Information Gain (Feature Goodness) is a criterion used in feature selection to evaluate how well a feature reduces uncertainty in a dataset. In the context of predictive learning, the "message" is the output feature or class in classification, and an information measure U is defined such that larger values represent higher levels of uncertainty. The information gain from a feature A, denoted as IG(A), is defined as the difference between the prior uncertainty and the expected posterior uncertainty using A. Formally, given an uncertainty function U and prior class probabilities P(ci) where i = 1, 2, ..., C (with C being the number of classes), the information gain is expressed as IG(A) = I(D) - \sum_{j=1}^{p} (|D_j| / |D|) I(D_j^A). In this formula, I(D) represents the information for the dataset D, D_j is the j-th child subset produced after splitting D using attribute A, |D_j|/|D| is the weight of child node j, and I(D_j^A) is the information for D_j due to partitioning D at A. A feature evaluation model inferred from this concept states that feature Ai is chosen instead of feature Aj if IG(Ai) > IG(Aj), meaning Ai reduces more uncertainty than Aj. This idea is used in algorithms like C4.5 for selecting a feature to generate new branches. However, Information Gain is biased toward attributes with many distinct values; for example, if an attribute has a unique value for each instance (such as an ID), a multiway split can create one pure child node per instance, resulting in zero weighted child entropy and maximal Information Gain.

expert_reference: Shannon entropy is a commonly used uncertainty function that serves as the standard measure for quantifying uncertainty in classification contexts. It is frequently employed to define information gain, which motivates the concept as a measure of uncertainty reduction. The null hypothesis (H0) is a formal statement in statistical testing that serves as the baseline assumption to be evaluated against observed data. It is explicitly defined alongside an alternative hypothesis (H1) to provide a rigorous framework for assessing whether an observed result is statistically significant. The null hypothesis represents the distribution of a test statistic under the assumption that no effect or difference exists; for example, in anomaly detection, H0 states that an instance belongs to the normal class, while in classifier evaluation, it states that the classifier has not learned a generalizable relationship between attributes and class labels.

The primary role of the null hypothesis is to enable the calculation of a p-value, which is the probability of falsely rejecting H0 when it is actually true. This allows for a more objective assessment of evidence compared to significance testing alone, which does not explicitly specify an alternative hypothesis. A critical distinction is that failing to reject the null hypothesis is not equivalent to "accepting" it; a non-significant result may still arise from the alternative distribution or a misspecified null model. Consequently, the null hypothesis provides the reference distribution against which the extremity of a test statistic is measured to determine if it falls within a critical region.

A test statistic, typically denoted R, is a numerical quantity used to quantify the evidence in an observed outcome with respect to a null hypothesis. It typically summarizes every possible outcome as a single count or real-valued value, enabling the computation of the probability of an outcome under the null hypothesis. The test statistic measures how 'extreme' an observed result is under the null hypothesis; for example, in a stockbroker problem, R could be the number of successful decisions made in a fixed number of trials, reducing a complex outcome to a single count.

The definition of 'extreme' depends on the choice of the null hypothesis and the design of the test statistic. An observed test statistic can be considered extreme if it is greater than or equal to a certain value (right-tailed), smaller than or equal to a certain value (left-tailed), or outside a specified interval (two-sided). These cases correspond to one-sided and two-sided tests, respectively.

In hypothesis testing, the test statistic is chosen to differentiate the behavior of results under the null hypothesis from the behavior of results under the alternative hypothesis. The distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis (the null distribution) and, sometimes, under the alternative hypothesis must be modeled. Given these distributions, the framework of hypothesis testing decides whether to reject or not reject the null hypothesis based on the evidence provided by the test statistic computed from an observed result. This decision is typically made by specifying a critical region—a range of possible values of the test statistic that are too extreme under the null hypothesis. If the observed test statistic falls in this region, the null hypothesis is rejected; otherwise, it is not rejected.

The p-value of an observed test statistic is the probability of obtaining that value or something more extreme from the null distribution. P-values capture the aggregate tail probabilities of the null distribution for test statistic values that are at least as extreme as the observed value. The reason for accounting for 'something more extreme' is that the probability of any particular result is often 0 or close to 0.

The test statistic is used in various contexts, including cluster analysis, anomaly detection, and association analysis. In cluster analysis, the test statistic is typically a cluster validity measure (e.g., SSE or silhouette coefficient) used to test whether the observed clustering is significant compared to random partitioning. In anomaly detection, the anomaly score of an instance serves as the test statistic, with the null hypothesis that the instance belongs to the normal class. In association analysis, the test statistic measures the deviation of an observed contingency table from the null hypothesis of no association among items; for example, the chi-squared test statistic is computed from the differences between observed and expected values in a contingency table.

A primary requirement for conducting statistical testing is knowing how the test statistic is distributed under the null hypothesis. This distribution can be estimated by fitting statistical models (e.g., normal or binomial) to test statistic values from data sets generated under the null hypothesis, or by using non-parametric approaches such as counting the fraction of times the test statistic generated under the null distribution exceeds the observed value. When the distribution of the test statistic depends on the number of samples, increasing the sample size helps obtain less variable estimates of the true null and alternative distributions. The minimum number of samples required for ensuring a low value of the significance level while having high power is often determined by power analysis.

expert_reference: The significance level, denoted by α, is a fixed threshold on p-values that is decided before any tests are performed. A result is called statistically significant if its p-value is lower than this threshold, which provides sufficient evidence to believe the observed result is a significant departure from the null hypothesis and convinces us to reject it. While every result has a different p-value, the significance level remains a constant for the testing process. Common choices for this level include 0.05 (5%) and 0.01 (1%). The p-value of a statistically significant result denotes the probability of falsely rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true. Rejecting the null hypothesis if the test statistic falls in the critical region is equivalent to evaluating the p-value and rejecting the null hypothesis if the p-value falls below the pre-specified threshold. In the context of multiple hypothesis testing, the significance level can be adjusted to balance power and false positives. For instance, in the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure, the significance level for the i-th p-value is computed as αi = i × α/m. This approach strikes a balance between the overly conservative Bonferroni procedure and the overly liberal naïve approach, resulting in higher power without producing too many false positives. The BH procedure declares the first k p-values as significant, where k is the largest index such that the p-value is lower than its significance level, guaranteeing that the False Discovery Rate (FDR) is smaller than α.

expert_reference: One-sided and two-sided tests are distinct approaches to statistical hypothesis testing that differ in how the probability of the null distribution is allocated across its tails. A one-sided test, which can be right-tailed or left-tailed, concentrates the entire probability of the significance level (such as 0.05) into a single tail of the distribution. In contrast, a two-sided test splits this probability equally between both tails, resulting in 0.025 probability in each tail when the significance level is 0.05. The choice between these tests depends on the specific research question: a one-sided test is used when the hypothesis is directional, such as testing whether one entity is better than another, while a two-sided test is used when the hypothesis is non-directional, asking whether two entities are different in either direction. A low p-value in either type of test indicates smaller probabilities in the tails of the null distribution, providing sufficient evidence to believe that the observed result is a significant departure from the null hypothesis and justifying its rejection. In the context of classifier comparison, a two-tailed test typically uses a threshold such as |Z| > 1.96 at a significance level of 0.05 to determine if classifiers are significantly different.

Hunt's algorithm is a generic procedure for growing decision trees in a greedy fashion. It is one of the earliest methods for this task and serves as the basis for many current implementations of decision tree classifiers, including ID3, C4.5, and CART. The algorithm is used because finding an optimal decision tree is computationally expensive due to the exponential size of the search space; Hunt's algorithm induces a reasonably accurate, albeit suboptimal, decision tree in a reasonable amount of time by making a series of locally optimal decisions about which attribute to use when partitioning the training data.

The decision tree is grown in a recursive, top-down fashion. The tree initially contains a single root node that is associated with all the training instances. The algorithm recursively applies itself to child nodes. A node is expanded if it contains training instances from more than one class. When a node is expanded, training instances are propagated to child nodes based on attribute values. For example, instances for which a specific attribute equals a specific value are propagated to one child, and the rest are propagated to the other child. If all instances associated with a node have an identical class label, the node becomes a leaf node labeled with that class.

Some child nodes created in the algorithm can be empty if none of the training instances have the particular attribute values. One way to handle this is by declaring each of them as a leaf node with a class label that occurs most frequently among the training instances associated with their parent nodes. Hunt's algorithm makes some simplifying assumptions that are often not true in practice, and possible ways for handling these assumptions are discussed in the source material.

expert_reference: Node impurity is a measure of how dissimilar the class labels are for the data instances belonging to a common node. It quantifies the uncertainty or lack of purity in a node's class distribution. In decision tree learning, impurity measures are used to evaluate the quality of a split; the goal is to find the attribute test condition that results in the purest child nodes. A node is considered pure if it contains instances from a single class, which yields a zero impurity value. Conversely, maximum impurity occurs when a node has an equal proportion of instances from multiple classes. The collective impurity of child nodes is computed as a weighted sum of the impurities of the individual child nodes, where the weight for each child is the fraction of the parent's training instances that reach that child. This collective impurity is compared against the parent's impurity to determine the gain from a split. The splitting criterion in the decision tree algorithm selects the attribute test condition that shows the maximum gain, which is equivalent to minimizing the weighted impurity of the children. A key limitation of impurity measures is that they tend to favor qualitative attributes with a large number of distinct values, as such attributes can produce pure partitions (zero impurity) by assigning a unique value to each instance, which may lead to overfitting. Therefore, the number of children produced by a splitting attribute should also be considered when selecting the best test condition.
