A cluster is fundamentally defined as a set of objects that share some property, a broad characterization that encompasses more specific structural definitions. In the context of understanding data, clusters are viewed as potential classes, and cluster analysis is the study of techniques for automatically finding these classes. The goal of clustering is to find useful groups of objects, where the usefulness of the groups is defined by the specific goals of the data analysis. Cluster analysis groups data objects based on information found only in the data that describes the objects and their relationships, distinguishing it from supervised methods that rely on external labels. 

Several specific definitions of a cluster exist depending on the underlying clustering approach. In prototype-based clustering, a cluster is a set of objects in which each object is closer (or more similar) to the prototype that defines the cluster than to the prototype of any other cluster. If the data is represented as a graph, where nodes are objects and links represent connections among objects, a cluster can be defined as a connected component. An entire collection of clusters is commonly referred to as a clustering. 

The definition of a cluster is central to the broader process of cluster analysis, which divides data into groups that are meaningful, useful, or both. Understanding the characteristics of data, clusters, and algorithms is important for a broad understanding of cluster analysis and provides the basis for deciding which technique to use in a specific situation. The type of clustering produced by an algorithm needs to match the type of clustering needed by the application for the algorithm to be appropriate.

expert_reference: Intra-cluster distance, also referred to as intra-cluster dissimilarity, measures the internal cohesion of a cluster by quantifying the distances between objects and the cluster's centroid. In K-means clustering, this metric is calculated as the summation of distances between the objects and the centroid of the cluster to which they are assigned. The centroid represents the mean value of the objects within that cluster. The primary objective of clustering is to divide a data set into groups based on object similarity while minimizing this intra-cluster dissimilarity. In the context of K-means Clustering Imputation (KMI), the distance between a centroid and an object is denoted as d(vk, xi), where vk is the centroid of cluster k and xi is the object. The KMI procedure involves randomly selecting K complete data objects as centroids, iteratively modifying the partition to reduce the sum of distances for each object from its cluster centroid, and finally filling in non-reference attributes for incomplete objects using a nearest neighbor algorithm. The process terminates when the summation of distances falls below a user-specified threshold or when no changes occur to the centroids in the last iteration. In hierarchical clustering, intra-cluster distances are explicitly excluded from inter-cluster distance calculations; for example, distances between points within the same cluster are not used to determine the height at which two distinct clusters are merged in a dendrogram. Clustering generally requires a meaningful distance or similarity measure to function effectively.
candidate_draft: Intra-cluster distance, also referred to as intra-cluster dissimilarity, is a measure of how closely related the objects within a single cluster are. In the context of K-means clustering, this dissimilarity is specifically measured by the summation of the distances between the individual objects and the centroid of the cluster to which they are assigned. This metric serves as a core component of the overall objective of clustering, which is to divide a data set into groups based on the similarity of objects while minimizing this intra-cluster dissimilarity. By focusing on the internal cohesion of a group, intra-cluster distance provides a basis for evaluating the quality of a clustering scheme and is distinct from measures that assess the separation or proximity between different clusters.

expert_reference: Inter-cluster distance is a measure of proximity or dissimilarity between two distinct clusters, used in hierarchical clustering and evaluation metrics. In the CURE algorithm, the distance between two clusters is defined as the minimum distance between any two representative points after those points are shrunk toward their respective centers. This approach is equivalent to centroid-based hierarchical clustering under specific conditions and roughly the same as single-link hierarchical clustering under others. In silhouette coefficient calculations, the inter-cluster component is represented by b(x), which is the smallest average distance from a point x to the members of any other cluster. This contrasts with the intra-cluster component, which is the average distance from x to the other points in its own cluster. In BIRCH, the distance between clusters can be computed using summary statistics, and the diameter (variance) of the merged cluster can also be used as a distance measure. Inter-cluster distance uses only cross-cluster pairs, excluding distances inside the same cluster. The height at which two clusters are merged in a dendrogram reflects the distance of the two clusters, as seen in single-link techniques where the distance between points or clusters determines the merge height.
candidate_draft: Inter-cluster distance, also referred to as cluster proximity, is a measure used to quantify the closeness or separation between two distinct clusters. In hierarchical clustering, this metric is essential because agglomerative techniques repeatedly combine the two closest clusters and are principally distinguished from one another by the way they define cluster proximity. A linkage method specifies how to compute this cluster-to-cluster distance. One approach, the group average technique, defines cluster proximity as the average pairwise proximity among all pairs of points in the different clusters. Another approach measures the separation between two clusters by the sum of the weights of the links from points in one cluster to points in the other cluster, where the links represent the proximity between data objects. Additionally, the distance between two clusters can be defined as the minimum distance between any two representative points after they are shrunk toward their respective centers. These definitions allow clustering algorithms to work with the proximity between clusters to determine the structure of the data.

expert_reference: The distinction between classification and clustering is defined by the source of the labels used to group objects. Classification involves assigning particular objects to pre-existing groups, a process that relies on a model developed from objects with known class labels to assign labels to new, unlabeled objects. In contrast, clustering involves dividing objects into groups based on shared common characteristics, where the labels are derived solely from the data itself. Because clustering creates a labeling of objects with class (cluster) labels without using pre-existing known labels, it is sometimes referred to as unsupervised classification. While both processes result in objects being grouped, clustering is the study of techniques for automatically finding these classes, whereas classification is the assignment of objects to those classes. This distinction is a core concept in understanding how data mining techniques divide data objects into groups.
candidate_draft: Classification and clustering are distinct data analysis tasks that both involve grouping data objects, but they differ fundamentally in their objectives and the nature of the groups they produce. Clustering is the process of grouping data objects so that objects inside the same group are similar, and objects in different groups are less similar. In this context, clusters are potential classes, and cluster analysis is the study of techniques for automatically finding these classes. Because clustering creates a labeling of objects with class (cluster) labels, it can be regarded as a form of classification, which is why cluster analysis is sometimes referred to as unsupervised classification. In contrast, when the term classification is used without qualification within data mining, it typically refers to supervised classification, where the goal is to assign particular objects to predefined groups. The distinction is also reflected in human cognitive processes: humans are skilled at dividing objects into groups (clustering) and assigning particular objects to these groups (classification). Understanding this distinction is important for deciding which technique to use in a specific situation, as the type of clustering produced by an algorithm needs to match the type of clustering needed by the application.

expert_reference: A core point is a data point located in the interior of a density-based cluster. Formally, a point is a core point if there are at least MinPts points within a distance of Eps, where MinPts and Eps are user-specified parameters. The count of points in the neighborhood includes the point itself. In density-based clustering algorithms like DBSCAN and SNN density-based clustering, core points are defined as points that strongly belong to one cluster. A core point can directly reach a border point, but a border point cannot directly reach back as a core-expanding point. In the DBSCAN algorithm, any two core points that are close enough—within a distance Eps of one another—are put in the same cluster. The use of core points adds considerable power and flexibility to density-based clustering approaches.
candidate_draft: In density-based clustering algorithms such as DBSCAN and SNN density-based clustering, a core point is a data object that strongly belongs to one cluster. The center-based approach to density allows a point to be classified as being in the interior of a dense region, which defines it as a core point. This classification distinguishes core points from border points, which are on the edge of a dense region, and noise points, which are in sparsely occupied regions. A core point starts and expands dense regions, serving as the foundation for cluster formation. In the DBSCAN algorithm, clusters are formed by connecting core points within a specified radius (Eps), and each connected component of core points becomes a separate cluster. The determination of a core point is governed by parameters such as Eps and MinPts; specifically, points for which the distance to their k-th nearest neighbor (k-dist) is less than Eps are labeled as core points, while other points are labeled as noise or border points. DBSCAN estimates density by counting points within the radius Eps, including the point itself, to identify these core regions.

expert_reference: A border point is a data point that is not a core point because it does not have enough points in its neighborhood to satisfy the core point condition, but it falls within the neighborhood of at least one core point. In the context of density-based clustering, a border point is located on the edge of a dense region. While a core point starts and expands dense regions, a border point can be attached to a dense region but does not expand it. This limitation exists because direct density-reachability requires the starting point to be a core point; consequently, a core point can directly reach a border point, but a border point cannot directly reach back as a core-expanding point. In cluster construction, border points attach to the core component formed by mutually connected core points. If a border point is close to core points from different clusters, a border tie occurs, requiring a convention to resolve the assignment, such as assigning the point to the first cluster that reaches it or the closest core point. A border point is distinct from a noise point, which is neither a core point nor a border point and is not assigned to any cluster.
candidate_draft: In the context of density-based clustering, specifically the DBSCAN algorithm, a border point is a data point that is not a core point but is located within the neighborhood of at least one core point. The DBSCAN algorithm operates by first identifying core points, which are strongly associated with a cluster, and then processing border points by attaching them to the clusters of their associated core points. This attachment process is a distinct step in the algorithm, occurring after core points are connected and before noise points are discarded. A border point is defined by its relationship to core points; it is 'close to' or 'associated with' them, but it does not itself meet the criteria to be a core point. If a border point is close to core points from different clusters, a tie or ambiguity arises, and the point must be assigned to one of the clusters of its associated core points. In some implementations, a border point associated with several core points is assigned to the closest core point, or to the first cluster that reaches it. Border points are one of three categories of points in DBSCAN, alongside core points and noise points. The identification of a point as a border point is part of the overall labeling process where all points are classified as core, border, or noise. The space requirement of DBSCAN is low because it only needs to keep the cluster label and the identification of each point as a core, border, or noise point. Border points are not discarded like noise points; instead, they are assigned to a cluster, making them part of the final clustering result. The concept of a border point is central to how DBSCAN handles the boundaries of clusters, allowing it to find clusters of arbitrary shapes and sizes by following dense connected regions.

In the context of density-based clustering, a noise point is defined as any point that is neither a core point nor a border point. This classification arises from a center-based approach to density, which categorizes data points into three distinct types: those in the interior of a dense region (core points), those on the edge of a dense region (border points), and those in sparsely occupied regions (noise or background points). A noise point is specifically characterized by its location in a sparsely occupied region, meaning it does not meet the density requirements to be a core point and is not within the neighborhood of a core point to qualify as a border point.

In the DBSCAN algorithm, noise points are handled by being discarded or omitted from the clustering process. This mechanism allows the algorithm to automatically classify low-density points as noise and remove them, thereby eliminating their negative effects on the clustering results. This is particularly important because atypical points or outliers can severely degrade the performance of clustering algorithms, especially prototype-based methods like K-means, or cause techniques like single link to join clusters that should not be joined. By identifying and discarding noise points, DBSCAN maintains the integrity of the discovered clusters.

The classification of a point as noise is sensitive to the algorithm's parameters. If the distance threshold (epsilon) is set too small, most neighborhoods become too small, causing many points to be classified as noise. Conversely, if the minimum points parameter (minPts) is set too large, real small clusters may disappear and be classified as noise. Thus, a noise point is a point that fails to satisfy the density connectivity conditions required to be part of a cluster under the given parameter settings.
candidate_draft: In the context of density-based clustering, specifically the DBSCAN algorithm, a noise point is a data object that is not assigned to any cluster. These points are typically located in low-density regions and are automatically classified as noise by the algorithm, effectively removing them from the cluster construction process. This classification allows DBSCAN to handle data with outliers and irregular shapes without forcing every point into a cluster, unlike algorithms such as K-means which require every point to be assigned to a centroid. The identification of a point as noise is one of the three possible classifications for any data point in DBSCAN, alongside core points and border points. The algorithm's ability to reject points as noise is a key advantage when dealing with datasets containing many isolated outliers or when the natural clusters are density-separated and non-spherical. However, the classification of points as noise is sensitive to the algorithm's parameters; for instance, if the Eps threshold is set such that certain regions are not dense enough to form clusters, the points in those regions, including those that might otherwise be part of a cluster, are marked as noise. This mechanism helps in sharpening the distinction between true clusters and random data or outliers, although it can also lead to small clusters being labeled as noise if the minimum points parameter is set too large relative to the cluster size.

expert_reference: DBSCAN requires two user-specified parameters, Eps and MinPts, to define its clustering behavior. Eps represents the maximum distance threshold for neighborhood calculations, while MinPts is the minimum number of points required within that Eps radius for a point to be classified as a core point. The point itself is included in the count of points within the Eps-neighborhood. For example, if MinPts is set to 3, a point must have itself and at least two other points within the Eps distance to be considered core. These parameters are global, meaning a single Eps and MinPts value are applied to the entire dataset. The selection of these parameters is critical because they determine the density threshold used to distinguish clusters from noise. A common method for determining Eps involves computing the k-dist (the distance to the k-th nearest neighbor) for all points, sorting these values, and identifying a sharp increase in the plot, which indicates a suitable Eps value. The value of k used in this process typically corresponds to the MinPts parameter. DBSCAN's reliance on a single global density threshold can be a limitation when cluster densities vary widely, as it may fail to separate clusters of different densities or merge them incorrectly depending on the chosen Eps.
candidate_draft: DBSCAN is a density-based clustering algorithm that requires two user-specified parameters: Eps and MinPts. These parameters are essential for the algorithm to function, as they define the criteria for identifying core points, border points, and noise points. The algorithm estimates density by counting the number of points within a radius of Eps, including the point itself. A point is considered a core point if it has at least MinPts points within its Eps-neighborhood. Border points are those that are within the Eps-neighborhood of a core point but do not have enough points to be core points themselves. Noise points are those that are neither core nor border points. The selection of appropriate values for Eps and MinPts is critical, as the algorithm's performance and the resulting clusters depend heavily on these parameters. For instance, in one example, Eps was set by looking at the distances of the fourth nearest neighbors, and MinPts was set to 4. The algorithm forms clusters by connecting core points within Eps, then attaching border points to associated core clusters and discarding noise. DBSCAN is particularly useful when the natural clusters are density-separated, non-spherical, noisy, and when the number of clusters is not known in advance. However, it can struggle with varying densities, high-dimensional data, and expensive nearest-neighbor search. The space requirement of DBSCAN is O(m), where m is the number of points, because it only needs to keep a small amount of data for each point, such as the cluster label and the identification of each point as a core, border, or noise point.

expert_reference: Directly density-reachable is a directional relationship between two points in density-based clustering. A point q is directly density-reachable from a point p if and only if two conditions are met: q must be in the ε-neighborhood of p (denoted as q ∈ Nε(p)), and p must be a core point. This relationship is asymmetric; specifically, a core point can directly reach a border point, but a border point cannot directly reach back as a core-expanding point. Consequently, while a border point can be assigned to a cluster, it does not expand the cluster because the definition requires the starting point of the reachability relation to be core. This concept serves as the foundational step for defining density-reachability, where a point q is density-reachable from p if there exists a chain of points from p to q such that each subsequent point in the chain is directly density-reachable from the previous one.

expert_reference: Density-reachability is a relationship defined between two points, p and q, within the framework of density-based clustering. A point q is considered density-reachable from p if there exists a chain of points starting at p and ending at q, denoted as p = p1, p2, ..., pn = q, such that each subsequent point in the chain is directly density-reachable from the preceding point. This concept relies on the definition of direct density-reachability, where a point q is directly density-reachable from p if q is contained in the epsilon-neighborhood of p (q ∈ Nε(p)) and p is a core point. Density-reachability is distinct from density-connectedness, which holds when there exists some point o such that both p and q are density-reachable from o. The framework assumes that the entire dataset can be evaluated using a single density standard. This approach contrasts with centroid-based methods like K-means, which may identify dense compact blobs but optimize for centroid compactness rather than density reachability.

expert_reference: Density-connected is a relationship between two points in a density-based clustering context. Two points, p and q, are density-connected if there exists some point o such that both p and q are density-reachable from o. This definition relies on the concept of density-reachability, where a point q is density-reachable from p if there is a chain of points from p to q such that each subsequent point in the chain is directly density-reachable from the previous one. The relationship is symmetric: if p and q are density-connected, they belong to the same cluster. This concept is central to DBSCAN, which identifies clusters as dense regions of objects surrounded by low-density regions. Unlike centroid-based methods that may cut through curved dense shapes, DBSCAN can follow dense connected regions when parameters are suitable. Density-connectedness allows DBSCAN to label points as noise instead of forcing them into a cluster, which is an advantage over K-means when density connectivity is the appropriate cluster model.

The concept is central to DBSCAN's ability to follow dense connected regions when parameters are suitable, distinguishing it from prototype-based methods that assume spherical clusters.

expert_reference: DBSCAN is a density-based clustering algorithm that locates regions of high density separated by regions of low density. Unlike K-means, which uses a prototype-based or centroid-based notion of a cluster, DBSCAN defines clusters based on a single density threshold. This approach allows DBSCAN to handle clusters of arbitrary shapes and sizes and makes it relatively resistant to noise. DBSCAN produces a partitional clustering where the number of clusters is automatically determined by the algorithm, rather than being specified as a parameter. A key characteristic of this definition is that points in low-density regions are classified as noise and omitted; consequently, DBSCAN does not produce a complete clustering of all objects. The algorithm operates by connecting core points that are within a distance Eps of one another into the same cluster, attaching border points that are close enough to a core point to that core point's cluster, and discarding noise points. Because it relies on a global density threshold, DBSCAN may struggle with data where cluster characteristics vary widely, and it can be computationally expensive for high-dimensional data where density is difficult to define.
candidate_draft: DBSCAN is a density-based clustering algorithm that defines clusters as dense regions of objects surrounded by low-density regions. Unlike center-based methods such as K-means, which typically assign every object to a cluster and assume globular shapes, DBSCAN uses a density-based definition that allows it to find clusters of arbitrary shapes and sizes, including curved, elongated, or ring-shaped structures. A key feature of this definition is the ability to identify and discard objects that do not belong to any dense region, classifying them as noise rather than forcing them into a cluster. This makes the algorithm relatively resistant to noise and outliers. The clustering process is based on connecting core points within a specified distance (Eps) and attaching border points to associated core clusters. Because the number of clusters is automatically determined by the algorithm based on the data's density structure, DBSCAN is particularly effective when the natural clusters are density-separated and the number of clusters is not known in advance. However, this density-based definition relies on a single density threshold, which can be a limitation when clusters have widely varying densities or when dealing with high-dimensional sparse data where density is difficult to define reliably.

expert_reference: DBSCAN is a density-based clustering algorithm that is relatively resistant to noise and can handle clusters of arbitrary shapes and sizes. Because it uses a density-based definition of a cluster, it can find many clusters that could not be found using K-means. DBSCAN is better when the density-cluster assumption matches the data, specifically when density connectivity is the right cluster model. It can label points as noise instead of forcing them into a cluster, unlike K-means which assigns every point to some centroid. However, DBSCAN has trouble with high-dimensional data because density is more difficult to define for such data. It can also be computationally expensive when the computation of nearest neighbors requires computing all pairwise proximities, as is usually the case for high-dimensional data. DBSCAN is a special case of DENCLUE, which provides a more flexible and potentially more accurate way to compute density. Neither DBSCAN nor K-means is universally better; K-means is better when the centroid-cluster assumption matches the data, such as when clusters are compact and centroid-like.
candidate_draft: DBSCAN is a simple and effective density-based clustering algorithm that identifies dense regions of objects surrounded by low-density regions. Its primary advantages include the ability to handle clusters of arbitrary shapes and sizes, resistance to noise and outliers, and the capacity to automatically determine the number of clusters without requiring it as a prior parameter. Unlike K-means, which assigns every point to a centroid, DBSCAN can label points as noise rather than forcing them into a cluster, making it particularly effective when natural clusters are density-separated, non-spherical, and noisy. The algorithm's space requirement is O(m), as it only needs to store the cluster label and the classification of each point as a core, border, or noise point. However, DBSCAN has significant limitations. It performs poorly on high-dimensional data because the traditional Euclidean definition of density does not work well in such spaces, and it struggles when clusters have widely varying densities. Additionally, the algorithm can merge clusters that overlap, and its performance is sensitive to the parameters used to define density neighborhoods. These characteristics make DBSCAN more reliable in low-dimensional spatial data than in high-dimensional sparse data.

expert_reference: Internal indices are unsupervised measures of cluster validity that evaluate the goodness of a clustering structure without respect to external information. These measures are termed internal indices because they rely exclusively on information present in the data set itself. Unsupervised measures of cluster validity are often further divided into two classes: measures of cluster cohesion, which determine how closely related the objects in a cluster are, and measures of cluster separation, which determine how distinct or well-separated a cluster is from other clusters. Within the broader classification of cluster validity indices, internal indices represent the category that assesses clustering quality based solely on internal data characteristics rather than external reference labels.
candidate_draft: Internal indices are a category of cluster evaluation measures that assess the quality of a clustering structure without using any external information. They measure the goodness of a cluster only by reference to the data itself, asking whether the clustering looks geometrically good by itself. This distinguishes them from external indices, which measure the extent to which the discovered clustering structure matches some external structure, usually the known class labels. Internal indices are unsupervised cluster evaluation measures that can be used to approximately determine the correct or natural number of clusters. The minimum and maximum values of these measures can provide some guidance in many cases. The silhouette coefficient is an example of an internal cluster evaluation measure. Understanding and enhancement of internal clustering validation measures is a key area of study in cluster analysis.

expert_reference:
SSE (Sum of Squared Errors) is an unsupervised, internal cluster evaluation measure that quantifies the goodness of a clustering structure without relying on external information. It functions as a centroid-quality measure, assessing how tightly data points sit around their assigned centroids; a smaller SSE indicates that points are closer to their centroids. In the context of K-means clustering, SSE serves as the objective function to be minimized, and for a fixed number of clusters (K), a lower SSE represents a better clustering solution.

The formal definition of SSE is the sum of the squared distances between each point and its assigned cluster centroid. This is expressed as SSE = ∑(i=1 to K) ∑(x ∈ Ci) (ci - x)², where K is the number of clusters, Ci is the set of points in cluster i, ci is the centroid of cluster i, and x is a data point. An equivalent formulation using a distance function is SSE = ∑(i=1 to K) ∑(x ∈ Ci) dist(ci, x)². The total SSE of a clustering is the sum of the SSE contributed by each individual cluster.

SSE is sensitive to the number of clusters used. Increasing the number of clusters (K) almost always reduces the SSE. In the extreme case where K equals the total number of points (n), every point becomes its own cluster, resulting in an SSE of 0, which is generally considered a useless clustering. Because of this property, SSE can be used to determine the number of clusters by observing where the measure stops decreasing significantly as K increases.

While K-means typically converges to a local minimum of SSE, various postprocessing techniques can be used to "fix up" the resulting clusters to achieve a lower SSE without increasing K. These techniques include alternating phases of splitting and merging clusters. Splitting strategies often involve dividing the cluster with the largest SSE or the largest standard deviation for a specific attribute, and introducing a new centroid (often the point farthest from any existing center). Merging strategies combine clusters to reduce the total number while attempting to minimize the overall SSE. Additionally, per-cluster SSE is useful as a diagnostic tool to identify which specific clusters are loose or spread out.

It is also known as scatter and serves as an objective function for clustering algorithms, particularly K-means, which aims to find clusters with low total SSE. Lower SSE values indicate better-quality clusterings, while higher SSE values suggest poorer cluster quality. In the context of bisecting K-means, the cluster with the largest SSE is typically chosen for splitting to reduce the overall SSE of the clustering. SSE is an internal measure, meaning it does not rely on external labels, unlike measures such as entropy or precision. Classification-Oriented Measures of Cluster Validity

expert_reference:
Cohesion is an internal measure of cluster validity that quantifies how closely related the objects within a single cluster are, often described as the compactness or tightness of the group. It is used to evaluate the goodness of a clustering structure without relying on external labels, using only information present in the dataset. Cohesion is distinct from separation, which measures how distinct or well-separated a cluster is from other clusters.

For prototype-based clusters, cohesion is defined as the sum of the proximity between each object in the cluster and the cluster's prototype (centroid). The formula is cohesion(C_i) = ∑_{x∈C_i} proximity(x, c_i), where C_i is the cluster, c_i is the prototype or centroid of the cluster, and proximity is a function that can represent either similarity or dissimilarity. When proximity is defined as squared Euclidean distance, this measure is equivalent to the cluster Sum of Squared Errors (SSE). For graph-based clusters, cohesion is defined as the sum of the pairwise proximities between all objects in the cluster, expressed as cohesion(C_i) = ∑_{x∈C_i} ∑_{y∈C_i} proximity(x, y).

The interpretation of the cohesion value depends on the type of proximity function used. If the proximity function is a similarity measure, higher values indicate better cohesion. If the proximity function is a dissimilarity measure, lower values indicate better cohesion. In the context of K-means clustering, which is a centroid-based algorithm, centroid-based cohesion is the appropriate measure. For non-Euclidean data, such as document data represented as a document-term matrix, cohesion can be defined using cosine similarity, where the objective is to maximize the similarity of documents to the cluster centroid. The total cohesion across all clusters is the sum of the cohesion of each individual cluster.

Cohesion is often related to separation. For some validity measures, the sum of total SSE (cohesion) and total SSB (separation) is a constant, meaning that minimizing cohesion is equivalent to maximizing separation. Cohesion can also be used to evaluate individual objects within a cluster; objects that contribute more to the overall cohesion are typically near the interior of the cluster, while those contributing less are near the edge. This information can guide clustering improvements, such as splitting a cluster with low cohesion into subclusters or merging clusters that are cohesive but not well separated.
candidate_draft: Cohesion is a measure of cluster validity that quantifies how closely related the objects within a single cluster are, often described in terms of compactness or tightness. It is a core component of unsupervised cluster evaluation, typically used alongside separation to assess the overall quality of a clustering. The definition of cohesion depends on the type of cluster model being evaluated. For graph-based clusters, cohesion is defined as the sum of the weights of the links in the proximity graph that connect points within the cluster. For prototype-based clusters, cohesion is defined as the sum of the proximities with respect to the prototype (centroid or medoid) of the cluster. In the context of K-Means, which represents a cluster by its centroid, the natural cohesion calculation uses point-to-centroid distances. While the graph-based and prototype-based approaches to measuring cohesion seem distinct, for some proximity measures they are equivalent. A cluster that has a high value of cohesion may be considered better than a cluster that has a lower value. Cohesion can be expressed either in terms of the sum of the similarities of objects in the cluster to the cluster centroid or in terms of the pairwise similarities of objects in the cluster. In some cluster validity measures, cohesion is used in combination with separation; for example, a measure based on both cohesion and separation is the sum of the pairwise similarities of all objects in the cluster with all objects outside the cluster divided by the sum of the pairwise similarities of objects in the cluster. Cohesion and separation can be combined into an overall measure of cluster validity by using a weighted sum. If the number of clusters is not too large, it can be useful to manually examine the cluster cohesion of each cluster and the pairwise separation of clusters. Most unsupervised cluster evaluation measures, such as the silhouette coefficient, incorporate both cohesion and separation. The goodness of a clustering is typically evaluated with the help of cluster validity measures that either capture the cohesion or separation of clusters, such as the sum of squared errors (SSE), or make use of external labels such as entropy.

expert_reference: Separation is an internal cluster validity measure that quantifies how distinct or well-separated a cluster is from other clusters. It is used to evaluate clustering quality by assessing the distance or dissimilarity between clusters, often in conjunction with cohesion measures. For prototype-based clusters, such as those produced by K-Means, separation is defined as the proximity (distance or dissimilarity) between the cluster's prototype (centroid or medoid) and either another cluster's prototype or an overall prototype. Specifically, the separation between two clusters Ci and Cj is given by separation(Ci, Cj) = proximity(ci, cj), where ci and cj are the prototypes of the respective clusters. Alternatively, the separation of a single cluster Ci from the overall dataset is given by separation(Ci) = proximity(ci, c), where c is the overall prototype. In graph-based or object-level definitions, separation is calculated as the sum of pairwise proximities between all objects in one cluster and all objects in another cluster: separation(Ci, Cj) = ∑_{x∈Ci} ∑_{y∈Cj} proximity(x, y). Another formulation, often used in normalized contexts, defines separation(Y) as the average normalized distance from a cluster's centroid to the centroids of all other clusters: separation(Y) = (1 / (|ζ| - 1)) ∑_{Y'∈ζ, Y'≠Y} d_N(center(Y), center(Y')). The choice of proximity function (similarity or dissimilarity) affects interpretation: for similarity, lower separation values indicate better separation; for dissimilarity, higher values indicate better separation. Separation is distinct from cohesion, which measures internal cluster compactness, and from external indices like Rand Index or Purity, which require ground truth labels.
candidate_draft: Separation is a core concept in unsupervised cluster evaluation that measures how distinct or well-separated a cluster is from other clusters. It is often paired with cohesion, which measures the compactness or tightness of objects within a cluster. Many internal measures of cluster validity for partitional clustering schemes are based on the notions of cohesion or separation. For example, the between group sum of squares (SSB) is a measure of separation between clusters. In graph-based cluster evaluation, separation can be defined as the total weight of the edges of the similarity graph that must be cut to separate the cluster from all other clusters, divided by the sum of the pairwise similarities of objects in the cluster. This graph-based measure of separation also incorporates cluster cohesion in its calculation. Separation is used to evaluate the quality of resulting clusters and to compare different clusterings to determine which is better. It is a key component in overall cluster validity measures, such as the silhouette coefficient, which incorporates both cohesion and separation. When clusters are poorly separated, meaning they touch or overlap, some clustering techniques may combine clusters that should be kept separate. Therefore, examining separation is crucial for assessing the effectiveness of a clustering algorithm and for deciding which technique to use in a specific situation.

expert_reference:
The silhouette coefficient is an internal cluster evaluation measure that does not use class labels. It evaluates whether a point is closer to its own cluster than to the nearest competing cluster by combining both cohesion (compactness) and separation.

For a point x in cluster X, the coefficient is computed using two components. First, a(x) is the average distance from x to the other points in its own cluster, defined as a(x) = (sum of d(x, u) for u in X excluding x) / (|X| - 1). Second, for another cluster Y not equal to X, the average distance from x to the members of Y is defined as bb(x, Y) = (sum of d(x, u) for u in Y) / |Y|. The value b(x) is the smallest average distance to another cluster, defined as b(x) = min over Y in the set of clusters excluding X of bb(x, Y).

The silhouette coefficient for point x is given by the formula: silhouette(x) = (b(x) - a(x)) / max(a(x), b(x)). When a(x) < b(x), the denominator is b(x), and the expression can be written as (b(x) - a(x)) / b(x) = 1 - a(x)/b(x). The value of the silhouette coefficient can vary between -1 and 1. We want the silhouette coefficient to be positive, and for a(x) to be as close to 0 as possible, since the coefficient assumes its maximum value of 1 when a(x) = 0.

The average silhouette coefficient of a cluster is computed by taking the average of the silhouette coefficients of points belonging to the cluster. An overall measure of the goodness of a clustering can be obtained by computing the average silhouette coefficient of all points.

When used with a partitional clustering algorithm such as K-means, the silhouette coefficient tends to decrease until the 'natural' set of clusters is found and start increasing once clusters are being split 'too finely' since separation will suffer and cohesion will not improve much. Thus, these measures can provide a way to determine the number of clusters. However, if the definition of a cluster used by the clustering algorithm differs from that of the cluster evaluation measure, then the set of clusters identified as optimal by the algorithm and validation measure can differ. In addition, if there actually are subclusters that are not separated very well from one another, then methods that incorporate both cohesion and separation may provide only a coarse view of the cluster structure of the data. The silhouette index did well on handling issues such as noise and differing sizes and density, but did not do well on handling arbitrary shapes.
candidate_draft: The silhouette coefficient is an internal cluster evaluation measure that assesses the quality of a clustering by combining both cohesion (compactness) and separation. It is computed for individual points, clusters, and the entire clustering. For a given point, the coefficient compares a(x), the average distance from the point to other points in its own cluster, with b(x), the minimum average distance from the point to points in any other cluster. The value for the point is calculated as (b(x) - a(x)) / max(a(x), b(x)). The resulting value ranges between -1 and 1. A strong cluster is characterized by a wide silhouette profile, where the bars of the cluster form a visual profile of that cluster. The average silhouette coefficient of a cluster is obtained by taking the average of the silhouette coefficients of the points belonging to that cluster. An overall measure of the goodness of a clustering is obtained by computing the average silhouette coefficient of all points. The silhouette coefficient is often used to determine the optimal number of clusters by plotting the average silhouette coefficient against the number of clusters and identifying a distinct peak. This method requires a meaningful pairwise distance matrix and is distinct from external indices that compare clustering to external structures.

expert_reference: For an internal cluster-validity index, statistical significance can be assessed by treating the validity index as a test statistic under a null hypothesis of no cluster structure. The source's first case generates many random data sets with similar overall ranges or properties but without the observed cluster structure, applies the clustering algorithm to each, and accumulates the resulting internal-index values to form a null distribution. The observed value, such as SSE, is then compared with that distribution to estimate how likely such a value would arise by chance.
candidate_draft: Models of Randomness (Approach 1) is a statistical testing procedure used to evaluate the significance of a discovered clustering by comparing it against a null hypothesis that the data contains no cluster structure. The core motivation is that data mining algorithms can find clusters in random data, so a validity measure must distinguish non-random structure from chance. This approach involves generating new instances that lack cluster structure to create a baseline distribution. For example, one can generate many random sets of points having the same range as the original data, apply a clustering algorithm like K-means to each set, and accumulate the distribution of a validity measure such as the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE). The observed clustering is then evaluated against this random distribution to determine if its structure is better than expected by random chance. This method is distinct from supervised measures of cluster validity, which rely on external information, and from internal indices that do not use statistical testing against a random model.

candidate_draft: Models of Randomness (Approach 2) is a statistical testing procedure used in cluster evaluation to assess the significance of a discovered clustering. The core motivation is to determine whether the observed cluster structure reflects non-random structure in the data or if it could have arisen by chance. This approach involves considering the null hypothesis that there is no cluster structure among the instances and that the clustering algorithm is producing a random partitioning of the data. By generating new instances that lack cluster structure (random data), one can evaluate the statistical significance of the cluster validity measure. If the validity measure for the actual data is unusually high (or low) compared to the distribution of measures obtained from random data, it suggests that the clusters reflect genuine non-random structure. This method helps distinguish whether non-random structure actually exists in the data, addressing the issue that data mining algorithms can find clusters in random data just as people find patterns in clouds.

For cluster i, let p_ij = m_ij/m_i be the fraction of objects in cluster i that belong to class j. Its entropy is e_i = -∑_{j=1}^L p_ij log₂ p_ij. candidate_draft: External Index: Entropy is a supervised cluster validity measure that evaluates how well the cluster labels match the external class labels. It is used when external labels are available to assess the goodness of a clustering, distinguishing it from internal measures like SSE that capture cohesion or separation without external labels. The total entropy for a set of clusters is calculated as the sum of the entropies of each cluster weighted by the size of each cluster. The entropy of each individual cluster is calculated using the standard entropy formula based on the class distribution within that cluster, where the number of classes is a parameter in the calculation. This measure is one of several supervised approaches to cluster validity, alongside purity and the Jaccard measure.

candidate_draft:
Purity is a supervised external index used to evaluate the quality of a clustering by measuring how well the resulting clusters align with known class labels. It is a classification-oriented measure that does not require the original feature values of the data points, relying instead solely on the cluster assignments and the true class labels.

The purity of a specific cluster is defined as the fraction of objects in that cluster that belong to the most frequent class within it. Formally, the class probability for class j in cluster i is calculated as pij = mij/mi, where mij is the number of objects of class j in cluster i, and mi is the total number of objects in cluster i. The purity of cluster i is then the maximum of these class probabilities: purity(i) = maxj(pij).

The overall purity of a clustering is computed as a weighted average of the purities of all clusters, where the weight for each cluster is its size relative to the total number of objects. The formula is: purity = Σi (mi/m) purity(i), where m is the total number of objects in the dataset.

In this metric, a purity of 1 indicates a perfect clustering where every cluster contains objects of only one class, while a purity of 0 indicates a completely random or poor clustering. However, purity is not a perfect measure of clustering quality; for instance, if every object is placed into its own singleton cluster, the purity is 1, but this is generally not considered a meaningful clustering. Therefore, high purity does not always imply a good clustering, and it should be interpreted alongside other validity measures.

expert_reference: The Rand Index and Jaccard Coefficient are external validation measures used to evaluate clustering by comparing the discovered cluster structure against an external structure, usually known class labels. They are classified as similarity-oriented measures because they operate by comparing pairs of objects rather than using classification-oriented metrics like purity or F-measure. The key distinction between the two lies in how they handle pairs that are correctly separated in both the class structure and the clustering (denoted as f00). The Rand Index includes these f00 pairs in its calculation, whereas the Jaccard Coefficient ignores f00 and focuses exclusively on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures. In a specific worked example where f00=4, f01=2, f10=2, and f11=2, the Rand statistic is computed as (2+4)/10 = 0.6, and the Jaccard coefficient is computed as 2/(2+2+2) = 0.33. The general methodology for computing these indices involves constructing class similarity and cluster similarity matrices. Additionally, a statistical significance assessment can be performed by generating M randomized sets of labels, computing the external index for each randomization, and defining the p-value as the fraction of randomizations where the index value exceeds the value obtained for the original set of labels.
candidate_draft: The Rand Index and Jaccard coefficient are external cluster evaluation measures used to assess the quality of clustering results. They operate by comparing pairs of points using a class similarity matrix and a cluster similarity matrix. This approach allows for the evaluation of how well the discovered clusters align with the known class labels.

expert_reference: External precision measures what fraction of a particular cluster belongs to a specified external class. For cluster i and class j, precision(i,j) = p_ij = m_ij/m_i, where m_ij is the number of objects of class j in cluster i and m_i is the size of cluster i.
candidate_draft: External Index: Precision is a cluster evaluation measure used to assess the goodness of clusters produced by a clustering algorithm. It is an external index, meaning it requires external labels (ground truth classes) to be available for evaluation; ordinary accuracy is not directly applicable for clustering unless such external labels exist. Precision is calculated for each cluster with respect to a specific class. The precision of cluster i with respect to class j is denoted as precision(i,j) = p_ij. This measure is part of a broader set of external indices that include recall and the F-measure, which can also be calculated for each cluster. The use of precision in this context is distinct from the general statistical concept of precision (related to significant digits and bias) and is specifically tied to the comparison of cluster assignments against known class labels.

expert_reference: Recall is an external index used in cluster evaluation to measure the extent to which a cluster contains all objects of a specified class. It is a classification-oriented measure that assesses how well the discovered clustering structure matches an external structure, typically known class labels. The recall of cluster i with respect to class j is defined by the formula recall(i,j) = m_ij / m_j, where m_j represents the number of objects in class j. This metric is one of several external indices, including purity, precision, F-measure, and similarity-oriented measures like the Rand Index and Jaccard Coefficient, used to evaluate clustering performance against ground truth data.
candidate_draft: Recall is a supervised measure of cluster validity used to evaluate the goodness of clusters produced by a clustering algorithm. In the context of cluster evaluation, the recall of a specific cluster with respect to a specific class is defined as the ratio of the number of objects in the intersection of that cluster and class to the total number of objects in the class. This metric is part of a broader set of evaluation tools, including precision and the F-measure, which are widely used in information retrieval and can be calculated for each cluster to assess performance. The calculation of recall is demonstrated in practical examples where it is computed based on the number of correctly identified positive instances relative to the total number of actual positive instances, yielding values such as 0.200, 0.600, or 1.000 depending on the specific data distribution and clustering outcome.

candidate_draft: The F-measure is a supervised cluster evaluation metric that combines precision and recall to assess the extent to which a cluster contains only objects of a particular class and all objects of that class. It is used to evaluate the quality of clustering results by comparing them against external class labels. For a specific cluster i and class j, the F-measure is calculated as the harmonic mean of precision and recall: F(i,j) = (2 × precision(i,j) × recall(i,j)) / (precision(i,j) + recall(i,j)). In the context of hierarchical clustering, the evaluation process involves computing the F-measure for each cluster in the hierarchy for every class, selecting the maximum F-measure attained for any cluster for each class, and then computing an overall F-measure as the weighted average of these per-class maximums, where the weights are based on class sizes. This approach is specifically designed to evaluate whether a hierarchical clustering contains, for each class, at least one cluster that is relatively pure and includes most of the objects of that class. The F-measure serves as an external index, distinguishing it from internal indices that measure clustering quality without using external information.

expert_reference: A dendrogram is a tree-like diagram used to graphically display hierarchical clustering. It visualizes both the cluster-subcluster relationships and the order in which clusters were merged (agglomerative view) or split (divisive view). In the diagram, the vertical height at which two clusters are merged reflects the distance between those two clusters. For example, if the distance between two points is 0.11, they are joined at a height of 0.11 in the dendrogram. Hierarchical clustering is sometimes used to generate K clusters by taking the clusters at the K-th level of the dendrogram, where the root is at level 1. This allows for the evaluation of hierarchical clustering behavior and comparison with K-means. If a final flat clustering is desired, the dendrogram must be cut at a specific level. When drawing a dendrogram by hand, the exact horizontal spacing does not matter, but the vertical merge heights and nested structure are critical. The leaf order must match the nested structure exactly, though branches can be flipped left-to-right. The dendrogram is distinct from the linkage criteria (such as single link, complete link, or group average) used to calculate the distances that determine the merge heights.

For example, if the distance between two points is 0.11, they are joined at a height of 0.11 in the dendrogram. A dendrogram should clearly show the order in which points are merged. Hierarchical clustering is often used to generate a specific number of clusters (K) by taking the clusters at a particular level of the dendrogram. By examining the clusters produced at different levels, one can evaluate the behavior of hierarchical clustering on different types of data and compare hierarchical approaches to other methods like K-means. The dendrogram is a standard output for agglomerative hierarchical clustering, which is a common category of clustering methods.

expert_reference: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering is a bottom-up method that produces a hierarchical clustering by starting with each point as a singleton cluster and repeatedly merging the two closest clusters until a single, all-encompassing cluster remains or a stopping rule is reached. This approach is a collection of closely related techniques where the definition of cluster similarity depends on the particular algorithm used. Some agglomerative algorithms, such as group average, base their notion of similarity on the strength of the connections between the two clusters (e.g., the pairwise similarity of points in the two clusters), while other techniques, such as the single link method, use the closeness of the clusters (e.g., the minimum distance between points in different clusters) to measure cluster similarity. The single-linkage distance is defined as the minimum distance between any point in one cluster and any point in the other: d_single(C_i, C_j) = min_{x∈C_i, y∈C_j} d(x, y). Other merging strategies include the centroid method, which merges the clusters with the closest centroids, and Ward's method, which is a greedy bottom-up clustering using the K-means SSE objective to merge the two clusters that result in the smallest increase in total SSE. Agglomerative clustering is distinct from divisive clustering, which splits clusters downward; in contrast, agglomerative clustering merges clusters upward. A key limitation of agglomerative hierarchical clustering is that it can never separate objects that have been wrongly put together, meaning it will only compound errors if the initial partitioning or merging decisions are incorrect. Additionally, if the data is very large, an agglomerative hierarchical clustering technique cannot be directly applied, often necessitating the use of divisive techniques or other methods like BIRCH that do not require all data to be in main memory.
candidate_draft: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering is a bottom-up method that produces a hierarchical clustering by starting with each point as a singleton cluster and then repeatedly merging the two closest clusters until a single, all-encompassing cluster remains. This approach is a second important category of clustering methods, distinct from partitional clustering, and is by far the most common type of hierarchical clustering. The key operation of the algorithm is the computation of the proximity between two clusters; it is the definition of cluster proximity that differentiates the various agglomerative hierarchical techniques. Agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithms tend to make good local decisions about combining two clusters because they can use information about the pairwise similarity of all points. The resulting hierarchical clustering is a set of nested clusters organized as a tree, which is often displayed graphically using a tree-like diagram called a dendrogram. This dendrogram displays both the cluster-subcluster relationships and the order in which the clusters were merged. A hierarchical clustering can also be viewed as a sequence of partitional clusterings, where a partitional clustering can be obtained by taking any member of that sequence. Agglomerative clustering is distinguished from divisive hierarchical clustering, which is a top-down method that splits clusters. While divisive approaches have also received some attention, agglomerative hierarchical clustering is the focus of most work in the area of hierarchical clustering.

expert_reference: Divisive hierarchical clustering is a top-down method that begins with all objects in a single cluster and repeatedly splits clusters into smaller clusters until singleton clusters or a stopping rule is reached. This approach is distinguished from agglomerative clustering, which merges clusters upward, by its downward splitting mechanism. Divisive clustering can be useful if the top-level split is meaningful or if a good splitter is available. One specific divisive hierarchical technique is the minimum spanning tree (MST) algorithm, which starts with the minimum spanning tree of the proximity graph and can be viewed as an application of sparsification for finding clusters; this algorithm produces the same clustering as single link agglomerative clustering. Divisive clustering is often considered when data is very large and agglomerative techniques cannot be directly applied, though the MST algorithm only works if the data set is not too large. Bisecting K-means is another divisive technique that works for many data sets, but it runs into problems if the data set is large enough that it cannot be contained completely in memory. In such large-scale situations, a technique such as BIRCH, which does not require that all data be in main memory, becomes more useful. The choice of clustering algorithm is often determined by the need to create a hierarchical clustering that extends only to the point of splitting data into a few hundred clusters rather than a complete hierarchy to individual objects.
candidate_draft: Divisive hierarchical clustering is a top-down method that operates by splitting clusters downward. It is one of two basic approaches for generating a hierarchical clustering, the other being agglomerative (bottom-up) clustering, which merges clusters. In divisive clustering, the process involves repeatedly splitting clusters, and the result depends strongly on the definition of the cluster split. A complete divisive clustering method requires a splitting rule to determine how the chosen cluster should be divided. This approach is useful when the top-level split is meaningful or when a good splitter is available. Specific examples of divisive hierarchical techniques include DIANA, a standard method found in the R cluster package, and MST, which starts with the minimum spanning tree of the proximity graph. Another technique, PDDP, is based on finding the first principal direction of the data. The resulting hierarchical structure is often displayed graphically using a dendrogram, which shows the cluster-subcluster relationships and the order in which the clusters were split.

expert_reference:
MIN (Single Linkage) is a linkage criterion used in hierarchical clustering to define the proximity between two clusters. The proximity of two clusters is defined as the minimum of the distance (or the maximum of the similarity) between any two points in the two different clusters. Formally, the distance between two clusters Ci and Cj is given by the formula: dsingle(Ci, Cj) = min d(x, y), where the minimum is taken over all pairs x in Ci and y in Cj. In this formula, dsingle(Ci, Cj) represents the single-linkage distance between clusters Ci and Cj, d(x, y) is the distance between individual points x and y, and the minimization is performed over all x in Ci and y in Cj.

The single-linkage technique operates by starting with all points as singleton clusters and adding links between points one at a time, shortest links first, which combines the points into clusters. This method is characterized by the "nearest bridge" intuition, meaning two clusters are considered close if at least one point in one cluster is close to at least one point in the other cluster. In terms of implementation, single linkage can use a precomputed distance matrix; the original point-distance matrix is computed once, and after a merge, the current matrix is updated using the minimum value.

The single-linkage technique is good at handling non-elliptical shapes, but it is sensitive to noise and outliers. It is distinct from complete linkage, which uses the farthest cross-pair, and centroid linkage, which uses the cluster centers.
candidate_draft: MIN, also known as single link or single linkage, is a specific agglomerative hierarchical clustering technique. It is distinguished from other agglomerative methods by its definition of cluster proximity: the proximity of two clusters is defined as the minimum of the distance (or the maximum of the similarity) between any two points in the two different clusters. In graph-theoretic terms, this corresponds to the shortest edge between two nodes in different subsets of nodes. In the basic agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithm, this proximity measure is used to repeatedly combine the two closest clusters until a single, all-encompassing cluster remains. The resulting hierarchical clustering is often displayed graphically using a tree-like structure, such as a dendrogram. In comparative evaluations, the hierarchical clustering produced by the single link technique has been observed to fit the data less well than the clusterings produced by complete link, group average, and Ward's method. The minimum spanning tree (MST) algorithm is noted as the divisive analog to single link, though it is restricted to data sets that are not too large.

expert_reference: MAX (Complete Linkage) is a version of hierarchical clustering in which the proximity of two clusters is defined as the maximum of the distance (or the minimum of the similarity) between any two points in the two different clusters. In graph terminology, if one starts with all points as singleton clusters and adds links between points one at a time, shortest links first, a group of points is not considered a cluster until all the points in it are completely linked, meaning they form a clique. This method is less susceptible to noise and outliers, but it can break large clusters and it favors globular shapes. The distance calculation is demonstrated by the formula d_complete({A, B}, C) = max(2, 1) = 2, where the distance between the cluster {A, B} and point C is the maximum of the individual distances. Another example is d_complete({A, B, C, D}, E) = max(4, 3, 2, 1) = 4. The procedure for complete linkage involves computing the original point-distance matrix once, and after a merge, updating the current matrix using the maximum value. Complete linkage says two clusters are close only if even the farthest cross-cluster pair is not too far. This contrasts with single linkage, which uses the nearest bridge, and centroid linkage, which uses the cluster centers.
candidate_draft: MAX (Complete Linkage) is a specific agglomerative hierarchical clustering technique that determines the proximity between two clusters by taking the maximum of the distance (or the minimum of the similarity) between any two points located in the two different clusters. In graph-based terms, this corresponds to selecting the longest edge between two nodes in different subsets of nodes. This definition of cluster proximity is the primary factor that differentiates MAX from other agglomerative hierarchical clustering methods, such as MIN (Single Linkage) or Group Average, which use different criteria to compute the distance between clusters. Because the algorithm relies on the farthest cross-pair to define cluster proximity, it tends to produce more compact, spherical clusters and is often observed to fit data better than single-linkage clustering, which can suffer from chaining effects. The method operates within the broader framework of agglomerative hierarchical clustering, where the algorithm repeatedly merges the two closest clusters until a single, all-encompassing cluster remains. The choice of MAX as the linkage rule is a critical decision in the clustering process, as it directly influences the shape and structure of the resulting hierarchical clustering.

expert_reference: Group Average Linkage is a graph-based agglomerative clustering technique that defines the proximity between two clusters as the average of the pairwise proximities (or average length of edges) of all pairs of points from different clusters. This approach bases its notion of similarity on the strength of the connections between the two clusters, such as the pairwise similarity of points, rather than relying solely on the closeness of the clusters measured by the minimum distance between points. In a full agglomerative clustering run, the distance between two specified clusters is calculated as one candidate distance, which must be compared with all other current cluster-pair distances before choosing a merge. The weighted version of group average, known as WPGMA, uses coefficients that are constants independent of cluster sizes, specifically alpha_A = 1/2, alpha_B = 1/2, beta = 0, and gamma = 0. General unweighted approaches are preferred unless there is reason to believe that individual points should have different weights. For clustering approaches like group average, outliers are potentially less problematic because they tend to form singleton or small clusters that do not merge with other clusters until much later in the merging process, allowing them to be removed by discarding these small clusters.

Ward's method is a greedy bottom-up hierarchical clustering technique that uses the same objective function as K-means clustering: minimizing the sum of squared errors (SSE). In this approach, each cluster is represented by its centroid, and the proximity between two clusters is defined as the increase in the total SSE that results from merging them. The algorithm proceeds by repeatedly evaluating all possible merges of existing clusters, computing the total SSE after each candidate merge, and selecting the merge that causes the smallest increase in total SSE. This process builds a hierarchy of clusters until all points are merged into a single cluster.

The SSE for a cluster C is defined as the sum of the squared distances of its points from the cluster centroid: SSE(C) = Σ ||x - μ_C||², where x is a point in C and μ_C is the centroid of C. The total SSE across all clusters is the sum of the individual cluster SSEs: SSE_total = SSE(C₁) + SSE(C₂) + ... + SSE(Cₖ).

Ward's method is distinct from centroid linkage, which also uses centroids but defines cluster proximity as the distance between centroids rather than the increase in SSE. Ward's method is mathematically similar to the group average method when the proximity between two points is taken to be the square of the distance between them. However, Ward's method is the correct hierarchical analog of K-means, as it directly optimizes the same SSE objective.

A key limitation of Ward's method is that once a merge is made, it cannot be undone, which prevents a local optimization criterion from becoming a global one. The clusters at each level do not represent local minima with respect to the total SSE, and a point in one cluster can be closer to the centroid of another cluster than to its own. Despite this, Ward's method is often used as a robust method for initializing K-means clustering. Outliers pose the most serious problems for Ward's method because they increase SSE and distort centroids, whereas in methods like single link, complete link, and group average, outliers tend to form singleton clusters that can be discarded.

expert_reference: Hierarchical clustering complexity refers to the computational and storage requirements of agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithms, which are defined by their use of a proximity matrix and iterative merging of clusters. The total space complexity is O(m²), where m is the number of data points, because the algorithm must store the proximities between all pairs of points (assuming a symmetric matrix) and track the state of the clusters. The time complexity is O(m² log m) when using a sorted list or heap to optimize the search for the two closest clusters; without such optimization, the time complexity is higher due to linear searches over the proximity matrix. These complexity bounds severely limit the size of data sets that can be processed directly, making the algorithm impractical for large-scale applications. The high computational cost arises because the general clustering problem is computationally infeasible to solve exactly, and the local merging strategy, while avoiding hard combinatorial optimization, still incurs significant overhead. Scalable alternatives, such as bisecting K-means or graph sparsification techniques, are often used to address these limitations by reducing the effective number of points or partitions before applying hierarchical methods.

Scalability approaches for clustering algorithms, including hierarchical clustering techniques, are discussed to address these limitations. A linear time hierarchical clustering algorithm has also been proposed to improve efficiency. The complexity of hierarchical clustering is a key factor in determining the appropriateness of the algorithm for a particular clustering task.

expert_reference: K-Means is a partitional clustering algorithm that directly divides data into K clusters, where K is a user-specified parameter representing the desired number of clusters. Each cluster is represented by a centroid, which is the representative centre of the cluster. For Euclidean K-Means, the centroid is defined as the mean of all points in the cluster; it is a mean position and does not have to be one of the original data points. If a cluster C_i contains m_i points, the centroid c_i is calculated as the mean of the points in that cluster: c_i = (1/m_i) * Σ_{x ∈ C_i} x. In two-dimensional space, this is expressed as c_i = (Σx/m_i, Σy/m_i). The algorithm operates by repeatedly assigning each point to the nearest centroid and then updating each centroid as the mean of the points assigned to it. This process of assignment and update is repeated until the assignments or centroids stop changing. K-Means is a centroid-based algorithm, and its behavior is characterized by the use of centroid-based cohesion and separation. The algorithm is simple and is guaranteed to converge for a number of choices of proximity function, centroid, and objective function. However, random initialization is often used, which is simple but can result in a clustering that represents a local minimum in terms of the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE).
candidate_draft: K-Means is a simple, centroid-based, partitional clustering algorithm that divides a data set into K clusters. It is one of the oldest and most widely used clustering techniques, and it is a prototype-based method that uses the centroid of the objects in a cluster as the prototype of the cluster. The basic procedure involves choosing initial centroids, which is considered the key step, and then assigning each point to the nearest centroid and recomputing centroids as means. The algorithm can be viewed as an optimization problem, and there are a number of choices for the proximity function, centroid, and objective function that can be used in the basic K-means algorithm and that are guaranteed to converge. The K-means algorithm has a long history, but is still the subject of current research. It is simple and can be used for a wide variety of data types. The K-means algorithm was named by MacQueen, although its history is more extensive. The K-means algorithm has a time complexity, but the specific value is not provided in the evidence. The K-means algorithm can be applied to a variety of different objective functions, such as minimizing the sum of the Manhattan distances of points from the center of their clusters. The K-means algorithm is distinct from K-medoid, which is another prominent clustering technique. The K-means algorithm is also distinct from hierarchical clustering algorithms, which are a different type of clustering technique. The K-means algorithm is also distinct from fuzzy clustering, which is a different type of clustering technique. The K-means algorithm is also distinct from DBSCAN, which is another clustering algorithm. The K-means algorithm is also distinct from Ward's method, which is similar to K-means but is the correct method for a different type of clustering. The K-means algorithm is also distinct from the K-means++ initialization approach, which is a specific initialization method for K-means. The K-means algorithm is also distinct from the K-means clustering imputation method, which is a specific application of K-means for imputing missing values. The K-means algorithm is also distinct from the fuzzy K-means clustering method, which is a specific variant of K-means. The K-means algorithm is also distinct from the parallel K-means clustering method, which is a specific implementation of K-means. The K-means algorithm is also distinct from the K-means clustering with background knowledge method, which is a specific variant of K-means.
