expert_reference: An ensemble classifier is a method that constructs a set of base classifiers from training data and performs classification by taking a vote on the predictions made by each base classifier. The base classifiers are often individually imperfect, but their combined decision can be more robust. For classification, a common combination rule is majority voting, where the final prediction is determined by the majority of the individual predictions. An alternate approach is to take a weighted majority vote, where the weight of a base classifier denotes its accuracy or relevance. The ensemble classifier predicts the class label of a test example by taking a majority vote on the predictions made by the base classifiers. If the base classifiers are identical, then all the base classifiers will commit the same mistakes, and the error rate of the ensemble remains the same as the individual classifiers. On the other hand, if the base classifiers are independent—i.e., their errors are uncorrelated—then the ensemble makes a wrong prediction only if more than half of the base classifiers predict incorrectly. In this case, the error rate of the ensemble classifier is lower than that of the individual classifiers. The ensemble classifier performs worse than the base classifiers when the base classifier error rate is larger than 0.5. Two necessary conditions for an ensemble classifier to perform better than a single classifier are: (1) the base classifiers should be independent of each other, and (2) the base classifiers should do better than a classifier that performs random guessing. In practice, it is difficult to ensure total independence among the base classifiers, but improvements in classification accuracies have been observed in ensemble methods in which the base classifiers are somewhat correlated. The ensemble of classifiers can be constructed in many ways, including by manipulating the training set, where multiple training sets are created by resampling the original data according to some sampling distribution and constructing a classifier from each training set. Bagging and boosting are two examples of ensemble methods that manipulate their training sets. The base classifiers for most of these approaches can be generated sequentially (one after another) or in parallel (all at once). Once an ensemble of classifiers has been learned, a test example is classified by combining the predictions made by the base classifiers. The final prediction of the ensemble classifier is obtained by taking a weighted average of the predictions made by each base classifier. The ensemble classifier can also enhance the representation of the target function; even though each base classifier is a decision stump, combining the classifiers can lead to a decision boundary that mimics a decision tree of depth 2. The ensemble classifier is a general method that can be applied to any classifier, and it is used to improve the performance of a single classifier by combining the predictions of multiple base classifiers.
candidate_draft: An ensemble classifier is a method that constructs a set of base classifiers from training data and performs classification by combining the predictions made by each base classifier. The final prediction is typically obtained by taking a majority vote or a weighted average of the individual predictions. Ensemble methods tend to perform better than any single classifier, showing the most improvement when used with unstable classifiers that are sensitive to minor perturbations in the training set. By aggregating the responses of multiple unstable classifiers, ensemble learning attempts to minimize their variance without worsening their bias. The ensemble of classifiers can be constructed in many ways, including bagging and boosting. Improvements in classification accuracies have been observed in ensemble methods even when the base classifiers are somewhat correlated. However, the ensemble classifier may perform worse than the base classifiers under certain conditions, such as when the base classifier error rate is larger than 0.5. The ensemble is strongest when the base classifiers are diverse and accurate.

expert_reference: Majority voting is a combination rule used in ensemble classification to derive a single final prediction from the outputs of multiple base classifiers. In this approach, each base classifier predicts a class label for a given instance, and the final prediction is the class that receives the most votes. This method is particularly common in random forests, where the final prediction is obtained by majority voting over the individual decision trees. The ensemble is strongest when the individual trees are reasonably accurate and their errors are not perfectly correlated, as this diversity helps reduce the high variance associated with single decision trees. A weighted majority vote is an alternative approach where the weight of a base classifier denotes its accuracy or relevance, but in standard majority voting, every vote has equal impact. In the context of k-nearest neighbors, majority voting assigns the test instance to the majority class of its nearest neighbors, with ties potentially resolved by random choice. The procedure involves sending a test instance through all base classifiers or trees and combining their predictions using this voting mechanism.
candidate_draft: Majority voting is a combination rule used in ensemble classification to determine the final prediction by taking a majority vote on the predictions made by each base classifier. In this approach, an ensemble method constructs a set of base classifiers from training data and performs classification by aggregating their individual outputs. For binary classification problems where class labels are either -1 or +1, taking the majority vote is equivalent to summing up the predicted values of y and examining the sign of the resulting sum. This method is a common combination rule for classification tasks, such as in random forests, where the final prediction is obtained by majority voting over the trees. The rationale for using majority voting is that if the models make different mistakes, the majority vote can be more reliable than a single model, and ensemble classifiers generally outperform a single decision tree classifier on many data sets. An alternate approach to simple majority voting is a weighted majority vote, where the weight of a base classifier denotes its accuracy or relevance, but the standard majority voting scheme treats each classifier's prediction equally in the vote count.

expert_reference: A random forest is an ensemble of decision trees, where each tree is trained using randomness so that the trees are not all identical. The method manipulates both the training instances and the input features to create diversity among the base classifiers. The training data is represented as a set of instances D = {(x1, y1), (x2, y2), ..., (xN, yN)}. The induction process for each tree b = 1, 2, ..., B involves drawing a bootstrap sample Db from the original training set by sampling N instances with replacement. A decision tree is then trained on Db, often grown deeply and without heavy pruning, meaning the trees are unpruned and allowed to grow until every leaf is pure. At every split, the tree considers only a random subset of features and chooses the best split from that subset. The number of attributes to be selected at every node, p, is a hyper-parameter of the random forest classifier. For classification, the final prediction is made by combining the trees using majority voting: ŷ = majority{h1(x), h2(x), ..., hB(x)}, where x is the test instance, hb is the b-th base classifier, and ŷ is the final ensemble prediction. The two main random components are bootstrap sampling of instances and random feature selection at each split. This approach reduces the variance of the trees without negatively impacting their low bias, making random forests robust to overfitting and computationally fast even in high-dimensional settings.
candidate_draft: Random forest is an ensemble method that uses decision trees as its base classifiers. It is designed to improve generalization performance by constructing an ensemble of decorrelated decision trees. The method was introduced by Breiman. Random forests build on the idea of bagging by using a different bootstrap sample of the training data for learning each decision tree. Additionally, random forests manipulate the input attributes by using different subsets of attributes at every internal node. This dual manipulation of training instances and input features distinguishes random forests from simple bagging. The base classifiers in a random forest are typically unstable classifiers that have low bias but high variance due to their large size. By aggregating the predictions of these strong and decorrelated decision trees, random forests reduce the variance of the trees without negatively impacting their low bias. Another property of the base classifiers is the lack of correlation among their model parameters and test predictions. For classification, the final random-forest prediction is obtained by majority voting over the trees. Random forests often grow trees deeply and rely on ensemble averaging or voting to control overfitting. Empirically, random forests have been found to provide significant improvements in generalization performance that are often comparable, if not superior, to the improvements provided by the AdaBoost algorithm. Because of their ability to consider only a small subset of attributes at every internal node, random forests are computationally fast and robust even in high-dimensional settings.

expert_reference: Boosting is an iterative ensemble procedure that adaptively changes the distribution of training examples so that base classifiers increasingly focus on examples that are hard to classify. Unlike bagging, boosting assigns a weight to each training example and may adaptively change the weight at the end of each boosting round. The algorithm begins by assigning equal weights to all examples, then draws a sample according to the sampling distribution to obtain a new training set. A classifier is built from this training set and used to classify all examples in the original data. At the end of each boosting round, the weights of the training examples are updated: examples that are classified incorrectly have their weights increased, while those classified correctly have their weights decreased. As the boosting rounds proceed, examples that are the hardest to classify tend to become even more prevalent in the sampling distribution. The final ensemble is obtained by aggregating the base classifiers obtained from each boosting round. In the AdaBoost implementation, the prediction made by each classifier is weighted rather than using a majority voting scheme, which allows the algorithm to penalize models that have poor accuracy. If any intermediate round produces an error rate higher than 50%, the weights are reverted back to their original uniform values and the resampling procedure is repeated. The training error of the ensemble decreases exponentially, leading to fast convergence, although the technique can be susceptible to overfitting due to its tendency to focus on wrongly classified examples.
candidate_draft: Boosting is an iterative procedure used to adaptively change the distribution of training examples for learning base classifiers so that they increasingly focus on examples that are hard to classify. By repeating this process multiple times, an ensemble of base classifiers is obtained, and the final prediction is made by aggregating the base classifiers obtained from each boosting round. An important analytical result of boosting shows that the training error of the ensemble is bounded by a specific expression, though the exact mathematical formula is not provided in the supplied evidence. AdaBoost, a variant of the boosting algorithm based on adaptive resampling and combining, has been shown to provide significant improvements in performance over base classifiers on a range of data sets. However, boosting algorithms have limitations, particularly regarding rare class modeling. In empirical comparisons, ensemble classifiers generally outperform a single decision tree classifier, with random forests often providing improvements comparable to or superior to those provided by AdaBoost.

expert_reference: The class imbalance problem is a practical issue in classification where the training set has an unbalanced representation of classes, typically with a minority class that is not well-represented. This imbalance poses two challenges for classification: first, many classification methods work well only when the training set has a balanced representation of both classes, and second, a classifier trained over an imbalanced data set shows a bias toward improving its performance over the majority class, which is often not the desired behavior. In the context of binary classification, the minority class is referred to as the positive class, while the majority class is referred to as the negative class. The problem is particularly relevant in model evaluation, where detection rate and false alarm rate are metrics that are not sensitive to skewness in the class distribution. In the presence of class imbalance, the behavior of an algorithm over small false positive rate values (also termed as early retrieval) is often more meaningful for comparison than the performance over all false positive rate values. This is because, in many applications, it is important to assess the true positive rate achieved by a classifier in the first few instances with highest scores, without incurring a large false positive rate. The precision-recall (PR) curve is an alternate approach for measuring the aggregate performance of a classifier, which is especially useful in the presence of class imbalance. The PR curve generally helps to magnify the differences between classifiers in the left portion of the PR curve, providing a deeper insight into the performance of classifiers than the ROC curves, especially in the early retrieval range of operating points.
candidate_draft: The Class Imbalance Problem is a data-related issue in classification where the degree of imbalance between classes varies across different applications and even across different data sets from the same application. This problem poses two primary challenges for classification. First, many existing classification models, when trained on an imbalanced data set, may not effectively detect instances of the rare class. Although some classifiers are more effective at handling imbalance in the training data than others, such as rule-based classifiers and k-NN, they are all impacted if the minority class is not well-represented in the training set. Second, accuracy, which is the traditional measure for evaluating classification performance, is not well-suited for evaluating models in the presence of class imbalance in the test data. Consequently, there are two primary considerations for building classifiers in the presence of class imbalance in the training set: first, presenting generic methods for building classifiers when there is class imbalance in the training set, and second, having learned a classification model, finding a way to adapt its classification decisions to best match the requirements of the imbalanced test set. Various alternative metrics that are well-suited for class imbalanced problems are available, including the precision-recall (PR) curve, which is especially useful in the presence of class imbalance. The precision-recall plot is more informative than the ROC plot when evaluating binary classifiers on imbalanced datasets. Statistical testing procedures for classification are directly relevant for avoiding false discoveries in supervised anomaly detection, with the additional challenge of building a model for imbalanced classes. In particular, the classification error metric used during statistical testing must be sensitive to the imbalance among the classes and give enough emphasis to the errors related to the rare anomaly class (false positives and false negatives).

expert_reference: Oversampling is a technique used to create a balanced training set by artificially generating new positive examples to address class imbalance. A simple approach involves duplicating every positive instance a specific number of times, where the duplication factor is determined by the ratio of the number of negative training instances to the number of positive training instances. This duplication method is analogous to doubling the weight of positive instances during the training stage, an effect that can alternatively be achieved by assigning higher weights to positive instances than negative instances, a method compatible with classifiers such as logistic regression, artificial neural networks, and support vector machines. However, a limitation of the duplication method is that replicated positive examples have an artificially lower variance compared to their true distribution, which can bias the classifier to the specific distribution of training instances and lead to poor generalizability. To overcome this limitation, the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) generates synthetic positive instances in the neighborhood of existing positive instances. The SMOTE procedure first determines the k-nearest positive neighbors of every positive instance, then generates a synthetic positive instance at some intermediate point along the line segment joining the instance to one of its randomly chosen k-nearest neighbors. This process is repeated until the desired number of positive instances is reached. A limitation of SMOTE is that it can only generate new positive instances within the convex hull of the existing positive class, meaning it does not improve the representation of the positive class outside the boundary of existing positive instances. Despite their complementary strengths and weaknesses, undersampling and oversampling provide useful directions for generating balanced training sets in the presence of class imbalance.
candidate_draft: Oversampling (SMOTE) is a technique for addressing class imbalance in training data by artificially generating new positive examples to create a balanced training set. This approach is distinct from undersampling, which reduces the frequency of the majority class to match the minority class. The specific method known as the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) operates by first determining the k-nearest positive neighbors of every positive instance. It then generates a synthetic positive instance at some intermediate point along the line segment joining a positive instance to one of its randomly chosen k-nearest neighbors. This technique is used to ensure that classification models can effectively detect instances of the rare class, which they may fail to do when trained on imbalanced data sets where the minority class is not well-represented.

expert_reference: Undersampling is a sampling method used to create balanced training sets in the presence of class imbalance by reducing the frequency of the majority class to match the frequency of the minority class. This approach is one of two primary strategies for ensuring that a learning algorithm is trained over a data set with adequate representation of both the majority and minority classes, the other being oversampling. To illustrate the procedure, consider a training set containing 100 positive examples and 1000 negative examples. To overcome the skew among the classes, a random sample of 100 examples is selected from the negative class and used with the 100 positive examples to create a balanced training set. Despite its utility, undersampling has specific limitations. One limitation is that some useful negative examples, particularly those closer to the actual decision boundary, may not be chosen for training, which can result in an inferior classification model. Another limitation is that the smaller sample of negative instances may have a higher variance than the larger original set. Undersampling and oversampling provide complementary directions for generating balanced training sets, each with distinct strengths and weaknesses.
candidate_draft: Undersampling is a sampling-based method used to address class imbalance in training data by reducing the frequency of the majority class to match the frequency of the minority class. This technique is one of two primary approaches for generating balanced training sets, the other being oversampling, which creates artificial examples of the minority class. The goal of undersampling is to ensure that the minority class is well-represented in the training set, as many classification models may fail to effectively detect instances of the rare class when trained on imbalanced data. A key limitation of undersampling is that it may discard useful negative examples, particularly those closer to the actual decision boundary, which can result in an inferior classification model. For example, in a training set with 100 positive and 1000 negative examples, undersampling would reduce the number of negative examples to match the positive count. Despite this limitation, undersampling remains a useful direction for handling class imbalance, especially when combined with other methods or when the majority class contains redundant information.

expert_reference: A cost matrix assigns a cost or benefit to each possible classification outcome, such as false negative, false positive, true positive, and true negative. The expected cost of a model is the probability-weighted sum of these outcome costs: C(M) = P(FN)c_FN + P(FP)c_FP + P(TP)c_TP + P(TN)c_TN. When costs are the decision criterion, models or operating points are compared by their expected cost and lower expected cost is preferred.
candidate_draft: A cost matrix is a tool used to evaluate cost-sensitive decision quality by accounting for the real consequences of different types of decisions. In the context of class imbalance, it is especially useful because it allows for the assessment of models where classes are not equally important. The best model is defined as the one that minimizes expected cost under the given cost matrix. This approach is distinct from standard accuracy-based evaluation, which may not reflect the relative costs of misclassified instances. The properties of a cost matrix have been studied in the context of incorporating cost information into learning algorithms, such as C4.5, through methods like wrapper methods, class distribution-based methods, and loss-based methods. Cost-sensitive learning can also be achieved through cost-proportionate example weighting, which trades off the relative costs of misclassified instances and the model. The cost matrix provides a framework for evaluating classification performance when the cost of errors varies by class, making it a critical component in handling imbalanced data sets.

expert_reference: Cost-Sensitive Classification is an approach to model evaluation and learning that accounts for the differing consequences of misclassification errors. It is motivated by the need for evaluation metrics that are sensitive to class skew and capture performance criteria beyond simple accuracy. The method involves evaluating decision quality using a cost matrix, where the choice of a model is determined by minimizing the expected cost. In a specific evaluation context, a model was selected based on having the lowest expected cost of 0.390. The foundations of this area include the study of cost matrix properties and various methods for incorporating cost information into learning algorithms, such as wrapper methods, class distribution-based methods, and loss-based methods. Algorithm-independent methods include AdaCost, MetaCost, and costing. Cost-sensitive boosting is also a recognized technique in this domain.
candidate_draft: Cost-Sensitive Classification is a method for building classifiers when there is class imbalance in the training set. It is one of the generic methods for handling imbalanced data sets, alongside sampling-based methods and alternative evaluation metrics. The approach involves incorporating cost information into the learning algorithm, such as through wrapper methods, class distribution-based methods, and loss-based methods. Algorithm-independent cost-sensitive learning methods include AdaCost, MetaCost, and costing. Cost-sensitive classification is particularly relevant when the classes are not equally important, and it helps address the issue that many existing classification models may not effectively detect instances of the rare class when trained on an imbalanced data set. The method is used to adapt classification decisions to best match the requirements of the imbalanced test set, ensuring that the classifier is appropriately tuned for the specific problem at hand.

expert_reference: RIPPER is a widely-used rule induction algorithm that implements a direct method for generating classification rules directly from data, distinguishing it from indirect methods that derive rules from decision trees. It is designed to work well with noisy data by using a validation set to prevent model overfitting. The algorithm typically employs a sequential covering scheme to induce rules. After generating a rule, RIPPER eliminates all positive and negative examples covered by that rule. The rule is added to the rule set provided it does not violate specific stopping conditions. One stopping condition is based on the minimum description length principle: if a new rule increases the total description length of the rule set by at least d bits, RIPPER stops adding rules; by default, d is chosen to be 64 bits. Another stopping condition requires that the error rate of the rule on the validation set must not exceed 50%. RIPPER also prunes rules to improve generalization errors based on their performance on the validation set. Pruning is done starting from the last conjunct added to the rule, removing a conjunct if a specific metric improves after pruning. This metric is monotonically related to the rule's accuracy on the validation set and involves the number of positive and negative examples in the validation set covered by the rule. While the original rule covers only positive examples, the pruned rule may cover some negative examples in the training set.
candidate_draft: RIPPER is a widely used rule induction algorithm that implements a direct method for generating classification rules directly from data. It operates by using the sequential covering algorithm to extract rules, a scheme typical of direct methods for rule-based classifiers. The algorithm begins with an empty decision list and extracts rules for each class based on an ordering specified by class prevalence. This class-based ordering strategy emphasizes giving higher priority to rare classes, making RIPPER particularly well suited for handling training data sets with imbalanced class distributions. In terms of performance, RIPPER scales almost linearly with the number of training instances. While rule-based classifiers generally produce descriptive models that are easier to interpret than decision trees, RIPPER's specific mechanism for prioritizing rare classes distinguishes it as a specialized approach for imbalanced data.

expert_reference: A receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots the true positive rate (TPR) on the y-axis against the false positive rate (FPR) on the x-axis as the classifier's score threshold is varied. Each point is an operating point corresponding to a particular threshold. The curve begins at (0,0) when every instance is predicted negative and ends at (1,1) when every instance is predicted positive; a perfect classifier reaches (FPR=0, TPR=1). Random guessing lies on the main diagonal: if an instance is predicted positive with fixed probability p irrespective of its attributes, then TPR = FPR = p, so the operating point is (p,p).
candidate_draft: The ROC curve, or receiver operating characteristic curve, is a graphical approach for displaying the trade-off between the true positive rate (TPR) and the false positive rate (FPR) of a classifier over varying score thresholds. It serves as a widely used tool for aggregate evaluation, facilitating the comparison of classifiers across a range of operating points. The basic approach for generating an ROC curve involves sorting the predictions according to their score values and then plotting the TPR and FPR for every possible value of the score threshold. Because the TPR monotonically increases with the FPR, the resulting curve exhibits a staircase pattern. A key characteristic of ROC curves is that they are agnostic to the skew in the test set, as both TPR and FPR are invariant to class imbalance. Consequently, the same ROC curve is obtained for two test sets with different class distributions but the same underlying classifier performance. A random classifier, which performs random guessing, resides at the point (p, p) along the main diagonal of the ROC curve, where p is the proportion of positive instances. A better ROC curve is closer to the top-left corner, indicating high TPR and low FPR. While the area under the ROC curve (AUC) is a common summary measure, a higher AUC does not guarantee that one classifier is always better than another, as ROC curves may intersect. Therefore, care must be taken when comparing AUC values, and visualizing the ROC curves is often preferred. The ROC curve does not automatically define the optimal threshold; rather, it provides hints, and a common heuristic is to choose the point closest to (0, 1). In the presence of class imbalance, precision-recall (PR) curves may provide deeper insight into classifier performance, especially in the early retrieval range of operating points, compared to ROC curves.

expert_reference: ROC space uses FPR on the x-axis and TPR on the y-axis. The point (0,0) represents predicting every instance as negative, (1,1) represents predicting every instance as positive, and (0,1) represents a perfect classifier with no false positives and all positives detected. Good operating points lie toward the upper-left corner, while random guessing lies on the diagonal from (0,0) to (1,1).
candidate_draft: ROC Space (TPR vs. FPR) is the two-dimensional coordinate system used to visualize the performance of a binary classifier, where the horizontal axis represents the False Positive Rate (FPR) and the vertical axis represents the True Positive Rate (TPR). This space serves as the foundation for the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve, which is a graphical approach for displaying the trade-off between TPR and FPR over varying score thresholds. A key characteristic of this space is that it is agnostic to the skew in the test set, because both TPR and FPR are invariant to class imbalance. In this coordinate system, a random classifier is expected to reside at the point (p, p) along the main diagonal, where p is the proportion of positive instances. The ROC curve within this space is monotonically non-decreasing, as the inclusion of a test instance in the set of predicted positives can either increase the TPR or the FPR. This space facilitates the comparison of classifiers over a range of operating points and allows for the evaluation of how well model scores rank positives above negatives across all thresholds.

expert_reference: The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is a measure used to summarize the aggregate behavior of a classifier across all operating points. It serves as a performance metric for machine learning algorithms, providing a single value that reflects overall classification quality. In terms of scale, a perfect classifier yields an AUC of 1, while an algorithm that performs random guessing results in an AUC of 0.5. The AUC is also described as the number of correctly ranked positive-negative pairs. A key property of the AUC is that it is insensitive to class skew in the test set, distinguishing it from the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUC-PR), which varies with changing skew. However, the AUC has significant limitations when used to compare classifiers. A higher AUC for one algorithm does not guarantee that it is strictly better than another, as this would require the ROC curve of the first algorithm to dominate the second across all operating points. If the ROC curves of two classifiers intersect, it is difficult to assess their relative quality using the AUC alone. Additionally, the AUC has been considered an incoherent measure of performance because it may use different scales when comparing different classifiers, although coherent interpretations have been proposed in the literature.
candidate_draft: The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is a performance metric used to summarize the aggregate behavior of a classifier across all operating points. It is derived from the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve, which is a graphical approach for displaying the trade-off between the true positive rate (TPR) and the false positive rate (FPR) over varying score thresholds. Because the TPR and FPR are invariant to class imbalance, the AUC is agnostic to the skew in the test set, making it a useful tool for aggregate evaluation in the presence of class imbalance. The AUC can be interpreted as a measure of how well the model scores rank positives above negatives across all thresholds. A perfect classifier has an AUC of 1, while an algorithm that performs random guessing has an AUC of 0.5. Although the AUC provides a useful summary of aggregate performance, it has limitations: a higher AUC for one algorithm does not guarantee that it is always better than another, as the ROC curve of the first may not dominate the second across all operating points. If the ROC curves of two classifiers intersect, it is difficult to assess their relative quality using the AUC measure alone. Therefore, care must be taken when comparing AUC values, and it is recommended to visualize the ROC curves rather than just reporting the AUC. An alternative measure, the area under the precision-recall curve (AUC-PR), is often more informative for imbalanced datasets, especially in the early retrieval range of operating points.

expert_reference: A classification threshold or cutoff converts a classifier score s(x) into a class decision: an instance is predicted positive when its score exceeds the selected threshold. Changing the threshold produces different operating points. The source selects an optimal threshold on validation data by (1) sorting the observed scores, (2) treating each unique score as a candidate threshold and computing a chosen evaluation measure E(s), and (3) selecting s* = argmax_s E(s). The selected s* is then treated as a learned hyper-parameter for classifying future instances.
candidate_draft: A classification threshold, or cutoff, is a value applied to the real-valued scores produced by a classification model to convert those scores into discrete class labels. The model generates a probability or score first, and the threshold subsequently determines the final prediction. The choice of a relevant threshold is generally guided by domain considerations, but it can also be informed by statistical procedures. Given a suitably chosen evaluation measure E and a distribution of classification scores on a validation set, the optimal score threshold S* can be obtained. The score threshold S* selected using this estimate of E can then be expected to produce optimal test performance with respect to E. Furthermore, the methodology of selecting S* on the validation set can help in comparing the test performance of different classification algorithms, by using the optimal values of S* for each algorithm. Although the threshold can theoretically be any value, the predicted labels change only when the threshold crosses one of the model scores. Assessing the performance of a classifier over a range of score thresholds is called aggregate evaluation of performance. ROC analysis was originally used in signal detection theory for performing aggregate evaluation over a range of score thresholds. ROC and AUC evaluate how well the model scores rank positives above negatives across all thresholds. ROC gives hints, but it does not automatically define the optimal threshold unless we define what “optimal” means. Precision, recall, and F1 evaluate the final predictions after choosing a specific threshold.

expert_reference: Changing the classification threshold changes the set of instances predicted positive and therefore changes the confusion-matrix counts from which precision and recall are computed. Raising or lowering the threshold can trade precision against recall. For any chosen threshold, F1 combines them as F1 = 2·precision·recall/(precision + recall). If a threshold is selected to optimize precision, recall, or F1, the source notes that class skew matters for skew-sensitive measures such as precision and F1.
candidate_draft: The threshold effect on precision, recall, and F1 describes how the choice of a classification score threshold determines the final predictions of a model, which in turn dictates the values of these evaluation metrics. Precision, recall, and F1 are fixed-threshold measures that evaluate the quality of predictions after a specific threshold has been selected. In contrast, ROC curves and the area under the ROC curve (AUC) evaluate how well a model's scores rank positives above negatives across all possible thresholds, focusing on the general quality of ranking rather than a single operating point. Because precision is impacted more strongly by false positives in the top-ranked test instances than the false positive rate (FPR) is, the precision-recall (PR) curve is often more informative than the ROC plot when evaluating binary classifiers on imbalanced datasets. Specifically, in the early retrieval range of operating points—corresponding to larger values of the score threshold—recall is close to zero while precision equals the fraction of positives in the top-ranked instances. Comparing different thresholds, such as 0.5 and 0.1, demonstrates how threshold choice directly changes precision, recall, false positives, and false negatives. This distinction is critical because while ROC analysis is agnostic to class skew due to the invariance of TPR and FPR, precision and recall are sensitive to the specific threshold chosen, making them essential for assessing performance under specific operational constraints or class imbalances.

expert_reference: Cost-based model selection compares ROC operating points using the expected cost implied by the class prior and a cost matrix. In general, C(M) = P(FN)c_FN + P(FP)c_FP + P(TP)c_TP + P(TN)c_TN. With positive-class prior p, TPR and FPR determine these outcome probabilities, allowing the expected cost of each ROC point or model to be computed. The preferred model or operating point is the one with the lowest expected cost under the specified costs and class prior.
candidate_draft: Cost-based model selection via ROC is a method for choosing among classification models by evaluating their performance in the ROC space, where the trade-off between the true positive rate (TPR) and the false positive rate (FPR) is displayed over varying score thresholds. This approach is used to compare classifiers over a range of operating points and to select the optimal score threshold on a validation set using a suitably chosen evaluation measure. In a cost-sensitive setting, the model with the lowest expected cost is selected as the best, even if it does not have the highest area under the ROC curve (AUC) or F1 score at a fixed threshold. The ROC curve facilitates this comparison by providing a graphical representation of classifier performance that is agnostic to class imbalance, as both TPR and FPR are invariant to the skew in the test set. However, the ROC curve does not automatically define the optimal threshold unless the definition of "optimal" is specified, such as through cost considerations. This method is distinct from simple accuracy-based model selection, which may be misleading due to model overfitting, and from AUC-based selection, which summarizes aggregate performance but may not reflect cost-sensitive decisions.

expert_reference: The holdout method is a model evaluation technique in which the available dataset is split once into two parts: a training set and a test set. The model is learned over the training set, and the resulting test error rate corresponds exactly to the performance of that specific model learned over that specific training set. This distinguishes the holdout method from k-fold cross-validation, where a different model is learned at every run and the performance of every one of the k models on their respective test folds is aggregated to compute the overall test error rate. In cross-validation, the computed error reflects the expected generalization error rate of the model selection approach when applied on a training set of the same size as one of the training folds, rather than the performance of a single model learned over a specific training set. The holdout method can be repeated several times to obtain a distribution of the test error rates, an approach known as random subsampling or the repeated holdout method. This repeated approach produces a distribution of the error rates that can be used to understand the variance of the test error rate.
candidate_draft: The holdout method is the most basic technique for partitioning a labeled data set for model evaluation. It works by randomly partitioning the entire labeled set D into two disjoint subsets: a training set (D.train) and a test set (D.test). The training set is used for model selection and learning a classification model, while the test set is used to compute the test error rate, which serves as an estimate of the generalization error rate. This approach involves a single split of the available data. The holdout method can be repeated several times to obtain a distribution of the test error rates, an approach known as random subsampling or the repeated holdout method. It is positioned as a foundational evaluation protocol alongside cross-validation, leave-one-out, and bootstrap methods.

expert_reference: Random subsampling is a model evaluation technique that repeats random hold-out splits several times and averages the resulting performance scores. This approach is more stable than a single hold-out split, which suffers from high dependence on one specific division of the data. However, random subsampling does not guarantee that every instance is tested exactly once; some instances may be tested repeatedly while others may not be tested at all. In the broader context of sampling techniques, random subsampling is related to simple random sampling, where there is an equal probability of selecting any particular object. Sampling can be conducted with or without replacement; in sampling with replacement, objects are not removed from the population as they are selected, allowing the same object to be picked more than once. This method is simpler to analyze because the probability of selecting any object remains constant during the sampling process, particularly when samples are relatively small compared to the data set size.
candidate_draft: Random subsampling is a model evaluation technique that repeats random train-test splitting multiple times and averages the resulting performance scores. It is also described as repeating random hold-out splits several times and averaging the results. This approach is used to estimate test error rates and is categorized as an estimation method for comparing performance metrics. It is distinct from k-fold cross-validation, which is a separate estimation method often compared against random subsampling in empirical studies. The technique involves randomly splitting data into training and test sets, a process that is repeated to generate multiple performance estimates.

k-Fold cross validation is a model evaluation technique that generalizes the holdout approach by segmenting the labeled data D (of size N) into k equal-sized partitions, or folds. In each of the k runs, one partition is designated as the test set (D.test(i)) while the remaining k-1 partitions are used as the training set (D.train(i)). This process is repeated until every fold has served as the test set exactly once, ensuring that every data instance in D is used for both training and testing across the full procedure. A different model is learned at every run, and the performance of each model on its respective test fold is aggregated to compute the overall test error rate. This aggregated estimate reflects the expected generalization error rate of the model selection approach when applied to a training set of the same size as one of the training folds, rather than the performance of a single specific model learned over a fixed training set.

The choice of k depends on the characteristics of the problem. A small value of k results in smaller training sets for each run, which can lead to a larger estimate of generalization error rate than expected for a model trained on the entire labeled set. Conversely, a high value of k results in larger training sets, reducing the bias in the estimate of generalization error rate. For most practical applications, choosing k between 5 and 10 provides a reasonable approach for estimating generalization error rate, as each fold can utilize 80% to 90% of the labeled data for training. An extreme case occurs when k equals N, known as the leave-one-out approach, where every run uses exactly one data instance for testing and the remainder for training. While this utilizes as much data as possible for training, it can be computationally expensive for large datasets because the procedure must be repeated N times.

Standard k-fold cross validation produces a single estimate of the generalization error rate without providing information about the variance of that estimate. To obtain variance information, one can run cross-validation for every possible partitioning of the data into k partitions, an approach known as complete cross-validation. However, this is usually too expensive for large datasets. A more practical solution is to repeat the cross-validation approach multiple times using different random partitionings of the data into k partitions at each iteration, and use the average test error rate as the estimate. Additionally, standard k-fold cross validation does not guarantee that the fraction of positive and negative instances in every partition is equal to the fraction observed in the overall data. A solution to this issue is stratified cross-validation, which performs stratified sampling of positive and negative instances into the k partitions to preserve class distribution.
candidate_draft: k-Fold Cross Validation is a model evaluation method that partitions a labeled dataset of size N into k equal-sized partitions, or folds. The method generalizes the basic train/test split by ensuring that every data instance is used for both training and testing across the k iterations. In each run, a different model is learned on the training folds, and its performance is evaluated on the held-out test fold. The overall test error rate is computed by aggregating the performance of all k models on their respective test folds. This approach aims to make effective use of all labeled instances for both training and testing, providing a robust estimate of generalization error. However, the computed error rate does not represent the performance of a single model learned over a specific training set, but rather an aggregate estimate. The choice of k depends on the characteristics of the problem, and the method does not guarantee that the fraction of positive and negative instances in every partition is equal to the fraction observed in the overall data. A common mistake is performing pre-processing operations, such as hyper-parameter tuning or feature selection, using the entire dataset rather than within the training fold of every cross-validation run. Cross-validation can also be used for model selection, but its usage for model selection is quite different than when it is used for model evaluation. Nested cross-validation is a related approach where an inner cross-validation framework is used for model selection while an outer cross-validation framework is used for model evaluation. This distinction is important to avoid bias in error estimation when using cross-validation for both hyper-parameter selection and model evaluation.

In this approach, the cross-validation procedure is repeated N times. In each run, exactly one data instance is held out for testing, and the model is trained on the remaining N − 1 instances. This configuration provides the maximum possible training data per run, which reduces the bias in the estimate of the generalization error rate compared to using a smaller number of folds. However, LOOCV is computationally expensive for large data sets because the model must be trained and evaluated N times. Additionally, because there is only one possible partitioning of the data for the leave-one-out approach, it is not possible to estimate the variance of the generalization error rate. LOOCV is distinct from standard k-fold cross-validation (where k is typically between 5 and 10), stratified cross-validation (which preserves class proportions), and bootstrap sampling (which samples with replacement and tests on out-of-bag instances).
candidate_draft: Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) is a specific model evaluation protocol that functions as a special case of k-fold cross-validation. In this method, the number of folds is set to N, where N is the total number of labeled instances in the dataset. Consequently, the data is partitioned into N folds, with each fold containing exactly one instance. During the evaluation process, the model is trained on all instances except the single one held out for testing, and this procedure is repeated N times so that every instance serves as a test case exactly once. This approach is designed to make effective use of all labeled instances for both training and testing. However, because the cross-validation procedure must be repeated N times, leave-one-out cross-validation can be computationally expensive for large datasets. It is distinct from standard k-fold cross-validation, which segments data into k equal-sized partitions where k is typically much smaller than N, and from stratified cross-validation, which preserves class proportions within folds.

expert_reference: Bootstrap sampling is a statistical resampling technique in which data instances are randomly selected with replacement from an original data set to create a synthetic collection of the same size as the original. Because the sampling is done with replacement, some instances may appear several times in the same training set, while others may be omitted. On average, a bootstrap sample of size N contains approximately 63.2% of the unique instances from the original data, leaving about 36.8% of the instances unselected. These unselected instances are known as out-of-bag instances and can be used as a test set for model evaluation. The procedure is typically repeated multiple times to generate different training and test sets, allowing for the computation of distributions of performance measures such as accuracy, precision, and recall, or to estimate the distribution of the support of a frequent itemset. In the context of ensemble methods like bagging (bootstrap aggregating), bootstrap sampling is used to train multiple classifiers on different subsets of the data, with the final prediction determined by majority voting. The method is distinguished from k-fold cross-validation, which systematically splits data into subsets, and from hold-out methods, which split data once into training and test sets.
candidate_draft: Bootstrap sampling is a resampling technique used for model evaluation and generating new data sets. It works by randomly selecting data instances with replacement from the original data set to form a new training set of the same size as the original. Because sampling is done with replacement, some instances are selected multiple times while others are not selected at all. On average, a bootstrap sample of size N contains about 63.2% of the unique instances from the original data, leaving about 36.8% of the instances out of the sample. These unselected instances, known as out-of-bag instances, can be used to evaluate the model trained on the bootstrap sample. The procedure is typically repeated multiple times, resulting in a different error rate for each run. The performance of a classification model trained and evaluated on a number of these bootstrapped data sets can then be used to generate a distribution for the measure of interest, such as the accuracy of a predictive model. This approach is useful for generating confidence intervals for various data mining results. Bootstrap sampling is an alternative to k-fold cross-validation, where the data set is systematically split into subsets for k number of times. While the bootstrap method provides a robust estimate of generalization performance with low variance, it may produce misleading results for highly complex models in certain conditions. Bootstrap sampling is also used in ensemble learning methods, such as bagging, where independent base classifiers are built on bootstrap samples of the training set.

expert_reference: Stratified k-fold cross validation is a model evaluation technique that extends standard k-fold cross validation by ensuring that each fold approximately preserves the class distribution of the full dataset. In standard k-fold cross validation, the labeled data is segmented into k equal-sized partitions, or folds. During each run, one partition is used for testing while the remaining partitions are used for training. This process is repeated until every fold has served as the test set once. A key limitation of standard k-fold cross validation is that it does not guarantee that the fraction of positive and negative instances in every partition is equal to the fraction observed in the overall data. Stratified cross validation addresses this by performing a stratified sampling of the positive and negative instances into the k partitions. This ensures that the proportion of class labels in every fold is kept the same as that of the overall data. This approach is particularly useful for classification tasks where class imbalance might otherwise skew the evaluation results. An empirical study by Kohavi suggests that ten-fold stratified cross validation is the best estimation method for performance metrics when compared to random subsampling and other k-fold variants. The method is distinct from leave-one-out cross validation, which is a special case where k equals the total number of instances N, and from bootstrap sampling, which samples with replacement to form training sets and evaluates on out-of-bag instances.
candidate_draft: Stratified k-fold cross-validation is a model evaluation method that modifies standard k-fold cross-validation by ensuring that each fold approximately preserves the class proportions of the original dataset. In standard k-fold cross-validation, labeled data is segmented into k equal-sized partitions, but this process does not guarantee that the fraction of positive and negative instances in every partition matches the fraction observed in the overall data. Stratified cross-validation addresses this limitation by maintaining the class distribution in each fold, which is usually preferred because it preserves class ratios. This approach is particularly relevant in supervised classification, where evaluation is an integral part of model development. While the right choice of k depends on problem characteristics, empirical studies suggest that ten-fold stratified cross-validation is often the best estimation method. The method is distinct from nested cross-validation, which is used for hyper-parameter selection, and from bootstrap sampling, which is a different resampling technique.

expert_reference: Feature selection chooses a subset of the original features according to an evaluation criterion. Its purpose is to remove irrelevant or redundant features, reduce dimensionality and acquisition or computational cost, and simplify the resulting model while retaining useful information. The source describes feature selection as a search over possible feature subsets, organized around a subset-evaluation measure, a search strategy, a stopping criterion, and validation. Standard approaches include embedded, filter, and wrapper methods. Unlike feature-construction methods, feature selection retains a subset of the original attributes rather than creating new combined attributes.
candidate_draft: Feature selection is a process that chooses an optimal subset of features according to a certain criterion. It is an effective form of dealing with the dimensionality reduction problem. While some irrelevant and redundant attributes can be eliminated immediately by using common sense or domain knowledge, selecting the best subset of features frequently requires a systematic approach. Conceptually, feature subset selection is a search over all possible subsets of features. The ideal approach to feature selection is to try all possible subsets of features as input to the data mining algorithm of interest, and then take the subset that produces the best results. The feature selection process is viewed as consisting of four parts: a measure for evaluating a subset, a search strategy that controls the generation of a new subset of features, a stopping criterion, and a validation procedure. Once a subset of features has been selected, the results of the target data mining algorithm on the selected subset should be validated. Feature selection techniques can help to improve the accuracy of decision trees by eliminating the irrelevant attributes during preprocessing. Feature selection is a topic well investigated in data mining, and it occurs naturally as part of the data mining algorithm.

Redundant features are attributes that duplicate much or all of the information contained in one or more other attributes. A common example is the purchase price of a product and the amount of sales tax paid, which contain much of the same information. In the context of feature selection, the objective is to identify important features and discard others as redundant or irrelevant. Redundant features can reduce classification accuracy and the quality of clusters found, and in probability models like Naive Bayes, they can cause similar evidence to be counted twice.

Inter-feature redundancy is typically assessed by measuring association or correlation between pairs of selected features. The choice of measure depends on the data type: Pearson correlation is used for numerical features, Spearman correlation for ordinal features, and the chi-square test for categorical features. If two input features are strongly related or associated, one may be redundant. However, removal decisions should also consider cost, missingness, interpretability, and performance. Consistency measures offer another approach by aiming to find a minimum number of features that separate classes as well as the full set, defined by the condition P(C|FullSet) = P(C|SubSet). An inconsistency occurs when two examples have the same feature values but different class labels. Using consistency measures allows for the removal of both irrelevant and redundant features. Decision trees can also handle redundant attributes because redundant attributes show similar gains in purity, leading the algorithm to select only one of them as a split condition.
candidate_draft: Redundant features are input attributes that duplicate much or all of the information contained in one or more other attributes. An attribute is considered redundant if it is strongly correlated with another attribute in the data, meaning that if two input features are strongly related, one may be redundant. Redundant features can cause similar evidence to be counted twice, which can reduce classification accuracy and the quality of the clusters that are found. While some redundant attributes can be eliminated immediately by using common sense or domain knowledge, selecting the best subset of features frequently requires a systematic approach. Redundancies in attributes can be detected using correlation analysis; for numerical attributes, checking whether they are highly correlated is useful to determine if they are redundant. Inter-feature redundancy can be assessed by measuring association or correlation between pairs of selected features. In feature selection, examples of handling redundancy include removing strongly correlated redundant features or ranking features by a statistical criterion. Even for two input features, removal should consider cost, missingness, interpretability, and performance. Some studies have shown that certain approaches work very well with data sets that contain highly redundant features, and rule-based classifiers can easily handle the presence of redundant attributes that are highly correlated with one other.

expert_reference: An attribute is defined as irrelevant if it is not useful for the classification task. Because irrelevant attributes are poorly associated with the target class labels, they provide little or no gain in purity and are typically passed over by other more relevant features. Consequently, the presence of a small number of irrelevant attributes will not impact the decision tree construction process. However, if the classification problem is complex, such as involving interactions among attributes, and there are a large number of irrelevant attributes, some of these attributes may be accidentally chosen during the tree-growing process because they may provide a better gain than a relevant attribute just by random chance. For example, students' ID numbers are irrelevant to the task of predicting students' grade point averages. Redundant and irrelevant features can reduce classification accuracy and the quality of the clusters that are found. Feature selection techniques can help to improve the accuracy of decision trees by eliminating the irrelevant attributes during preprocessing. In minimum subset techniques, an algorithm returns a minimum feature subset and no difference is made for features in the subset; whatever is relevant within the subset is otherwise irrelevant. In search directions where the feature set shrinks and the subset grows, the subset may store only the irrelevant features.
candidate_draft: Irrelevant features are defined as attributes that contain almost no useful information for the data mining task at hand. Their presence in a dataset can reduce classification accuracy and the quality of clusters found, and can distort commonly used proximity measures, especially when the number of irrelevant attributes is large. Because irrelevant attributes typically show poor information gain, rule-based classifiers can avoid selecting them if other relevant attributes show better information gain. Some learning algorithms handle irrelevant attributes intrinsically; for example, Naïve Bayes classifiers are robust to them, linear SVMs can handle them by learning zero weights, and logistic regression can handle them by learning weight parameters close to 0. While some irrelevant attributes can be eliminated immediately using common sense or domain knowledge, selecting the best subset of features frequently requires a systematic approach. Feature selection techniques can help improve the accuracy of decision trees by eliminating irrelevant attributes during preprocessing. The number of relevant features is a parameter that is often not known by the practitioner, and the presence of a large number of irrelevant or redundant attributes is a significant issue in high-dimensional data.

expert_reference: The curse of dimensionality is the phenomenon that data analysis becomes increasingly difficult as the number of attributes grows. The data space expands rapidly and observations become sparse, which can make distances and density differences less informative and local neighborhoods less meaningful. These effects can degrade methods that depend on proximity or density, including clustering and classification methods. This is a major motivation for dimensionality reduction and feature selection. Kernel methods can avoid explicitly constructing coordinates in a transformed high-dimensional feature space, but that computational device does not eliminate the broader high-dimensional data problem.
candidate_draft: The curse of dimensionality is the phenomenon where many types of data analysis become significantly harder as the dimensionality of the data increases. This difficulty arises because, as the number of dimensions increases, the data space grows very quickly, making high-dimensional data sparse. This sparsity makes distance and density relationships less meaningful for clustering. Consequently, many clustering and classification algorithms have trouble with high-dimensional data, leading to reduced classification accuracy and poor quality clusters. Dimensionality also constitutes a serious obstacle to the competence of most learning algorithms, especially due to the fact that they are usually computationally expensive. The curse of dimensionality is often associated with high-dimensional data and can be encountered when computing similarity in a high-dimensional space. It is a key reason why dimensionality reduction techniques, such as feature selection and principal components analysis, are used to improve the performance of data mining algorithms.

expert_reference: The Filter Approach is one of three standard approaches to feature selection, alongside embedded and wrapper methods. It operates independently of the data mining method subsequently employed, a property that distinguishes it from wrapper approaches which are typically coupled to a specific learner. The name 'filter' derives from the process of filtering undesirable features out before the learning phase begins. Within a common feature selection architecture, filter methods share components such as a measure for evaluating a subset, a search strategy, a stopping criterion, and a validation procedure; however, they differ from wrapper methods specifically in the way they evaluate a subset of features. Because the filter approach is independent of the downstream model, filter methods are usually faster than their wrapper counterparts. While the literature also recommends filtering for the detection and treatment of noisy data, the Filter Approach in the context of feature selection is defined by its pre-learning feature evaluation and selection mechanism.
candidate_draft: The Filter Approach is a standard method for feature selection in data mining where features are selected before the data mining algorithm is run, using an approach that is independent of the data mining task. In this approach, the evaluation technique used to assess feature subsets is distinct from the target data mining algorithm itself. The measures employed in the filter approach attempt to predict how well the actual data mining algorithm will perform on a given set of attributes. The primary reasons for using filter approaches include noise removal, data simplification, and increasing the performance of any data mining technique. While the ideal approach to feature selection involves trying all possible subsets of features as input to the data mining algorithm of interest and selecting the subset that produces the best results, the filter approach provides a distinct strategy by decoupling the evaluation from the specific learning algorithm. Once a subset of features has been selected using this method, the results of the target data mining algorithm on the selected subset should be validated.

It applies a criterion to score each feature independently and uses those scores to produce an ordering or ranking of the features. The subsequent learning process, or a user-defined threshold, then determines how many of the highest-ranked features are retained. Like other filters, ranking is performed independently of the particular learning algorithm that will later use the selected features.

expert_reference: The wrapper approach is a feature selection strategy that uses a learning algorithm as a black box to evaluate feature subsets, aiming to improve the predictive performance of that specific learner. Unlike filter methods, which cannot allow a learning algorithm to fully exploit its bias, wrapper methods are designed to select features that accomplish the highest predictive accuracy for a fixed learning algorithm. The process typically involves two stages: first, feature subset selection where the best subset is chosen using the accuracy provided by the learning algorithm on training data as the criterion; and second, re-learning the data mining model with the best subset. To avoid overfitting, the wrapper approach employs statistical validation, such as cross-validation, to agree on a predictive measure. While wrapper approaches are an interesting choice in some domains, they require higher computational costs and are usually slower than filter methods, which can be a crucial factor under time constraints. Experimental studies have shown that results vary among learners, often recommending wrapper approaches for each kind of learner to optimize performance.
candidate_draft: The wrapper approach is a feature selection strategy in which the evaluation of feature subsets is performed using the target data mining algorithm itself. Unlike filter methods, which use an evaluation technique distinct from the target algorithm, the wrapper approach treats the learning algorithm as a black box. It uses statistical validation, such as cross-validation, to avoid over-fitting and to select the best feature subset based on a predictive measure. In this approach, the subset evaluation function is simply the criterion normally used to measure the result of the data mining. The wrapper approach allows a learning algorithm to fully exploit its bias, whereas filter models do not. It is possible to encompass both the filter and wrapper approaches within a common architecture, as they differ only in the way in which they evaluate a subset of features. Wrapper approaches have proven to be an interesting choice in some domains, provided they can be applied with the same classifiers, but they require higher computational costs. The embedded approach is similar to the wrapper approach in the sense that the features are specifically selected for a certain learning algorithm, but in the embedded approach, the features are selected during the learning process. Wrapper methods have been extensively studied by using classifiers such as SVMs, or frameworks to jointly perform feature selection and SVM parameter learning. An empirical evaluation comparing wrapper approaches with consistency-based feature selectors concluded that both perform similarly in accuracy, but the consistency-based feature selector is more efficient. Filters are thought to be more appropriate for some practical factors in feature selection rather than wrapper-based feature selectors. The method GAMIFS can be viewed as a genetic algorithm to form a hybrid filter/wrapper feature selector. Finally, once a subset of features has been selected, the results of the target data mining algorithm on the selected subset should be validated.

The filter versus wrapper trade-off in feature selection concerns the choice between two distinct evaluation strategies: filters evaluate features before learning, whereas wrappers evaluate subsets by using the learner. Both approaches can be encompassed within a common architecture that includes a measure for evaluating a subset, a search strategy that controls the generation of a new subset of features, a stopping criterion, and a validation procedure; filter methods and wrapper methods differ only in the way in which they evaluate a subset of features.

A wrapper model consists of two stages: (1) feature subset selection, which selects the best subset using the accuracy provided by the learning algorithm (on training data) as a criterion; and (2) a stage that is the same as in the filter model. Since only the best subset is kept in stage 1, the data mining model must be learned again with the best subset. Wrapper models can achieve the purpose of improving the particular learner's predictive performance.

The trade-off is that filter models cannot allow a learning algorithm to fully exploit its bias, whereas wrapper methods do. However, wrapper methods are usually slower than filters, and it may be crucial to determine the best feature selection choice under time constraints. In such cases, filters are thought to be more appropriate than wrapper-based feature selectors.
candidate_draft:
The trade-off between filter and wrapper approaches in feature selection is defined by how each method evaluates subsets of features. Filter methods and wrapper methods differ only in the way in which they evaluate a subset of features. In a filter approach, features are selected before the data mining algorithm is run, using an evaluation technique that is distinct from and independent of the target data mining algorithm. These measures attempt to predict how well the actual data mining algorithm will perform on a given set of attributes. In contrast, wrapper methods use the target data mining algorithm itself to evaluate feature subsets. The wrapper approach treats the learning algorithm as a black box, often using statistical validation to avoid over-fitting, and selects the best feature subset based on the criterion normally used to measure the result of the data mining.

The primary trade-off involves computational cost and algorithmic bias. Wrapper methods are usually slower than filters and require higher computational costs, which can be crucial when determining the best feature selection choice under time constraints. Conversely, filter models cannot allow a learning algorithm to fully exploit its bias, whereas wrapper methods do. Filters are generally thought to be more appropriate for scenarios requiring speed, such as noise removal and data simplification, while wrappers are an interesting choice in some domains provided they can be applied with the same classifiers. Both approaches can be encompassed within a common architecture, and the goal in both cases is to improve the data mining analysis with respect to time, cost, and quality.

expert_reference: Sequential Forward Generation (SFG) is a forward feature-subset search direction. It starts with an empty selected set S and adds one feature at a time according to the feature-subset criterion until the stopping condition is met or all features have been considered. A stopping rule may specify the desired number of selected features or another criterion. In the source taxonomy, forward generation describes the direction of search; whether the overall search strategy is exhaustive, heuristic, or nondeterministic is a separate design choice.
candidate_draft: Sequential Forward Generation (SFG) is a feature set generation algorithm used in feature selection. It operates by starting from the empty set and adding the next best feature until the selected set satisfies the criterion. This forward search direction contrasts with Sequential Backward Generation (SBG), which starts with the full set and removes features one at a time. SFG is one of four feature set construction methods presented in the lecture, alongside SBG, Bidirectional Generation (BG), and Random Generation (RG). The search space for SFG, when a threshold m of minimum features is established, is defined as the sum of combinations from 0 to m features, independent of the forward or backward generation direction.

expert_reference: Sequential Backward Generation (SBG) is a heuristic feature selection method that starts with the full set of features and iteratively removes features one at a time. The algorithm is defined by the function SBG(F, U), where F is the full set of features and U is the measure or criterion used to evaluate subsets. The procedure initializes a set S to hold the removed features. In a repeat loop, the algorithm selects the next feature to remove using f = GetNext(F) (or f = FindNextWorst(F, U) in the heuristic variant), removes it from the current set via F = F \setminus \{f\}, and adds it to the removed set via S = S \cup \{f\}. The loop continues until the remaining set F fails to satisfy the criterion U or until F becomes empty. When the stopping condition is met, the algorithm returns F \cup \{f\}, where f is the last removed feature. This return value is justified because f was the last feature removed, and after removing it, the remaining set failed the criterion. SBG is distinguished from Sequential Forward Generation (SFG), which starts from an empty set and adds features, and from Bidirectional Generation (BG), which combines forward and backward search directions. SBG is a heuristic method because it uses greedy choices to select the next worst feature to remove.
candidate_draft: Sequential Backward Generation (SBG) is a feature set construction method used in feature selection. It operates by starting from the full feature set and removing the next worst feature until the remaining set fails the criterion, then adding the last removed feature back. SBG is one of four feature set construction methods presented in the lecture, alongside Sequential Forward Generation (SFG), Bidirectional Generation (BG), and Random Generation (RG). The search space for SBG is independent of the forward or backward generation direction, defined by the threshold m of minimum features to be selected. SBG is distinguished from SFG, which builds the feature set forward, and BG, which combines forward and backward search. The method is part of the broader feature selection process, where feature subset generation methods and search categories are analyzed.

This approach takes advantage of both SFG and SBG by combining forward and backward search. The search terminates under one of two conditions: (1) when one search finds the best subset comprised of m features before it reaches the exact middle, or (2) when both searches achieve the middle of the search space.
